text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally striking a man with his vehicle during an enforcement operation in Houston is expected to turn himself in Monday.

A grand jury indicted Mario Alberto Morales on Friday on a charge of second-degree aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, according to the Harris County District Attorney’s Office.

Morales' lawyer, David Lindenmuth, told several outlets that Morales plans to surrender between 8:30 a.m. and 10 a.m. at the 488th District Court.

Lindenmuth said Morales did not intend to strike Miguel Parra Hernandez on Oct. 10 while pursuing him and another person who ran from the scene.

“It was an accident. It was nothing more than accident, but the DA to score political points right before elections decided to bring charges,” Lindenmuth told ABC News.

District Attorney Sean Teare said surveillance video contradicts ICE’s account that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of Morales’ vehicle. The footage, Teare said, shows a Jeep Cherokee speeding over a median and driving toward Parra Hernandez as he runs. Another vehicle blocks the view of any impact, but the Jeep appears to pass within inches of him. Parra Hernandez is then seen on the ground.

At a news conference Friday, Teare also played Morales’ body-camera footage. It shows Morales driving and talking about pursuing someone. The vehicle appears to shake as it goes over something. Morales then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is on the ground holding his leg and yelling in pain.

Morales is heard saying, “He got hit with a car, bro,” and, “I was coming in and I hit him with the car.”

Parra Hernandez was later taken into custody with a broken leg.

ICE called the allegations “RECKLESS and FALSE” and described the indictment as “a political stunt.” The agency also said local officials do not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties.

“The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct,” an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill.

Lindenmuth said Morales is a former corrections officer who joined the Army, worked as a detention and processing officer at the Port Isabel Detention Center and later worked with DHS as an ICE contractor. Morales joined ICE as a federal immigration officer in August 2025.

text:
Mario Alberto Morales, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer indicted by a grand jury last week, surrendered himself in a Harris County District Court Monday.

In Harris County 488th District Court, Morales entered in a gray suit and purple tie alongside his legal team David Lindenmuth and newly added co-counsel former Harris County District Attorney Kim Ogg.

In one-word answers, Morales acknowledged he understood the charge against him. Lawyers for the district attorney’s office requested a $75,000 bond due to the "violent nature" of the incident and some "admissions of prior drug use" they uncovered in their investigation.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

Morales' lawyer David Lindenmuth countered and requested a $25,000 bond, arguing his client posed no flight risk and that there is no on-going threat to the community.

Judge Matthew Peneguy, who presided over the hearing, ordered a $30,000 bond.

Morales was indicted for a second-degree felony offense of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. The agent is accused of striking Miguel Parra-Hernandez with his vehicle, breaking his leg and ankle, on Oct. 10. An ICE spokesperson claimed Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the agent’s vehicle while agents were trying to arrest a different man and said he fled the scene after an attempted traffic stop.

Parra-Hernandez's family, his lawyer and immigrant rights advocacy groups have disputed ICE's account.

Surveillance video and footage from Morales' body camera, released by the Harris County District Attorney's office, show Morales pursuing Parra-Hernandez as he ran away from the agent's unmarked vehicle. Morales' car is seen jumping the median to make a left turn into a parking lot, then hitting Parra-Hernandez from behind and coming to a stop several feet after running him over.

The indictment was announced Friday by Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare and Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez.

Gonzalez said investigators developed serious concerns over Morales' actions, including how he pursued Parra-Hernandez and the manner in which Parra-Hernandez was struck.

"No badge, title, or position places anyone beyond scrutiny or accountability," Gonzalez said. "As sheriff, I take seriously our responsibility to protect everyone who lives, works, or travels through Harris County; that includes holding ourselves and our fellow law enforcement professionals to the highest standards."

David Lindenmuth, the lawyer representing Morales, called the indictment "political prosecution" in an interview with Houston Public Media. He said the collision was “nothing more than an accident”

"This officer was doing his job, and a fleeing individual caused the chaotic circumstances that led to this unfortunate incident," Lindenmuth said. "And it was unfortunate. Nobody wishes harm on this individual, including Mr. Morales, but it was not a crime. It has been manufactured to be a crime by a politically minded district attorney."

Teare said he hoped the indictment would do more than seek justice for Parra-Hernandez and his family.

"I hope that it also sends a loud and clear message to every ICE officer who feels that they have a free pass to terrorize our streets," Teare said. "The time to stop is now, and if you don’t you will be held accountable."

In a statement shared with Houston Public Media, an ICE spokesperson called allegations Morales struck Parra-Hernandez intentionally "reckless and false" and said the indictment was a "political stunt."

RELATED: ICE says its agent can’t be locally prosecuted for Houston crash. Legal experts disagree

The indictment is a rare but not unprecedented instance of state agencies prosecuting a federal agent. A federal grand jury in Minnesota indicted Texas-based ICE agent Christian Castro for making false claims to the Federal Bureau of Investigations over the shooting of a Venezuelan man in January. A legal battle ensued between the states over the extradition of the agent. Castro was ultimately arrested when he returned to Minnesota for a court appearance.

If Morales is convicted, the assault charge carries up to 20 years in prison.

Morales' background

Teare said Morales joined ICE during a hiring surge as the agency ramped up border security efforts under the second Trump administration, and he questioned Morales' qualifications to join the agency after reviewing his background.

"I can unequivocally tell you that I’ve reviewed thousands of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around this state, and I’m not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person," Teare said.

According to his lawyer, Morales held several different law enforcement type jobs over the last 12 years. He spent roughly two years in the army as a military police officer and paratrooper, but was honorably discharged in 2014 after a series of health setbacks including two traumatic brain injuries.

After the army, Lindenmuth said Morales held a couple of "courier-type" jobs, before becoming a correctional officer with the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. Two years later in 2018, he moved on to work as a processing and detention officer at the immigrant detention facility in Port Isabel.

He then worked as a contract transportation officer with ICE until becoming an official agent in August 2025.

Morales also briefly ran in the Republican primary to represent Texas' 34th congressional district. Lindenmuth addrd Morales has also worked as a pastor.

"This is also a man who’s devoted his life to God and Jesus as a pastor for his Christian church," Lindenmuth said. "So this is not the monster that the [district attorney] would have you believe that he is."

title: ICE enforcement in Orange County raises red flags for misuse of government databases
authors: JODY AGIUS VALLEJO Los Angeles Times, whtnone
description:
These arrests raise troubling questions: How are immigration agents identifying the people they stop?
These deeply rooted lives can be upended in an instant through routine encounters facilitated by an expanding infrastructure of immigration surveillance.
A June 2025 CalMatters investigation documented more than 100 instances in roughly one month in which Southern California law enforcement agencies shared license plate reader data with ICE, despite California law prohibiting such sharing.
University of Washington researchers also documented federal immigration agents querying the license plates of U.S. citizens observing ICE operations.
The same infrastructure used to identify people for immigration enforcement can be used to monitor those exercising their 1st Amendment rights to legally observe law enforcement.
text:
Inside an abandoned work truck in northern Orange County one recent Saturday sat a steaming cup of coffee and a Danish with a bite taken out of it. The remnants of an ordinary morning, suddenly interrupted.

The truck belonged to a man who had gone out for gas and a car wash before the workweek. He never made it home. ICE agents had taken him into custody after a roadside stop, leaving his truck in a nearby parking lot.

Shortly afterward, I accompanied another community volunteer to tell his wife what had happened. She cried out, and her body began to shake. Her husband had lived and worked in the United States for decades. Now she, a U.S. citizen and their U.S.-born children faced the urgent task of locating him, ensuring he received lifesaving medication, and figuring out how their family would survive without him. His story is becoming increasingly familiar across Orange County.

As the Trump administration escalates immigration enforcement across Southern California, local rapid-response groups report a disturbing new pattern: federal agents stopping Latino men driving landscaping and construction trucks, taking them into custody and leaving their vehicles behind.

These arrests raise troubling questions: How are immigration agents identifying the people they stop? What role are government databases and surveillance technologies playing? As a sociologist who studies immigration, I see two connected issues: the devastation enforcement inflicts on families and communities, and the expanding surveillance infrastructure that gives the government greater power to identify and target people in their everyday lives.

According to research I co-authored at USC’s Equity Research Institute, approximately 211,000 undocumented immigrants live in Orange County. Roughly three-quarters have lived in the United States for more than a decade. They are deeply rooted residents who have built families, businesses and community ties. Undocumented immigrants account for approximately 33% of workers in building and grounds cleaning and maintenance occupations and 29% in construction trades. Fifteen percent of employed undocumented adults in the county ages 25 to 64 are small business owners. These workers are integral to our economy. Removing them from the workforce disrupts businesses, reduces household spending and can create labor shortages that raise costs throughout the county.

Immigration enforcement is often framed as removing individuals who lack legal status. But people do not live as isolated individuals. Our research estimates that approximately 491,000 Orange County residents are undocumented or live with undocumented family members, including more than 216,000 U.S. citizens.

Detaining one person can destabilize an entire network of relationships and economic support built over decades. These deeply rooted lives can be upended in an instant through routine encounters facilitated by an expanding infrastructure of immigration surveillance.

A new investigation by the University of Washington’s Center for Human Rights documents how federal immigration agents use state motor vehicle records to facilitate roadside arrests. Researchers describe a process that can unfold in minutes. Agents identify a vehicle, run its license plate to obtain the registered owner’s name and cross-reference that information against federal databases. The information can then be used to identify people for detention.

The researchers identified four pathways through which immigration authorities obtain motor vehicle information: direct DMV access, interstate law enforcement networks, commercial data brokers, and information shared by state or local police. One important pathway is Nlets, the International Justice and Public Safety Network, which allows law enforcement agencies to query driver’s license and vehicle registration records across state lines. California Vehicle Code 1808.48 prohibits the use of noncriminal DMV records for immigration enforcement. Yet interstate networks like Nlets raise questions about whether federal authorities can obtain information through indirect channels despite these restrictions.

In just the first five months of 2026, the University of Washington study found that DHS agencies conducted more than 1 million searches of Washington state’s driver and vehicle records. These searches occurred despite Washington’s Keep Washington Working Act, which restricts state agencies’ participation in federal immigration enforcement and limits certain disclosures of personal information. Maryland has faced similar concerns despite a state law requiring a judicial warrant for federal immigration authorities to access protected motor vehicle information.

The findings expose a troubling reality: States can enact laws to protect residents’ privacy, but those protections can be undermined when federal agencies obtain the same information through interconnected law enforcement networks.

Privacy protections mean little if the government can simply find a way around them.

California was among the states researchers sought to examine, but they could not obtain the records needed to determine whether its protections are working. Evidence from Orange County shows why these concerns are far from hypothetical.

A June 2025 CalMatters investigation documented more than 100 instances in roughly one month in which Southern California law enforcement agencies shared license plate reader data with ICE, despite California law prohibiting such sharing. The Orange County Sheriff’s Department was among the agencies identified.

The searches involved technology provided by Flock Safety, whose license plate readers have sparked “ bipartisan backlash” over mass surveillance, police misuse and the erosion of civil liberties. By recording vehicle movements and making that information searchable across jurisdictions, these systems can enable law enforcement to reconstruct people’s movements, associations and daily routines without individualized suspicion or a judicial warrant.

The danger is not simply that the government has access to more information about us. It is that this information can expand the government’s power to decide who becomes a target of suspicion, surveillance and detention. And these surveillance systems are not socially neutral. The decision about whose plate to search is made by human beings. If ICE agents disproportionately single out landscaping trucks, construction vehicles or drivers they perceive to be Latino, seemingly neutral technology can facilitate racial profiling while giving discriminatory enforcement the appearance of objective policing.

This expanding surveillance does not stop at immigration enforcement. University of Washington researchers also documented federal immigration agents querying the license plates of U.S. citizens observing ICE operations. The same infrastructure used to identify people for immigration enforcement can be used to monitor those exercising their 1st Amendment rights to legally observe law enforcement. This signals not simply a loss of individual privacy, but a weakening of the democratic freedoms that allow people to challenge government power. Immigration enforcement is becoming a testing ground for the expansion of surveillance and the limits of constitutional protections.

California cannot allow these practices to become normalized. Protecting civil liberties requires more than laws on the books. It requires meaningful oversight and accountability. California’s attorney general should investigate whether federal immigration authorities access DMV records, particularly through Nlets. In July, Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta issued guidance under S B 580 addressing database safeguards, audits and vendor oversight. California must ensure these protections are enforced, not merely adopted on paper.

Today, these surveillance systems are being used to identify and target our immigrant community. But the infrastructure being built does not distinguish between immigrants and citizens. Once we normalize the government’s power to track people, monitor their movements and transform ordinary activities into opportunities for surveillance and enforcement, we put everyone’s civil liberties at risk.

text:
U.S. District Court in California orders immediate release rather than a bond hearing following a federal habeas corpus petition.

LOS ANGELES, CA, UNITED STATES, November 2, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- A client represented by Jorge Munoz Law Firm has returned home to his family after nearly two months in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention. A federal court ordered his immediate release after finding that ICE had unlawfully taken him back into custody.

The federal court litigation was handled by Jorge Muñoz, founder and immigration attorney at Jorge Munoz Law Firm. Muñoz represents immigrants facing deportation and those held in ICE custody, including clients seeking to challenge potentially unlawful detention in federal court.

On Aug. 21, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California granted a habeas corpus petition filed by Muñoz on behalf of the client (Case No. 5:26-cv-03927-ACCV). A habeas corpus petition allows someone in government custody to challenge the legality of their detention before a federal judge. Rather than ordering a bond hearing to determine whether the client could be released, the court ordered ICE to release him immediately.

ICE had re-detained the client at his home on June 27, 2026, without prior notice or a hearing. He was subsequently held at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in California. Muñoz filed the habeas corpus petition on July 14, challenging the government's authority to continue holding him.

According to Muñoz, the client was granted temporary permission to enter the United States in 2022 through an immigration process known as parole. He complied with his parole conditions for more than three years while pursuing an asylum claim.

"He had a valid work permit, no criminal record and a pending asylum case," Muñoz said.

The government argued that the client was entitled, at most, to a bond hearing under a California class-action judgment. A bond hearing would have allowed an immigration judge to decide whether the client could be released from custody on bond, but it would not have guaranteed his release. Muñoz argued that immediate release, rather than a bond hearing, was the appropriate remedy for his client's unlawful detention. The federal court rejected the government's position.

"The court held that re-detaining him without notice or a hearing violated his Fifth Amendment due process rights, and it ordered his immediate release," Muñoz said.

The court also required ICE to return the client's property, certify compliance within three days and observe due process requirements in any future enforcement action involving him.

Following the client's release, the firm obtained a change of venue, transferring his removal proceedings from the Adelanto detained docket to the non-detained Los Angeles Immigration Court. His asylum application remains pending, and Muñoz continues to represent him.

For representation or media inquiries regarding immigration detention, deportation defense or federal immigration litigation, contact Jorge Munoz Law Firm.

About Jorge Munoz Law Firm

Founded in 2023, Jorge Munoz Law Firm represents individuals and families facing immigration proceedings. With offices in North Charleston, South Carolina, and Houston, Texas, the firm serves clients nationwide.

text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has threatened to take legal action against Immigration and Customs Enforcement over allegations the agency’s officers at the agency are using parking lots owned by New York City for operations in the area.

In a letter to the Trump administration, Mamdani noted the agency’s use of property owned by the city was “unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers City residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access City property”.

He added, “if your agents continue any unauthorized use of these lots, New York City will take legal action to prevent this unlawful commandeering of City property.”

The letter called on the Department of Homeland Security and other ICE officials to issue guidance immediately to ICE agents that stipulates they are prohibited from using any New York City parking lots to stage or conduct operations.

New York City has been a sanctuary city for immigrants since Mayor Ed Koch’s administration in 1989.

The Mamdani administration has criticized the Trump administration over ICE activity in New York City, calling for ICE to be abolished in the wake of a shooting by an ICE officer of Oscar Belgal, 28, while he was picking up his five-year-old child from school.

Lawyers for Belgal claimed the ICE agent did not identify himself while wearing plainclothes before he ran up to Belgal’s car, smashed in the windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.

The Trump administration recently lost a legal challenge of New York City’s sanctuary laws filed in July 2025.

The Mamdani administration and more than 100 elected officials in New York have also urged private owners and operators of parking garages to prohibit ICE from using their private property for operations in the city.

“Our neighbors should not live in fear that the parking lot down the block could become a staging ground for an operation that puts their communities at risk,” Mamdani wrote in a 15 October letter to more than a thousand parking garage owners and operators in New York City. “I am asking every garage and lot owner in this city to stop giving them that option. Do not rent your property to ICE. Do not lend it to them. Tell them they are not welcome.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told the New York Times in response to the letter: “ICE’s presence in public parking lots is fully authorized under federal law and is a standard practice for law enforcement agencies nationwide.

“Mayor Mamdani should be grateful to our brave law enforcement officers for cleaning up the streets of NYC since he won’t.”

text:
NORTH HOLLYWOOD, LOS ANGELES -- A video going viral online shows masked ICE agents violently taking a man into custody in North Hollywood, California, on Friday morning.

The video shows the man handcuffed as ICE agents drag him to a vehicle. Three agents were seen picking the man up by his arms and legs as he cried out in pain.

The family of the man arrested identified him as 27-year-old Angel Luis Gonzalez Lobo from Venezuela. His brother said he does not know why he was arrested.

Soon after, an agent approaches a neighbor on the sidewalk walking his two dogs, appearing to point his gun in his face and pushing him into a bush. The neighbor appeared to be unarmed.

Just before the interaction, he picked up what appeared to be a canister of pepper spray off the sidewalk, but quickly threw it to the side as officers rushed toward him, exclaiming, "I thought it was his!"

Neighbors say they are upset with the way the situation escalated.

“It was a no-questions-asked thing. They just came up on him, and it was a tussle in the bushes," said witness Damari Butler.

Butler pulled out his camera and rolled on the struggle.

"The guy with the dogs, he stepped in a little bit. The ICE agent pulled out a gun, backed him up in the bushes with the gun to his face, which was insane," Butler said. “At that point, I'm going to be honest with you, I thought that was the end for him.”

The agent eventually walked back to the man being arrested on the ground.

“At one point, it did look like they may have tased him while he was on the ground and then they tried to hogtie him and then they threw him in the truck," Butler said.

A second car then pulled up as agents attempted to get the man into the vehicle.

In the meantime, the video shows the man with two dogs pick something else up from the ground. An agent then rushes after him and tells the neighbor to put it down before appearing to spray something at him.

“It just felt very chaotic. It didn’t feel like anybody actually knew what they were doing on that side. It just felt like, 'If we need to use excessive force to get what we need -- do it,'" Butler said.

Another witness said she felt scared for the man who was taken by agents.

"Until you actually witness it, it's actually really sad. It's really sad this is going on," neighbor Nancy said. "Whether I was with my child or not, I was a bit scared. I was scared for the man that was being dragged. I was scared for myself and my son. I just didn't feel safe walking outside my apartment building."

Our sister station KABC-TV reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for more information but has yet to hear back.

Meanwhile, the shocking video sparked area leaders to demand answers.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass issued the following statement:

“This is unacceptable and will not be tolerated in L.A. I’m engaging the Attorney General’s Office to investigate and prosecute any wrongdoing by these federal agents. Additionally, I referred this matter to the Office of U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat leading oversight on federal immigration enforcement abuses.

We beat Trump and ICE in court, and new state laws have implemented accountability measures for ICE agents to protect our communities.”

Councilwoman and mayoral candidate Nithya Raman wrote the following on social media:

"I am outraged by reports of violent ICE kidnappings in North Hollywood. L.A. is not a playground for the Trump regime’s inhumane operations, and Angelenos should not have to live in fear of going to work, taking their kids to school or living their life."

text:
School districts across the metro are still grappling with the Trump Administration’s ongoing immigration enforcement months after federal agents targeted students, bus stops and school parking lots during Operation Metro Surge.

"Thin I.C.E.", a new docuseries from FOX 9 Documentaries, includes interviews with Minnesota education officials and ICE observers who tried to protect schools and students during Operation Metro Surge. Part one premieres Wednesday, Nov. 4 at 10:35 p.m. CT. on FOX 9.

Fewer students after Operation Metro Surge

Big picture view:

School districts with large immigrant populations, like Columbia Heights, Saint Paul and Minneapolis have reported losing dozens of students and millions of dollars in funding because of declining enrollments attributed to Operation Metro Surge.

Saint Paul Public Schools are now considering teacher layoffs because of the financial impact attributed to the immigration operation.

Why you should care:

Schools, once deemed sensitive locations that were off-limits to Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, were regularly targeted during the Trump Administration’s enhanced immigration operations.

"They absolutely came onto our school property," said Columbia Heights Superintendent Zena Stenvik.

Stenvik became one of the most vocal critics of Operation Metro Surge after a 5-year-old boy and his father were detained on the way home from school.

Pictures of Liam Ramos wearing a blue bunny hat and a backpack while being surrounded by armed federal agents went viral and forced the Trump Administration to publicly defend the operation.

"I did not have an understanding of how far it would go and how much it would really touch the hearts of the entire world," Stenvik said.

From school to an ICE plane

What they're saying:

A former elementary school principal reflected on the emotional toll Operation Metro Surge had on students, families and staff, including what he called the "worst day" of his career.

Jason Kuhlman, then the principal at Valley View Elementary, said a parent asked him to bring her two children to the Whipple Federal Building where she had been unexpectedly detained during an immigration check-in.

"I get emotional about it just because that’s not what we signed up to do. That’s against my morals and my values to bring kids down where they’re going to be detained," Kuhlman said.

Kuhlman said those students were sent to a detention center in Dilley, Texas within hours even though the district presented paperwork proving the family was actively seeking asylum.

"The agent didn’t look at the paperwork at all, just stuck them on a plane and away they were," Kuhlman recalled.

Other students suddenly disappeared without the district knowing whether they had already been deported or were simply in hiding.

"We knew they were missing, we knew we lost contact with them, but we didn't know where they were," Kuhlman said.

No more safe places

The other side:

Rep. Walter Hudson (R-Albertville) defended federal agents who patrolled school zones during Operation Metro Surge.

"I don't think there's anywhere you should be able to go where you're no longer subject to the laws of the land in which you live," Hudson said, while acknowledging that school districts can deny agents who do not have judicial warrants.

"The school can tell you that we don't want you in here and your administrative warrant doesn't override their authority over that space, but you most certainly can sit in the parking lot, sit across the street, wait outside," Hudson said in the upcoming documentary.

In response, ICE observers monitored playgrounds and bus stops for months.

"The middle schooler who lives near me called me and asked if ICE was chasing him home from the bus stop, if he could hide in my house," said Tippy Amundson, who helped families in Brooklyn Park during the surge.

"I put that 12-year-old in my car and I drove him down the street and I said, 'you can hide in that house, you can hide in the house, you can hide in that house.'"

"Thin I.C.E." is a three-part series by FOX 9 Documentaries detailing the Trump Administration's immigration operations in Chicago and Minneapolis that resulted in constitutional challenges, violent tactics and deadly shootings.

text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent accused of intentionally striking a man with his SUV during an immigration operation in west Harris County is expected to surrender to authorities Monday morning.

Mario Alberto Morales is expected to turn himself in between 8:30 a.m. and 10 a.m. at the 488th District Court, according to his attorney.

Morales was indicted Friday by a Harris County grand jury on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in connection with an October 10 incident that left Miguel Parra Hernandez seriously injured.

Body-camera video captures moments before crash

Newly released body-camera video shows the moments leading up to the incident near Clay Road and Highway 6.

In the recording, an agent can be heard saying, “We got a runner,” as Parra Hernandez runs from immigration officers.

Moments later, prosecutors allege Morales intentionally struck Parra Hernandez with his SUV.

Parra Hernandez suffered serious injuries to his leg that required surgery.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said the evidence, including body-camera and surveillance video, supports the criminal charge against Morales.

“I hope that also sends a loud and clear message to every ICE officer who feels that they have a free pass to terrorize our streets,” Teare said.

ICE agent’s attorney disputes allegations

Morales’ attorney maintains that the collision was an accident and that his client never intended to strike Parra Hernandez.

Morales faces a second-degree felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. If convicted, he could face between two and 20 years in prison.

What happens next?

Morales is expected to surrender at the Harris County Criminal Courthouse Monday morning.

His attorney confirmed the surrender could happen as early as 8:30 a.m. and as late as 10 a.m.

The court proceedings could provide additional details about his bond and the next steps in the criminal case.

title: We studied the impact of ICE enforcement on the job market. It isn't pretty. - The Boston Globe
description:
Before enforcement intensified, jobs in these cities were growing slightly faster than in the rest of the country.
Applying our average estimates suggests Boston had 12,000 fewer jobs than it otherwise would have had six months after the surge of ICE enforcement began with “Operation Patriot” in May 2025.
Other researchers have found that surges in ICE arrests in the community reduced consumer spending.
We expect 287(g) to be an increasingly important channel for enforcement in the coming year.
As in the past, we can expect these new 287(g) agreements to drive job loss in the communities that implement them.
text:
Our research focused on a specific bundle of policies that spread fear beyond those arrested: militarized “shock and awe” raids, arrests made “at-large” in the community, and indiscriminate targeting of migrants including those with pending asylum claims or legal status.

We looked for communities where enforcement surged most sharply. We defined 64 “surge cities” as those that experienced both an outsized jump in total arrests and in arrests relative to their population. Boston is one of them.

Before enforcement intensified, jobs in these cities were growing slightly faster than in the rest of the country. After the surges, this trajectory changed for the worse and did not recover. In the average surge city, employment fell 0.43 percent below its expected path six months after enforcement intensified and 0.69 percent below by month 11.

This may sound like a small change. It isn’t. Boston illustrates the scale. ICE made about 3,000 more arrests in the city in 2025 than it did in 2024. Applying our average estimates suggests Boston had 12,000 fewer jobs than it otherwise would have had six months after the surge of ICE enforcement began with “Operation Patriot” in May 2025.

While jarring, these estimates almost certainly understate the true economic toll. We compared cities where enforcement surged with similar cities where it did not — a conservative comparison, designed to isolate ICE’s effect from tariffs, inflation, and other economic shocks. Our estimates therefore captured only the additional damage added by an intense crackdown, not the full national cost of the mass deportation campaign.

Community-based arrests — at worksites, homes, and traffic stops — appear to be doing most of the damage. These arrests spread fear across a much broader population, creating further knock-on economic effects. Other researchers have found that surges in ICE arrests in the community reduced consumer spending. In Los Angeles, spending in immigrant-heavy neighborhoods fell 20 to 25 percent in the two months after a major ICE operation was announced, costing the region roughly $625 million in lost sales. Nationwide, foot traffic near enforcement sites fell about 3 percent and spending fell about 6 percent, regardless of a neighborhood’s demographics, suggesting that fear, not just removals, is suppressing economic activity.

Yet the economic and human toll has not led the administration to modify its enforcement strategy, nor has it changed Congress’ willingness to fund it. If anything, arrests since the start of 2026 have accelerated, even as the human costs become harder to ignore.

The acceleration was driven in part by the administration’s increased use of 287(g) agreements, particularly the controversial task force model, which deputizes local police and sheriffs to question, stop, and arrest immigrants in the community during routine patrols and traffic stops. According to our research these highly visible, at-large arrests are extremely disruptive to local economies. Nationwide, active 287(g) agreements grew from 135 in January 2025 to more than 2,600 by October 2026, with task force agreements accounting for roughly three-quarters of the growth.

Though Massachusetts has prohibited local law enforcement from entering 287(g) partnerships, agencies in the two New Hampshire counties within the Boston metro area have signed on. Because labor markets span state lines, New Hampshire’s choice to turn local officers into de facto immigration agents has the potential to trigger additional job losses in Massachusetts and within Greater Boston.

We expect 287(g) to be an increasingly important channel for enforcement in the coming year. Thousands of newly deputized local officers are now funded in ways that reward immigration enforcement rather than public safety. As in the past, we can expect these new 287(g) agreements to drive job loss in the communities that implement them.

Immigration policy doesn’t have to cause job loss and economic damage. We can craft a sensible approach that provides legal status for immigrants who have spent years building lives and careers here, focuses enforcement resources at the border and on the small number of people who pose a genuine threat, and offers legal migration channels that meet the American economy’s labor demands and complement American workers.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani is demanding that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement immediately stop using city-owned property for immigration enforcement operations, threatening legal action if the agency does not comply.

“ICE has no right to use our property as a base for tearing families apart. That goes for every park and every lot this City owns. title: Interfaith migration policy summit seeks common ground on welcoming the stranger
description:

The summit came during what participants described as a challenging time for their cause.
Enid Almanzar, board chair at the National Latino Evangelical Coalition, said in remarks at the summit, "Migration is not a footnote in the biblical narrative."
Multiple panelists at the summit shared concerns about that policy change.
"A nation should be able to uphold its laws without surrendering its conscience, and faith communities have a responsibility to remind our leaders and ourselves of that truth."
text:
WASHINGTON (OSV News) -- An Oct. 29-30 interfaith immigration policy summit hosted by the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, also known as CLINIC, brought together faith leaders, legal practitioners, advocates and scholars from Catholic, Protestant and Jewish faith traditions to find areas of commonality in their work serving immigrant communities.

Anna Gallagher, executive director of CLINIC, said in remarks at the summit, "We have much to learn from one another."

"Across the traditions represented here, we encounter teachings about hospitality, justice, compassion, refuge, and responsibility," she said.

The summit came during what participants described as a challenging time for their cause. A joint report from the National Association of Evangelicals, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Migration and Refugee Services, the Center for the Study of Global Christianity at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, and World Relief estimated that more than 10 million Christians living in the U.S. would be vulnerable to deportation under Trump administration policies implemented in 2025, and 61% were Catholic.

It also found more than 1 in 6 Catholics are either vulnerable to deportation themselves or could see a family member deported, barring law or policy changes.

In reference to their interfaith dialogue, the Rev. Enid Almanzar, board chair at the National Latino Evangelical Coalition, said in remarks at the summit, "Migration is not a footnote in the biblical narrative."

"Even Jesus began his earthly life as a child whose family had to flee political violence and seek refuge in Egypt," she said.

Acknowledging broader doctrinal differences between the organizations, Rev. Almanzar said, "we may not agree on some of the larger theological questions, but we don't have to agree on every doctrine to recognize the moral urgency of protecting the vulnerable."

"Because ultimately, compassion without action becomes sentimentality and conviction without courage becomes rhetoric, and so our calling is to move beyond both to become communities where dignity is defended, where families are accompanied, and where love is made visible," she said.

The summit also came shortly after a divided panel of the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia allowed a lawsuit against the federal government from a coalition of more than two dozen religious organizations to proceed. The group is challenging a Trump administration policy that rescinded long-standing restrictions on arrests at sensitive locations, also including schools and hospitals, with exceptions for public safety or national security threats. Multiple panelists at the summit shared concerns about that policy change.

It also came soon after the Archdiocese of St. Louis filed a separate lawsuit against the federal government over a policy it said prohibits priests from distributing holy Communion to and hearing confessions of Catholics detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Pope Leo XIV sent a special message of support to the summit, thanking CLINIC for its work, "together with that of the many people, families, civic bodies and church communities who strive to uphold the dignity of migrants and refugees."

"Too often, these most vulnerable members of society are caught in situations which strip them of their human rights -- an injustice that cries out to heaven," he said. "It is my hope, therefore, that this summit will encourage the participants to stir the hearts and minds of their fellow citizens to overcome that indifference and detachment which reduces the human person to a statistic."

Pope Leo said he would pray the meeting "will help find new ways to awaken consciences to our shared moral duty for these brothers and sisters of ours, who, as Sacred Scripture and the saints untiringly remind us, are Christ visiting us in disguise."

Gallagher said Pope Leo's message was "a meaningful charge for the beginning of an interfaith gathering."

"We are here to learn from one another, to strengthen our work, and to consider how we can help our communities see more clearly and respond more faithfully," she said.

Rev. Almanzar argued that religious communities are well suited to advocate for humane immigration policies.

"Maybe the most prophetic thing we can do in this environment is refuse that false binary choice between security and humanity," she said. "A nation should be able to uphold its laws without surrendering its conscience, and faith communities have a responsibility to remind our leaders and ourselves of that truth."

"As faith communities," she added, "I think we can be leaders in reframing the conversation and casting a vision about a future where people flourish, where people are welcome, where people are loved, and there's not that false binary choice."

Gallagher added, "Migration brings us into contact with questions that are central to religious life. Where do we belong? What do we owe one another? How do we respond to suffering? What does it mean to welcome someone whose language, history, or circumstances differ from our own?"

After our own review, we conclude that Appellants lack Article III standing to challenge the Nondisclosure Policy.
The purported Nondisclosure Policy is simply Appellants’ conclusory label that describes practices whereby various Agencies make varying degrees of information available by varying means in various proceedings.
As we see it, because Appellants have failed to establish the existence of the so-called Nondisclosure Policy occurring throughout the entirety of DHS in a uniform manner, we cannot conclude that their alleged injury is ‘concrete.’ … “Moreover, even if we assume, for the sake of argument, that a Nondisclosure Policy does exist, we find Appellants’ arguments in support of organizational standing unpersuasive.
… “In sum, if we accepted Appellants’ theory of standing in this case, it could functionally eliminate the Article III standing requirements for any lawyer who seeks to invalidate a government policy.
text:
Where the appellants — two immigration attorneys, a law firm and a legal services organization — filed suit to enjoin the Department of Homeland Security from routing discovery in immigration proceedings through Freedom of Information Act requests, the dismissal of the complaint should be affirmed because the appellants do not have standing to assert their claims.

“A group of two immigration attorneys, a law firm, and a legal services organization (collectively, the ‘Appellants’) filed suit to enjoin the Department of Homeland Security (‘DHS’) from routing discovery in immigration proceedings through Freedom of Information Act (‘FOIA’) requests. Appellants brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act (‘APA’), 5 U.S.C. §706, et seq., challenging this alleged ‘Nondisclosure Policy’ as violative of the Due Process Clause, the Immigration and Nationality Act, and DHS regulations. The district court dismissed all the claims at the motion to dismiss and summary judgment stages. Appellants appealed those decisions. After our own review, we conclude that Appellants lack Article III standing to challenge the Nondisclosure Policy. Accordingly, we affirm the district court’s judgment for the government, albeit on different grounds. …

“Appellants’ sweeping challenge is based on examples of FOIA referrals which occurred within different component agencies of DHS, i.e., removal proceedings undertaken by ICE, and asylum adjudications conducted by USCIS. But specific, disjointed instances of such referrals, without more, do not amount to an ‘agency action’ in the form of an agency-wide policy. … Further, because the ‘action’ Appellants allege is a collection of decentralized immigration interactions that vary in their details among the varying Agencies, it is not even entirely clear whether the harm that is asserted (i.e., the withholding or delay in making information available) will even occur in any specific instance. For example, the complaint itself alleges, and the summary judgment record confirmed, that the information a noncitizen obtains in affirmative asylum proceedings depends on a wide range of factors, including the discretion of the asylum officer. The purported Nondisclosure Policy is simply Appellants’ conclusory label that describes practices whereby various Agencies make varying degrees of information available by varying means in various proceedings. As we see it, because Appellants have failed to establish the existence of the so-called Nondisclosure Policy occurring throughout the entirety of DHS in a uniform manner, we cannot conclude that their alleged injury is ‘concrete.’ …

“Moreover, even if we assume, for the sake of argument, that a Nondisclosure Policy does exist, we find Appellants’ arguments in support of organizational standing unpersuasive. Appellants liken their bid for standing to the plaintiff organization in Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982). There, says Appellants, the Supreme Court found that the plaintiff organization suffered an injury in fact because defendants’ actions affected their ‘core business activities.’ …

“We do not think Appellants’ alleged injury is analogous to the harm present in Havens. …

“Havens‘ core-business-activities exception cannot mean that any lawyer, law firm, or ‘organization that provides free legal assistance’ may assert organizational standing, in lieu of representing an individual plaintiff, by alleging that a challenged policy increases the cost of representation or limits the size of a client roster. …

“In sum, if we accepted Appellants’ theory of standing in this case, it could functionally eliminate the Article III standing requirements for any lawyer who seeks to invalidate a government policy. If a lawyer wished to package his disagreement with the policy in a case or controversy, all he would have to do is represent a client whom the policy regulates. Then the lawyer could walk into court, leave the client at the door, and claim for his own sake that the policy makes it harder to represent the client. We do not think that this is what the Supreme Court had in mind as falling within Havens‘ context. …”

Greater Boston Legal Services, et al. v. United States Department of Homeland Security, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 01-240-26) (21 pages) (Gelpí, J.) Appealed from a decision by Casper, J., in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Sandra H. Masselink, with whom Adriana Lafaille, John T. Montgomery, American Civil Liberties Union Foundation of Massachusetts, Inc., and Ropes & Gray were on brief, for the plaintiffs-appellants; Susan M. Finegan, Emily Kanstroom Musgrave, Gabrielle Brown, Alexa Greco, Cassandra Harris, Savannah Wormley, Mintz, Levin, Cohn, Ferris, Glovsky, and Popeo, P.C., and Nicholas A. Butto on brief for American Immigration Lawyers Association, amicus curiae for the appellants; Simon G. Jerome, with whom Brett A. Shumate, Leah B. Foley and Charles W. Scarborough were on brief, for the defendants-appellees (Docket No. 25-1799) (Oct. 29, 2026).

name: Litigation
title: Immigrant advocacy groups file lawsuit against TN over drivers license policies
description:
A new legal battle is brewing in Tennessee.
Immigrant advocacy groups have filed a lawsuit against the Department of Safety and Homeland Security over an abrupt shift in driver’s license policies.
The lawsuit, filed by the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition and the National Immigration Law Center, challenges a state rule restricting the federal documents accepted for temporary licenses.
Advocates say the change suddenly excludes thousands of legally authorized residents—including DACA recipients and work permit holders—who have driven safely in the state for decades.
The state has declined to comment on the pending litigation, but plaintiffs are asking a Davidson County court to immediately halt the policy, arguing it was implemented unlawfully without public input.

title: ICE, inflation and Trump: gen Z readers share their concerns heading into the voting both
description:
Gen Z readers across the country highlighted to the Guardian the issues shaping their views ahead of the election.
Charlie, a 22-year-old library worker in Ohio, pointed to healthcare and affordability as the most important issues shaping their vote.
Emily, a 28-year-old living in central Illinois, identified artificial intelligence, Israel’s war on Gaza and ICE as among the biggest concerns shaping the political landscape.
Similar concerns about the prospect of Democratic underperformance were raised by Connor Long, a 29-year-old remote sales representative in Orlando, Florida.
Long said he was “excited to see how this election is shaping up but am leery of the data we are seeing.”
text:
The 2026 US midterms are approaching against a backdrop of growing political uncertainty, with young voters increasingly mobilizing around concerns about the country’s future.

Although nearly 50 million Americans aged 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the midterms, almost half remain either unregistered or civically disengaged, according to US Census Bureau data.

Gen Z readers across the country highlighted to the Guardian the issues shaping their views ahead of the election. Among their biggest concerns were the rising cost of living, federal immigration policies, the climate crisis, election interference and the rollback of civil rights.

For Tyler, a 24-year-old working at a community church in Richfield, Minnesota, “ICE, inflation and worries about [Donald] Trump’s military force have been … huge factor[s] in voting this year.”

“I like going to the grocery store but I don’t like seeing the price increase amid this unpopular and illegal war,” Tyler said, adding: “​​Fascism is taking hold and I want there to be some semblance of accountability, and I want to make sure that we actually have a real opposition party that we’re not seeing at the moment, aside from some candidates.”

However, even a Democratic victory would not necessarily ease concerns about election integrity, with Tyler worrying that “there will be some trickery and subversion of results or another version of January 6”.

Charlie, a 22-year-old library worker in Ohio, pointed to healthcare and affordability as the most important issues shaping their vote.

“Advocating against universal healthcare indicates, to me, a deep disregard for the actual wellbeing of the American people. Also, the wealth disparity in the US is astronomical, so advocating for a greater tax on the ultra-wealthy is important to me as well. People who have to work to survive are doing so poorly right now, all I want is to see life become affordable again,” Charlie said.

For a 25-year-old maintenance worker in Connecticut, the financial pressures of everyday life can also make civic participation difficult.

“I do want to vote, but that depends on how accessible it is. If I have the time and energy I go out and vote. I do work a lot. I have a lot of bills to pay (car, car insurance, rent, utilities, student loans, medical bills). It is hard to find time to do just about anything,” they said.

They also expressed frustration with the candidates on offer, saying that a lack of confidence in either party could make deciding how to vote difficult.

“The problem is I am worried that if I vote, I will vote wrong because I don’t really trust any of the people up for office … I don’t want to vote for a Republican, but I also don’t want to vote for [Connecticut governor Ned] Lamont because his track record of doing what he said he would (even trying) is not very good and he has put more money into corporate pockets than into the working class,” they said.

“I am concerned that any meaningfully good legislation will have bullcrap logrolled into it for things that our communities don’t want. I also worry that the almighty American dollar will blind every politician in the race and none of them will have actual integrity,” they added.

Emily, a 28-year-old living in central Illinois, identified artificial intelligence, Israel’s war on Gaza and ICE as among the biggest concerns shaping the political landscape.

“Our refusal to acknowledge the cruelty and absurdity of this administration has normalized it into our culture, if it wasn’t there already. Any attempt to criticize it is shot down with claims of hysteria or wokeness. Our … participation in this modern propaganda will have lasting impacts. I am deeply concerned how the world looks at us, and how we will look back at ourselves,” Emily said.

Looking ahead to the election, Emily said the hope is to see “any politician that looks like they actually have a backbone and won’t just tweet that someone should do something about this”.

The climate crisis and immigration enforcement are also shaping how young voters view the election.

Matthew Doutt, a 26-year-old accountant in Knoxville, Tennessee, said: “This administration has done deep damages to the guardrails meant to defend against climate change, and we need someone – anyone – to get us back on track … Unfortunately, with me being in a conservative state that’s been heavily gerrymandered, no one stands out in my state in a positive way.”

He also raised concerns about the potential presence of federal immigration agents at polling locations.

“Tennessee is one of several states that has partnered with ICE for local enforcement. I’m expecting to see ICE at polling locations to supposedly prevent against undocumented immigrants [from] voting but I expect it to be more about intimidating liberals,” Doutt said.

For Niamh Catterall, an 18-year-old university student from Texas currently studying in Ireland, the election will mark her first time voting. She plans to cast her ballot by mail, with the war, cost of living, protections for minorities and immigrants, and the separation of church and state among her main concerns.

“I am hopeful of a break from party politics and a renewed focus on how a candidate can help a society or individual. In the case of many of the candidates who I support, such as [Gina] Hinojosa or [James] Talarico, their platforms go beyond experience or big picture, federal politics like being aligned with Trump and actually focus on what groups within the state need, whether that is healthcare or cost of living,” Catterall said.

For Nathan, a 21-year-old computer science student in Texas, LGBTQ+ rights and datacenter expansions are key issues amid the performances of Democratic candidates in the state.

“It really excites me to see how well Talarico is doing! The idea of a blue Texas is mind-blowing to me,” Nathan said, adding: “I know that Democratic candidates in southern states almost always lose. I also really wish that more people my age voted.”

However, for Scott, a 29-year-old software engineer in Washington who has already voted, concerns about the future span both sides of the political aisle.

“I’m extremely concerned with the lack of leadership from both parties, but especially with the imminent harm from the Republican party, and Trump in particular. This level of corruption is unprecedented and unacceptable. Although my state is not competitive on the national stage, I felt it was at least something I could do,” Scott said.

He also described a growing sense of economic and political uncertainty among young Americans, alongside frustration with what he sees as a lack of a compelling vision from Democrats.

“My career went from a sure thing to unknown in less than 10 years. I, and many others, especially my age, are not optimistic for the future … I’m emotionally raw, and very tired. My biggest concern is that Democrats won’t rally behind a unifying coherent vision for the future that we can get excited about. I’ve literally heard Democrats say we need a vision for years. They need to get one now … It doesn’t need to be perfect, and it’s OK if there’s unknowns, but it needs to be something that the vast majority of Americans can rally behind,” he added.

Similar concerns about the prospect of Democratic underperformance were raised by Connor Long, a 29-year-old remote sales representative in Orlando, Florida.

Long said he was “excited to see how this election is shaping up but am leery of the data we are seeing.”

title: Why Immigration Agents Don't Quit in Protest | The New Yorker
description:
Still, there was a feeling among immigration agents that they were being shackled by the new Administration.
By 2024, the Border Patrol had lost a quarter of its workforce, with many longtime agents opting for early retirement.
The operation was so unpopular with the rank and file that Border Patrol and ICE struggled to find personnel for the deployment.
In a conversation with Vox about why Border Patrol agents obey immoral orders, he warned against placing the moral onus on individuals over institutions.
And yet, the more I learned about Barry’s movement, the more I imagined the possibility of a similar community of former immigration agents.
text:
In the winter of 2018, Joshua Childress was sent to the Yuma Regional Medical Center, in southwest Arizona, to guard a man who’d fallen from a thirty-foot-high border wall. Childress was in his seventh year in the United States Border Patrol and had grown accustomed to doing hospital watch, in which agents monitor recently apprehended migrants to insure that they don’t escape while receiving care. To Childress’s surprise, the injured man spoke fluent English. Childress asked why he had come to the U.S. “Because this is my home,” the man replied.

The man, who appeared to be in his early twenties, had lived in Arizona since he was eight years old—longer than Childress had been in the state himself. A few months earlier, the man had hosted a barbecue at his house, and neighbors had called in a noise complaint. The police came, asked for the man’s I.D., and reported him to immigration authorities, who deported him to Mexico. Childress asked why the man hadn’t sought Dreamer status under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which provides protection from deportation for certain undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children. The man explained that he had wanted to, but his father had been afraid that the paperwork was a trick meant to entrap them.

Childress listened as the man described the mountain town where he’d grown up, a place that sounded much like the community where Childress was raised, in rural Colorado. “I barely speak Spanish,” the man told Childress. “I don’t know anybody in Mexico. I’ve been down there wandering around for three months, trying to figure out what to do, and I decided, You know what? I’ll take my chances and come back here. And then I fell from the fence and broke my leg.”
