title: Exercise Your Constitutional Rights to Protect the Rule of Law - Bloomberg Law
description:
What can citizens do when federal officials charged with protecting their legal rights disregard them or enforce them only selectively?
The first ten amendments to our Constitution, the Bill of Rights, provide guarantees to every citizen that are legally enforceable.
It didn’t start with this administration, but in the last year, the assault on personal rights has increased dramatically.
Judge Philip Pro was appointed by President Reagan to the US District Court for the District of Nevada.
Judge Paul Watford was appointed by President Obama to the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.
text:
What can citizens do when federal officials charged with protecting their legal rights disregard them or enforce them only selectively? Our Constitution gives every citizen the rights of peaceful assembly and freedom of speech. Exercising those rights in these circumstances is the very essence of citizenship.

The first ten amendments to our Constitution, the Bill of Rights, provide guarantees to every citizen that are legally enforceable. They include the basic freedoms all Americans enjoy but many take for granted. Together, they are meant to ensure that all of us are free from lawless government interference with our personal liberty.

These rights include the right to speak freely; worship freely; associate freely with persons or organizations of our choice; vote freely in elections; to be free from arbitrary arrests and unreasonable searches and seizures, particularly in our homes; to protest peacefully; and to ask government for relief from grievances.

The Constitution, the basic and highest law of the land, assigns to the executive — the president and his subordinates — the duty to see that laws embodied in the Constitution and statutes are fully and fairly implemented. For nearly 250 years, this duty almost always has been, in the words of Article II of the Constitution, “faithfully executed.”

In recent times, the executive branch has undermined the law and impeded those rights. The transition from guarantor to degrader of rights has evolved gradually, incrementally, almost unnoticed, over many years. It didn’t start with this administration, but in the last year, the assault on personal rights has increased dramatically.

For example, recent presidential executive orders seek to impede or deny the right to vote, by restricting mail-in ballots and use of electronic voting machines, “inspecting” state voter registration rolls with the goal of removing names, and other similar measures. These actions ignore the Constitution’s explicit assignment to the states of the power to set the “time, place and manner” of elections.

Although the Constitution authorizes Congress to protect the electoral process, neither the Constitution nor Congress has provided any such authority to the president. He has no lawful role with respect to how elections are conducted. The president nevertheless has acted with unbounded assertiveness as if it were his right and responsibility.

The executive has also burdened our legal system with unwarranted investigations and threats to law firms if they represent clients or causes the executive dislikes. Some firms have capitulated rather than risk loss of revenue. Other institutions, including many leading universities, major corporations, non-profits, and news organizations, have been subjected to unwarranted lawsuits, have been investigated without cause, or even have received unjustified demands for payment.

When lawyers have challenged these actions, the government frequently has delayed or evaded compliance with court orders enforcing legal rights, particularly with respect to immigration. In some cases, Justice Department attorneys have misinformed judges and openly disregarded judicial directives. The result is a crisis of confidence in the DOJ’s commitment to justice that has no precedent in American history.

Judges have been subjected to malicious personal attacks by high-ranking members of the executive and legislative branches, including virally on social media. Although the executive hasn’t explicitly threatened any judge with harm, its extreme rhetoric about decisions of which it disapproves has led others to threaten judges and their families or to introduce meritless impeachment resolutions simply for doing their constitutional duty of applying the law as objectively and impartially as possible.

Scholars tracking the combined effects of these actions have called this progression of escalating assaults on the rule of law a “rolling coup.” The executive appears determined to assert as much control over the government as possible, ignoring Congress, the courts, and the rights of the states.

So far, Congress has done little in response. And although lower federal courts have restrained many of these lawless actions, the executive often outraces reviewing courts, which inherently are slow and deliberative. One recent example is the White House ballroom case, in which the judiciary intervened only after the fact. Relief that comes only after harm is inflicted is no relief at all.

The harms aren’t limited to the systematic evasion of our constitutional system of checks and balances among the executive, legislative, and judicial branches. Many executive actions directly hurt individual citizens. As noted, voting rights of millions of American citizens have been the target of actual or threatened interference. Largely peaceful protests have been violently suppressed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, troops have been needlessly deployed to our cities, individuals have been arbitrarily arrested, and homes have been searched without judicial warrants, all at the direction of the executive.

These transgressions are difficult to explain unless the executive is determined to overpower the other two branches, gain unrestrained power and retain it, possibly in disregard of the results of the elections in 2026 and 2028. Although the administration has misused emergency powers that were granted by past Congresses, it also claims even greater secret emergency powers implemented in dozens of pre-written presidential directives never approved or even seen by Congress. The potential for further abuse exists and constitutes a clear and present danger to the republic.

Similar patterns of progressively seizing power have been seen in other nations, including Poland, Hungary, and Turkey, where autocrats gradually but substantially interfered with democratic institutions. Unfortunately, the playbook seen elsewhere is beginning to be seen here.

We are confident that if the American people knew the full extent of this overreach, they would demand that it end. The question is: Will they know in time? Will they make their voices heard through free speech, peaceful assembly, and at the ballot box?

Keep Our Republic’s Article III Coalition, a bi-partisan group of 61 former federal judges to which we belong, seeks to be today’s Paul Revere, alerting citizens to the grave dangers facing the nation.

We encourage all citizens to exercise their constitutional right to vote this Election Day and to elect candidates who will fulfill their role as a check on the other branches of government. We urge Americans to contact their representative in Congress and their two senators, strongly encouraging them to apply the Constitution’s existing safeguards and where appropriate to erect new statutory ones.

There may well be an approaching tipping point beyond which it is too late. The time for citizens to speak up and act is now.

This article does not necessarily reflect the opinion of Bloomberg Industry Group Inc., the publisher of Bloomberg Law, Bloomberg Tax, and Bloomberg Government, or its owners.

Author Information

The authors are all retired US judges and are members of the Executive Committee of Keep Our Republic’s Article III Coalition. They write, however, solely in their individual capacities.

Judge Robert Cindrich was appointed by President Bill Clinton to the US District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania and by President Jimmy Carter to be the US Attorney for that district.

Judge Bernice Donald was appointed by President Clinton to the US District Court for the Western District of Tennessee and by President Barack Obama to the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

Judge Allyson Duncan was appointed by President George W. Bush to the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

Judge Jeremy Fogel was appointed by President Clinton to the US District Court for the Northern District of California and is also a former director of the Federal Judicial Center.

Judge John Jones was appointed by President George W. Bush to the US District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and is the president of Dickinson College.

Judge Paul Michel was appointed by President Ronald Reagan to the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit and is also a former Watergate Assistant Special Prosecutor.

Judge Philip Pro was appointed by President Reagan to the US District Court for the District of Nevada.

Judge Deanell Tacha was appointed by President Reagan to the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit and was dean of the Pepperdine University School of Law.

Judge Thomas Vanaskie was appointed by President Clinton to the US District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and by President Obama to the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

Judge Paul Watford was appointed by President Obama to the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

title: Politicians ignore permanent migration program planning at their peril
description:
DESPITE THE NOW strong focus on their respective Net Overseas Migration (NOM) targets, Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all either ignored or suppressed the challenges of managing the permanent migration program.
Both Labor and Coalition policy is to maintain the permanent migration program at 185,000 per annum within a NOM target of 225,000 and 100,000, respectively.
Partner visas The Migration Act makes it abundantly clear that partner visas must be managed on a demand-driven basis.
Long-term migration planning requires a plan for managing both NOM and the permanent program.
One Nation’s immigration policy manifesto just ignores the permanent migration program altogether, suggesting it is oblivious to the challenges.
text:
Australia’s major political parties are failing to address growing permanent visa backlogs, risking legal challenges, longer processing times and mounting pressure from employers and families. Dr Abul Rizvi writes.

DESPITE THE NOW strong focus on their respective Net Overseas Migration (NOM) targets, Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all either ignored or suppressed the challenges of managing the permanent migration program. There are serious legal, policy and political implications of doing so.

Both Labor and Coalition policy is to maintain the permanent migration program at 185,000 per annum within a NOM target of 225,000 and 100,000, respectively. One Nation has decided, in its eagerness to announce its negative NOM target for three successive years, that it will simply avoid talking about the permanent migration program altogether.

There are two major challenges that are being ignored/suppressed. First is the ongoing growth in the partner visa backlog — this is a visa category that by law must be managed on a demand-driven basis. The second is pressure from employers and state/territory governments for additional places to meet their needs, which are currently well in excess of the places allocated.

Partner visas

The Migration Act makes it abundantly clear that partner visas must be managed on a demand-driven basis. The Department of Home Affairs (DHA) knows this and accordingly puts a footnote to the annual planning levels and outcomes for this visa that proudly states DHA manages this visa on a demand-driven basis. It is a totally misleading footnote, as the Department over the last decade has always delivered partner visa numbers to whatever planning level the Government sets irrespective of demand.

For example, in both 2024-25 and 2025-26, the partner planning level was 40,500 and the outcome was – you guessed it – 40,500. The planning level is clearly being used as a cap when s87 of the Migration Act makes it clear partner visas cannot be capped.

The illegal behaviour started around 2014-15 when former Immigration Minister Peter Dutton and his Secretary, Mike Pezzullo, decided either to ignore the requirements of the law or were not advised of it — the latter would seem unlikely.

In the face of a forthcoming audit of partner visa processing by the Auditor-General, the then-new Immigration Minister, Alex Hawke, quickly cleared the backlog in 2020-21 by allocating a record 72,000 places for partner visas. New applications also fell during COVID, assisting DHA to be able to tell the Auditor-General that it was indeed managing partner visas on a demand-driven basis.

After the audit, the Coalition Government went back to limiting places for partner visas to around 40,000 per annum. The new Labor Government, which had been critical of the Coalition Government’s illegal practice and had encouraged the Auditor-General to call out the illegal practice, went back to doing the same — limiting places for partner visas and allowing the backlog to blow out. In 2025-26, with places limited to 40,500 and new applications during that year at 66,916, the backlog blew out to an astonishing 116,917 by end June 2026.

In 2026-27, the Government has marginally increased the number of places for partners to 41,500. If new applications in 2026-27 are again over 65,000 (highly likely), that means the backlog will grow further, possibly to around 130,000. And the Government will continue to pretend that it is abiding by the law and managing partner visas on a demand-driven basis.

But at some stage, it will be forced by either the courts or the Ombudsman to face the reality of its illegal behaviour.

Demand from employers and state/territory governments

Unlike partner visas, the Government has tried to manage the booming demand for permanent employer-sponsored visas in a manner that is slightly more responsive to demand.

Applications have increased from 41,992 in 2022-23 to 87,055 in 2025-26. To try to deal with this, the Government has increased places for this visa from 26,103 in 2021-22 to 44,022 in 2025-26. The increased number of places has not, however, kept pace with rising applications and hence the backlog has boomed from 27,523 at end June 2023 to 99,144 at end June 2026.

For 2026-27, the Government has further increased places to 58,040. This has been achieved by shifting places from the Regional Visa, where places in 2026-27 have been reduced by around 14,000. That has made a number of states/territories and regional authorities angry, with the Government struggling to reach agreement with them on their respective allocations for 2026-27.

The larger number of places for the permanent employer-sponsored visa in 2026-27 will not be enough, even to cover the current application rate, let alone reduce the backlog. Applications will continue to be high due to the very large number of people on the temporary employer-sponsored visa, which at end September 2026, was almost 280,000 and rising.

That means the permanent employer-sponsored visa backlog will keep rising through 2026-27 and most likely into 2027-28. Processing times will continue to blow out and employers will become increasingly angry.

Poor long-term planning

The situation the Government finds itself in is due to its failure to respond adequately and quickly enough to the boom in NOM in 2022-23 and 2023-24. The flow-through of that surge to pressure on the permanent program was inevitable. Despite committing to developing a long-term migration plan prior to the 2025 Election, Labor reneged on that commitment.

It has at last committed to managing NOM to a target. But that is not sufficient. Long-term migration planning requires a plan for managing both NOM and the permanent program. Labor has no such plan.

The NOM target and immigration policies announced by the Coalition will in fact exacerbate the challenges of managing the permanent migration program, as it proposes to significantly boost places in the temporary employer-sponsored visa. That will inevitably flow through to the permanent employer-sponsored visa and increase the backlog and processing times even further. While the Coalition would not intentionally make employers angry, that is what its currently announced policies would do.

One Nation’s immigration policy manifesto just ignores the permanent migration program altogether, suggesting it is oblivious to the challenges.

Dr Abul Rizvi is an Independent Australia columnist and former Deputy Secretary of the Department of Immigration. You can follow Abul on Twitter @RizviAbul or Bluesky @abulrizvi.bsky.social.

text:
ERBIL (Kurdistan24) — Afghanistan's Taliban authorities on Monday expressed serious concern over reported plans by US President Donald Trump's administration to deport more than 150 Afghan immigrants through Pakistan for eventual return to Afghanistan, warning that the move could endanger people who previously assisted US forces.

The planned deportations reportedly include relatives of Afghans who worked alongside the US military before the Taliban regained power in August 2021, according to US media reports and AfghanEvac, an organisation supporting former Afghan allies.

In a statement, Afghan Foreign Ministry spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi urged Washington to adopt a "responsible and measured approach" and coordinate with Kabul before making decisions affecting Afghan citizens.

"The Afghan side is ready to interact in this regard in a practical and mutually understanding manner," Balkhi said.

The Taliban authorities said they were concerned about Afghans who had yet to obtain legal residency documents in Pakistan and called for their rights and legitimate interests to be considered.

Washington cannot directly arrange deportations to Afghanistan because it does not maintain diplomatic relations with the Taliban government. US officials have reportedly said Pakistan would oversee the deportees' transfer across the border into Afghanistan.

Advocacy groups have warned that former US allies and their relatives could face persecution, detention or retaliation if returned.

Although the Taliban announced a general amnesty after taking power and have repeatedly promised that former government employees and Western allies could safely return, the United Nations has documented reports of extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detentions and other abuses.

Pakistan's mass deportation campaign

The planned US deportations come amid Pakistan's ongoing campaign to expel Afghan nationals without valid residency documents, a policy that has forced millions of Afghans to return home after decades of displacement and conflict.

Earlier this year, Islamabad ordered law enforcement agencies nationwide to arrest undocumented Afghan citizens as part of its repatriation policy, raising concerns among humanitarian organisations about the treatment of vulnerable families.

Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have also deteriorated significantly since the Taliban takeover in 2021. Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Taliban authorities of allowing militant groups, particularly the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), to operate from Afghan territory and launch attacks inside Pakistan. Kabul has rejected the accusations.

Tensions escalated following deadly border clashes in October 2025, bringing relations to a new low and resulting in the near-total closure of major border crossings.

The deteriorating security situation has further complicated the return of Afghan refugees, many of whom fled the country following the Taliban takeover or during earlier decades of war.

Trump's immigration crackdown

The proposed deportations are part of Trump's broader immigration crackdown, which has included travel restrictions affecting Afghanistan and efforts to end deportation protections previously granted to some Afghan nationals.

Following the Taliban's return to power in 2021, thousands of Afghans who had worked with US forces, diplomatic missions and international organisations were evacuated or sought protection abroad, fearing reprisals from the new authorities.

Some were granted special immigrant visas or other forms of protection because of their assistance to the United States during its 20-year military presence in Afghanistan.

The prospect of returning former allies and their families has prompted warnings from veterans' organisations and refugee advocacy groups, which argue that the deportations could expose individuals who supported US operations to serious danger.

The United States completed its military withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021, ending its two-decade intervention and paving the way for the Taliban to regain control of the country.

The latest dispute highlights the continuing consequences of that withdrawal, as Washington's immigration policies, Pakistan's deportation campaign and Afghanistan's human rights situation converge over the fate of Afghans who sought refuge abroad.

text:
WARREN — Terri Yendrek recalled childhood occasions in which she got into trouble after standing for what she felt was right.

The “now” is a vastly different set of circumstances for her, however, than the “then.”

“I’m here mainly to remember people harmed and killed by ICE,” Yendrek, of Brookfield, said.

Rather than facing negative trouble for standing up for her beliefs, Yendrek joined those who are part of Good Trouble Trumbull for a peaceful two-hour rally Saturday afternoon at Courthouse Square to remember and honor those who have died at the hands of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents since January 2025.

Good Trouble Trumbull takes its name from the late Georgia congressman and civil rights icon John Lewis, whose mantra was advocating for getting into good and necessary trouble, if necessary, in nonviolently fighting against injustices and for fairness and equality.

Yendrek, a counselor who has worked with people who have developmental challenges, said another motivator for her to join a few dozen who attended the gathering was to be a voice for those who are unable to advocate for themselves. In addition, she wanted to support immigrants, many of whom she said she feels continue to be demonized and dehumanized by some people who relish dividing others, and who see them as an enemy.

Saturday’s rally was among 83 such events that had been planned nationally. The local gathering also aligned with Disappeared in America, a project launched last year to document the names and stories of children, families and workers — and the overall human cost associated with them being swept up in a mass deportation policy that began last year.

According to Disappeared in America’s website, more than 605,000 people have been deported, more than 400,000 have been detained, and at least 117,400 children have been separated from their families.

In addition, Saturday’s rally was part of a national Day of the Dead, an occasion in which the living remember and connect with those who have died, Laura Liberman, a Good Trouble Trumbull organizer, noted.

In her remarks, Liberman provided a series of grim statistics, as well as an action plan to work toward counteracting the actions of many ICE agents.

“Since January 2025, ICE has shot and killed at least six people in the streets, half of whom were U.S. citizens. These people were not charged, they were not tried, they were shot,” she said. “An additional 62 people died in ICE custody, also without a trial.”

Too often, unidentified ICE agents have kidnapped unsuspecting people going to work, dropping off their children and in other circumstances, forced them into unmarked vehicles and taken them to detention centers, which is home to an estimated 65,000 people, Liberman added.

“So, we have mass incarceration of civilians kidnapped by masked agents, shipped off to places outside the legal process – concentration camps – where they disappear or die,” she said, adding, “That doesn’t secure the border; that doesn’t secure anybody. It makes us all less safe, and it has to stop.”

The six to whom Liberman alluded were Ruben Ray Martinez, 23, who was fatally shot March 15, 2025, in South Padre Island, Texas; Silverio Villegas Gonzalez, 38, who was killed Sept. 12, 2025, during a traffic stop near Chicago and left two young sons; Alex Pretti, 37, an intensive care unit nurse who was shot Jan. 24 in Minneapolis; Renee Good, 37, who was killed Jan. 7 in Minneapolis while driving away from an ICE agent; Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, a construction worker who was fatally shot July 7 in Houston while driving a work crew to a construction site; and Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, 25, a Colombian immigrant who was killed July 13 during a traffic stop in Biddeford, Maine, after an ICE agent shot at his vehicle five times.

Liberman also was among several Good Trouble Trumbull members who read aloud the names of more than 60 people who lost their lives while in ICE custody.

Also at the rally, information was available about several adults and children who died directly or indirectly from decisions ICE agents made.

They included Linda Davis, 55, who was killed Feb. 16 in Savannah, Georgia, after her vehicle was struck by a driver on a high-speed chase fleeing from ICE agents, and Mario David Coronado Juarez, 36, who died in a car crash Sept. 20 following an attempted ICE traffic stop in Grand Rapids, Michigan.

Others who were remembered were Nurul Amin Shah Alam, 56, a visually-impaired legal refugee who was found dead Feb. 24 on a Buffalo, New York, street after a Border Patrol agent left him at a coffee shop ahead of a major snowstorm without notifying his family or attorney; Orlin Hernandez Reyes, 3, who was tortured and killed March 4 after ICE left him with a violent estranged relative, and after his mother had been deported in January without due process; and Mohammad Nazeer Paktiawal, 41, whose asylum was pending from aiding the U.S. Army. He died March 14 in a Dallas hospital one day after ICE had taken him into custody.

In addition, Liberman read aloud an action plan that, in a sense, took on added urgency a few days before Tuesday’s midterm elections.

“We stay informed, we protect our community — and we vote. We vote for leaders who will get this ICE violence out of our communities, who will close the concentration camps and who will stop rewarding this un-American behavior with billions of dollars, when people can’t afford gas, groceries and healthcare,” she said, adding, “And after we elect those leaders, we write to them and call them and tell them that’s what we voted for them to do.”

Liberman also read aloud a poem she wrote, titled “People Should Never Get Shot in the Street.”

text:
WASHINGTON, United States (CMC) — The United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency says Caribbean nationals are among several foreign nationals arrested or investigated in connection with alleged voter fraud and election-related offences.

In a statement on Friday, ICE said the cases form part of a nationwide crackdown on illegal voting and include individuals who allegedly registered to vote or cast ballots unlawfully in US elections.

The agency identified nationals of Jamaica, Haiti, Cuba and the Bahamas, along with individuals from Guatemala, India, Liberia, Canada, Russia, Nicaragua, Ghana, Peru, the Philippines and Mexico.

“Secure elections protect our nation’s sovereignty and Americans’ sacred right to vote,” said ICE Public Affairs Assistant Director Micah Bock.

“We have uncovered hundreds of cases of election fraud and the extent of this problem continues to expand,” he added.

Bock said the crackdown reflects the Trump administration’s commitment to addressing what he described as immigration policies that had undermined election integrity.

Among the cases highlighted was that of Jamaican Lawrence Cole, who ICE said had previously been convicted of felony drug offences.

The agency alleged that Cole voted illegally in the 2004 and 2008 general elections, as well as the 2008 presidential primary.

ICE also identified Cuban Carlos Javier Alamo-Sorino, who is currently in custody. It said Alamo-Sorino, who was paroled into the United States during the Obama administration, had previous convictions for sexual offences, robbery, larceny and harassment.

According to ICE, he admitted to voting illegally in an election.

Haitian Cliff Medgy Sanon was also named. ICE said Sanon, who has a conviction for receiving stolen property and is subject to a final removal order, voted in the 2022 election.

In another case, the agency alleged that Anthony Tyrone Higgs, a lawful permanent resident originally from The Bahamas, voted illegally in a 2020 election.

ICE said Higgs has previous convictions for armed robbery, grand larceny, domestic violence, assault and resisting arrest.

The agency said the cases represent only a portion of its ongoing investigations and arrests involving alleged election-related offences.

It added that federal authorities would continue pursuing voter fraud investigations as part of efforts to safeguard the integrity of US elections.

Afghanistan's Taliban authorities voiced concern on Monday over reported plans by Washington to deport scores of Afghan immigrants to Pakistan with the aim of their eventual return to their home country.

More than 150 Afghans in the United States would be deported via Pakistan to Afghanistan, including relatives of those who assisted US forces before their 2021 withdrawal, according to US media reports and an advocacy group.

Read more'Suffocating restrictions' shadow five years of Taliban rule in Afghanistan

"The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan expresses its serious concern over reports that the United States intends to deport some Afghan refugees to Pakistan who have not yet been able to obtain legal residency documents in that country," foreign ministry spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi said in a statement.

Advocacy groups have warned that the removal of former allies and their families could endanger their lives.

After regaining power, Taliban authorities announced a general amnesty for Afghans who worked with Western-backed forces and governments and have repeated promises this year that their former foes could safely return home.

However, the United Nations has recorded reports of extrajudicial killings, detentions and abuses.

President Donald Trump's administration last year issued travel bans for a number of countries, including Afghanistan, as part of a broad immigration crackdown.

Watch moreTrump admin's hardline deportation policy an 'attempt to break the global refugee and asylum system'

His administration sort to sought to end deportation protections for Afghans, some of whom were granted special immigrant visas following the 2021 takeover by Taliban authorities.

Among those expected to be deported are relatives of Afghans who assisted the US military in the country prior to the fall of Kabul, according to AfghanEvac, a group seeking to help former Afghan allies.

While the United States cannot arrange deportations directly to Afghanistan, anonymous US officials told The New York Times that Pakistan will oversee their expulsion to Afghanistan.

In recent years, Germany and Turkey have deported Afghan nationals directly to Afghanistan, despite concerns from human rights groups over the risks facing returnees.

Read moreGermany deports Afghan nationals for first time since Taliban takeover

Balkhi said Taliban authorities urged "the United States of America to adopt a responsible and measured approach in this regard and to take any decisions and measures regarding the fate of Afghan citizens with clear mutual understanding, necessary coordination, and consideration of the rights and legitimate demands of the individuals concerned".

"The Afghan side is ready to interact in this regard in a practical and mutually understanding manner," he added.

Read moreMapped: Inside the Trump administration's secret deals to deport people to third countries

Pakistan's government earlier this year ordered law enforcement nationwide to arrest Afghan citizens without visas as part of a years-long repatriation policy that has pushed back millions of Afghans who fled throughout decades of war.

Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been fraught since the Taliban authorities took power and worsened after deadly border clashes last October that led to near-total closure of the border.

title: WFYI: ICE detainees sue over alleged abuse, conditions at Indiana prison
description:
Immigration detainees held at Indiana’s Miami Correctional Facility are suing state and federal agencies for what they say are inhumane and unconstitutional conditions.
The lawsuit covers the three named plaintiffs and all other detainees at the correctional facility north of Kokomo.
Officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE and Indiana Department of Correction are listed as plaintiffs.
‘Further litigation forthcoming’ Hickey said she hopes this lawsuit forces changes but also gets answers to what has occurred at Miami Correctional Facility.
After speaking with people held at the prison he said the state needed to end its holding of ICE detainees there.
text:
By Samantha Horton

WFYI Public Media

October 30, 2026

This story was updated Oct. 31, 2026 with a response from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

Immigration detainees held at Indiana’s Miami Correctional Facility are suing state and federal agencies for what they say are inhumane and unconstitutional conditions.

The 72-page court filing details medical neglect, cells flooded with human waste, and abusive punishments detainees claim to have experienced at the maximum security prison used by the Trump administration for its immigration enforcement policies.

The lawsuit also alleges conditions at the facility violate the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment due process clauses because the detainees are civil detainees, not under criminal convictions, and are facing punitive punishments like lockdowns and solitary confinement.

The ACLU of Indiana and Illinois filed a class action lawsuit Thursday, Oct. 29, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana. The lawsuit covers the three named plaintiffs and all other detainees at the correctional facility north of Kokomo.

“Frankly, they are experiencing physical decline, potential long-term medical consequences, and, like, severe emotional distress and suffering,” said Katie Hickey, an attorney with the ACLU of Illinois representing the plaintiffs.

Officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE and Indiana Department of Correction are listed as plaintiffs.

A DHS spokesperson replied Oct. 30 to WFYI’s request for comment and said the allegations in the lawsuit are false.

“ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens,” the DHS spokesperson wrote in an email.

The spokesperson said detainees are provided three meals a day, clean water, clothing, toiletry items, phones to communicate with family and lawyers, and comprehensive medical care – physical, dental and mental healthcare. In cases of a detainee showing signs of self-harm the agency has a strict protocol including 15-minute checks while one is on suicide watch.

The lawsuit comes after continued reports from detainees, lawyers and advocates about the conditions at the prison. This summer Gov. Mike Braun called for an audit to review the private healthcare provider the state contracts to work in the facilities after reports from the IndyStar on delays in medical care for detainees.

Indiana began housing Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees at Miami Correctional in October 2025 through a two-year contract with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Miami Correctional is a maximum security facility for men.

Since detainees began to arrive, there have been two reported deaths.

In the lawsuit, plaintiff Cynthia Acevedo said healthcare providers at the facility switched her to a different seizure medication that is ineffective at preventing seizures. Even then, Acevedo, a transgender woman, does not regularly receive the medication and has multiple seizures a week. When she goes to get medical treatment, no Spanish translator is made available.

Sergei Vasenin and Kemoye Muslar, the other plaintiffs, share their experiences of slow and limited medical care and regular solitary confinement and lockdowns.

During a 10-day lockdown, Muslar said his cell flooded over with sewage for three days. He was not provided cleaning supplies or hygiene products.

The detainees also allege guards call them racial slurs, threaten death and physically beat them without any reason.

The lawsuit details a case of a recent suicide attempt by a detainee. It alleges, staff were notified of concerns for the man’s mental health. It goes on to say that guards locked him alone in his cell where he went on to use a cable and hang himself according to witnesses. The lawsuit says the condition and whereabouts of the detainee remain unconfirmed.

The DHS spokesperson confirmed to WFYI an Iraqi detainee is at Parkview Hospital in Fort Wayne. This individual is the one the lawsuit detailed attempted to take his life while being held at Miami Correctional.

The plaintiffs are asking for the court to declare the facility’s medical and mental health care and conditions inadequate and in violation of the the Fifth Amendment and Fourteenth Amendment due process clause.

‘Further litigation forthcoming’

Hickey said she hopes this lawsuit forces changes but also gets answers to what has occurred at Miami Correctional Facility.

“The people who have died, the recent suicide attempt. There’s been no transparency from the government about all of that, so we hope that we can learn a lot more about all of these things in Miami over the next; over the coming months,” Hickey said.

For more than a year religious leaders have gathered monthly at or near the prison to pray for the detainees being held there and their families. André Carson visited Miami Correctional in April demanding answers to the deaths in the facility. After speaking with people held at the prison he said the state needed to end its holding of ICE detainees there.

Other groups including the Indiana Organizing Project have held events across the state calling on the governor to end the contract with ICE or at least not renew it.

Indiana Organizing Project Executive Director Stuart Mora said nothing in the lawsuit surprised him and it comes as conditions fail to improve.

“I think that there will be further litigation forthcoming,” said Mora. “Our team has not seen significant changes in Miami Correctional, since the governor called for an investigation several months ago.”

The ACLU was joined by the National Immigrant Justice Center, Macarthur Justice Center and law firm Dunn Issaacson Rhee in filing the lawsuit on behalf of the detainees.

description:

But advocates say the state is now limiting the types of documents certain noncitizens can use to qualify for a temporary driver's license.
That leaves some people who have held Tennessee driver's licenses for years, or even decades, suddenly being denied when they attempt to renew.

text:
Immigration advocates are suing the state of Tennessee, arguing a new policy is unfairly preventing some non-U.S. citizens who are here legally, from obtaining temporary driver's licenses.

The lawsuit challenges changes made by the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security that advocates say could leave thousands of immigrants unable to drive — despite having federal permission to be in the United States.

Under the previous policy, Tennessee accepted work permits and other federal documents as proof of legal authorization to remain in the country.

But advocates say the state is now limiting the types of documents certain noncitizens can use to qualify for a temporary driver's license.

Under the new requirements, applicants must present a valid visa, an I-94, an I-94W or a temporary green card.

That leaves some people who have held Tennessee driver's licenses for years, or even decades, suddenly being denied when they attempt to renew.

RELATED COVERAGE | ICE: Man arrested outside Nashville airport known or suspected Tren de Aragua gang member

"Under its new rule, TDOS will only issue driver's licenses to certain non-citizens who present a valid visa, an I-94 or an I-94W or somebody with a temporary green card," said Jazmin Ramirez, advocacy director for the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition.

"As a result, people who have held a driver's license for years or even decades are now being turned away and denied renewals for the first time."

The Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition filed the lawsuit, arguing the policy excludes people who have federal authorization to live and work in the United States.

Immigration attorney Kathleen Martinez says the state is effectively treating people with work permits as if they do not have authorized immigration status.

"They're treating everyone with a work permit as if they are not here with authorized stay," Martinez said in a post on social media.

DACA recipients among those affected

During a virtual news conference, advocates described how the changes are affecting immigrants who depend on their ability to drive to work, take their children to school and handle everyday responsibilities.

DACA recipients are among those potentially impacted. Many have federal work authorization but are not issued the specific immigration documents Tennessee now requires.

One person who spoke during the news conference, but asked to remain anonymous, described how losing their license has affected their job.

"Currently, I am employed at a Level 1 trauma center but cannot show up to work because I am without a license and live an hour away," the person said.

Advocates say the consequences could extend to thousands of people who previously qualified for temporary licenses but no longer meet the state's revised documentation requirements.

Lawsuit questions state's authority to make changes

The lawsuit argues Tennessee officials implemented the new restrictions without following the proper legal procedures.

Attorneys contend the Department of Safety and Homeland Security overstepped its authority by changing which federal documents are accepted and failed to give the public an opportunity to weigh in before the policy took effect.

The legal challenge comes after Tennessee passed sweeping immigration legislation that went into effect this year.

State officials have reportedly interpreted the new law as allowing the department to impose stricter requirements for temporary driver's licenses.

However, advocates argue the state cannot use the legislation to deny licenses to people who have otherwise been authorized to live and work in the country under federal law.

The lawsuit asks the court to intervene and challenge the state's new licensing requirements.

WZTV reached out to the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security for comment.

The department responded that it does not comment on ongoing litigation.

text:
President Donald Trump's administration is planning to deport Afghans detained in the U.S. back to their home country via Pakistan, according to court documents obtained by The Associated Press — a move advocacy groups say could put their lives at risk.

Immigrant rights organizations say those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban. Thousands fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.

“This is absolutely unconscionable," said Shawn VanDiver, a U.S. Navy veteran and president of the advocacy group #AfghanEvac. “It seems like there’s no end to their willingness to break the law and violate people’s human rights.”

The U.S. intends to initially deport Afghan immigrants as early as Monday on flights from Louisiana, where the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan, according to court documents.

The plan to deport Afghans to Pakistan was first reported by Bloomberg on Monday. On Friday, The New York Times reported that the immigrants were going to be sent to Afghanistan after arriving in Pakistan.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in an email to the AP on Saturday that ICE does not comment on future immigrant-removal operations, citing operational security and personnel safety. Officials at the Pakistani Embassy in Washington did not immediately return email messages.

Afghans caught up in Trump's immigration crackdown

U.S. officials confirmed the Afghan deportations in sealed court documents obtained by the AP.

In a document filed in federal court in Virginia on Friday, a senior ICE official acknowledged that an Afghan immigrant had been scheduled to be on an upcoming charter flight from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan, “with further transport onward to Afghanistan.” The document was filed in the case of an immigrant who is not in custody and is challenging efforts to deport him.

In another federal court case in Oklahoma, federal prosecutors filed a document on Monday disclosing that another Afghan immigrant was scheduled to be deported to Afghanistan sometime next week.

The Trump administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. It has done this in some instances when it is unable to send them to their own countries because the US does not have formal relations, like with the Taliban government in Afghanistan. In other instances, it has been used as a deterrent.

In many cases, a U.S. immigration judge has determined their lives would be in jeopardy if sent to their home countries. It was not immediately clear if any designated for return to Afghanistan have protective orders against being sent there.

Immigrant groups and Democrats decry deportation plan

Human Rights First, an advocacy group for refugees and asylum seekers that tracks U.S. deportation flights, said Saturday that it had confirmed a scheduled flight from Louisiana to Pakistan on Tuesday carrying Afghan immigrants.

“It is beyond egregious that this administration plans to carry out an unprecedented mass deportation flight of Afghans, forcibly sending them through Pakistan and into the hands of the Taliban,” Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said in an email to the AP.

“This follows previous unconscionable deportation flights we have tracked under this administration, including Iranian Christian converts and political dissidents removed via Qatar and Kuwait to Iran, as well as a Russian political dissident removed via Egypt to Russia,” Arvey said.

Some Democratic members of Congress took to social media to criticize the Afghan deportations after seeing the Times story on Friday.

“It is reprehensible that the Trump Administration plans to deport hundreds of Afghans, including women, children and those who supported U.S. forces, to Pakistan — who then risk being sent back into the hands of the Taliban. Congress must stand against this," Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire posted on X.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut added in his own X post, “We made a promise to our Afghan allies — that after aiding & protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them. This Administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture & death.”

Thousands fled war and persecution in Afghanistan

In September, Trump's administration finalized a last-minute reprieve to avoid the closure of a camp in Qatar that houses more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted America’s war effort or are the relatives of U.S. service members. The administration extended for nine months the life of Camp As Sayliyah, which had been due to close Sept. 30 at the end of the U.S. budget year.

Upon entering his second term, Trump, a Republican, paused his Democratic predecessor’s Afghan resettlement program as part of a series of executive orders cracking down on immigration, including dramatically altering refugee admissions to focus on white South Africans.

text:
A federal court has put the brakes on indiscriminate enforcement actions by federal immigration authorities in Southern California based on race and appearance. Specifically, the court ordered that residents must not be stopped or detained solely because they are Latino, low-income, or part of the working class.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California issued a preliminary injunction on the 23rd in the lawsuit ‘Vasquez Perdomo v. Mullin,’ prohibiting racially discriminatory immigration enforcement by the Trump administration.

This order applies to seven counties, including Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino, Ventura, Santa Barbara, and San Luis Obispo.

The court ruled that for immigration enforcement agents to stop or detain a resident, there must be specific grounds supporting reasonable suspicion. It stated that individuals cannot be targeted simply because they appear Latino, low-income, or belong to the working class.

The court also specified that evaluating the legitimacy of enforcement actions requires a comprehensive consideration of the circumstances and context at the time. However, enforcement actions conducted at border-adjacent locations such as border crossing checkpoints are excluded from this order.

The court partially certified a class action lawsuit filed by residents who suffered damages from such enforcement practices.

This lawsuit originated from allegations that federal immigration authorities indiscriminately stopped and detained residents based on race and occupation during large-scale operations in the Los Angeles area starting in June of last year.

Plaintiffs argued that immigration enforcement agents violated constitutional rights by detaining Latino workers at car washes, streets, and farms without reasonable suspicion.

Mohammad Tajsar, an immigrant rights attorney at the ACLU of Southern California, stated that federal agents conducted widespread racially discriminatory enforcement against Southern California Latino residents, adding that they will closely monitor whether the court order is properly implemented.

Flor Melendrez, executive director of CLEAN, a car wash worker advocacy group that participated in the lawsuit, pointed out that agents appeared at car washes without warrants and took workers away, emphasizing that the law requires more than mere prejudice or guesswork.

Carl Bergquist, legal counsel for the immigrant rights organization CHIRLA, urged strict compliance, stating that the order clarifies that unconstitutional enforcement must stop immediately.

However, this order does not completely ban immigration enforcement itself. It restricts indiscriminate crackdowns based solely on race or occupation, while enforcement based on reasonable suspicion remains permitted.

text:
After more than four years in the U.S., a Beaumont resident was detained and deported by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, leaving his fiancée and two young daughters without him.

Fabian Camilo Medina Rodriguez said he entered the U.S. from Colombia in February 2022, was detained by Border Patrol, applied for asylum and went to Houston two days later.

RELATED: Local counties join ICE program under new Texas law

Medina Rodriguez met his fiancée, Danielle Bienvenu, while living in the U.S. Bienvenu receives Social Security disability benefits because of several disabilities, including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Her 3-year-old daughter has autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and the couple also has a 1-year-old daughter

After entering the U.S., Medina Rodriguez was enrolled in an ICE alternatives-to-detention program. ICE said he violated the program's requirements at least 14 times over two years, including by failing to keep his monitor charged, leaving his assigned area without notice and failing to answer or return calls from compliance officers. The agency said he was terminated from the program twice, including an initial termination on Nov. 17, 2022, before he was allowed to reenter.

Medina Rodriguez disputed that account, saying he remained in the program. He said he followed the requirements, attended immigration appointments and submitted weekly photos through an app. ICE said an immigration judge ordered him deported on Oct. 1, 2024. Medina Rodriguez said his lawyer appealed the order and that officials later told him at an appointment, “You have a pending petition,” and instructed him to keep sending weekly photos.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

While living in the U.S., Medina Rodriguez worked in construction. On July 31, 2026, he went to a monthly immigration appointment in Houston. He said four ICE agents arrested him as he was leaving, forcibly took his phone and did not allow him to call Bienvenu or arrange for someone to retrieve his vehicle. Bienvenu learned he was in custody through a text from a woman whose husband had also been arrested that day. Medina Rodriguez said he was held for five hours before he could call Bienvenu and that he received no answer when he asked whether ICE had a legal order to hold him.

Kept telling him" is conversational and slightly editorialized; the simpler construction is more neutral. Medina Rodriguez said he believed a judge's review of his lawyer's documents and his family's circumstances could have helped his case. He said he believed his due process rights had been violated. Bienvenu said she and Medina Rodriguez's attorney had visited him, but he was told they had not.

“[Immigration] literally told him, ‘No one has come for you. No one has reached out for you. No one has done any of this,’” Bienvenu said. “They want them to lose their will to stay. Texas is his home. He has a family here, and we were trying to get him out, and they're lying to him, telling him other things.”

RELATED: Port Arthur ESL program boosts English skills for new students

Medina Rodriguez said the first detention center had 12 beds and that some elderly detainees did not receive adequate care. He also said detainees were told they would have to pay $250 for clothing.

“They do not let you go out; you do not see the sun,” he said.

Medina Rodriguez said he was later moved to cells in a prison, where he said guards were aggressive, detainees had trouble obtaining medicine and ICE staff visited twice a week. He said he has no criminal record in the U.S. or Colombia. Medina Rodriguez said he was taken to Louisiana and deported by plane to Bogotá, Colombia, on Aug. 21. He said he had chains on his hands and feet and a metal chain around his neck and waist during the flight. He described the experience as being “chained like slaves.”

text:
A federal judge in the United States ordered immigration agents to stop making arrests based solely on Latin appearance or racial stereotypes, in a decision that sets new boundaries for the operations of federal immigration agents, including those from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in seven counties in Southern California.

Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong ruled that agents must have reasonable and individualized suspicion before detaining a person for immigration reasons, rather than relying solely on their physical appearance or their apparent status as a low-income worker.

The decision, signed on October 23 and made public on Thursday the 29th, responds to a lawsuit alleging racial profiling during immigration operations under the administration of Donald Trump.

According to the original court ruling, consisting of 84 pages, having a Latino appearance, even when combined with the perception of belonging to the working class, does not in itself provide sufficient legal justification to detain someone.

Recordings and messages from agents reveal discriminatory practices

The judge based her decision on numerous pieces of evidence, including recordings from body cameras, internal communications, and testimonies regarding the detention of Latin individuals, including U.S. citizens.

According to , some messages included racial slurs against migrants, while other testimonies described operations in which agents detained Latino workers without intervening against white individuals present at the same locations.

The judge noted that the evidence suggested an unwritten but officially supported practice of detaining individuals based on their appearance as Latin or working-class Latin individuals.

He also questioned the government’s defense of its training programs while the documented actions of the agents showed possible violations of constitutional rights.

Where is the prohibition applied?

The measure includes Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino, Ventura, Santa Barbara, and San Luis Obispo, the seven counties that make up the Central District of California.

However, the order does not prohibit all immigration arrests nor does it apply across the entire United States.

Agents may continue to make arrests when there are individualized legal grounds. The resolution also includes exceptions for entry ports, border checkpoints, and other locations considered equivalent to the border.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), one of the organizations that initiated the lawsuit, celebrated the decision and announced that it will monitor its compliance.

Trump's administration rejects the accusations and appeals

The Trump administration denied that its agents maintained a policy of racial profiling and appealed the decision to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.

Government attorneys also questioned the interpretation of the evidence presented by the plaintiffs, as reported by El País.

The controversy has an important precedent: in September 2025, the Supreme Court suspended a previous order from the same judge that restricted immigration arrests based on certain factors, such as ethnic appearance and language.

However, the new resolution incorporates evidence obtained later during the judicial process.

Frimpong clarified that this is a preliminary measure, not a final ruling on the existence of an illegal government policy.

text:
Federal immigration authorities asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday to hear the case of a Mexican national whom agents arrested last year in Racine. The petition is the latest escalation in a legal fight over the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants facing deportation.

The justices’ decision will determine whether tens of thousands of immigrants currently in federal detention can seek release on bond.

“The question of mandatory detention thus boils down to one question: Can we lock up noncitizens without giving them a day in court first?” said Jenifer Bizzotto, the Wisconsin attorney representing Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, the man at the center of the case. “The stakes could hardly be higher.”

Arrested as ‘collateral’

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents turned up at then-24-year-old Cirrus Rojas’ apartment in June 2025 in search of a prior tenant. They instead arrested Cirrus Rojas, who entered the U.S. in 2018 without a visa, as “collateral.” Wisconsin court records show no criminal convictions under his name.

He spent most of the next nine months in custody at the Dodge County Detention Center in Juneau, entangled in a new White House policy barring ICE detainees from posting bond — a departure from decades of precedent.

The 1996 Immigration Reform Act requires immigration authorities to detain — without bond — anyone found crossing the U.S. border without authorization. Prior administrations applied that rule narrowly, allowing many immigrants arrested in the country’s interior to seek a bond hearing in immigration court.

The Trump administration bucked that approach in July 2025, when ICE Director Todd Lyons issued a new legal interpretation requiring detention without bond regardless of where immigrants are arrested.

The Board of Immigration Appeals, a panel of judges who set the rules for the federal immigration court system, later signed off on the interpretation.

With bond off the table, tens of thousands of immigrants in ICE custody turned to a backup option: filing habeas corpus petitions in federal district courts to challenge their detention.

Unlike immigration courts, which are part of the U.S. Department of Justice, federal district courts belong to the judicial branch and, therefore, are technically independent of the White House. When a federal district court grants a habeas petition, it generally orders an immigration court judge to hold a bond hearing.

Wisconsin’s Western and Eastern District courts have received more than 100 habeas petitions over the past year.

A federal appeals court split

The 7th Circuit ruled 2-1 in Cirrus Rojas’ favor in July, joining appellate courts based in New York, Cincinnati, Denver, Atlanta and San Francisco in rejecting the policy.“If Congress had indeed demanded — but not funded — no-bond detention for all unlawful entrants, that may well have thrown the nation’s immigration system into chaos,” Judge Joshua Kolar, whom Joe Biden appointed to the court, wrote in the court’s majority opinion. “Immigration authorities might have found themselves quickly overwhelmed by a colossal unfunded mandate to arrest and detain millions.” Judge Diane Sykes, a George W. Bush appointee, dissented alone.

“At this point, only the Supreme Court can bring uniformity and settle this question once and for all,” she wrote. “I anticipate that it will do so soon.”

Cirrus Rojas left custody earlier this year after a federal district court judge in California vacated the mandatory detention rule. The San Francisco-based 9th Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that decision less than a month later.

The 7th Circuit allowed his case to move forward because federal authorities plan to re-detain him.

Supreme Court could have final say

“Nothing, absent our intervention, stops the government from making good on its promise,” Kolar wrote.The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, is now asking the Supreme Court to step in.

The court agreed to take up another mandatory detention dispute earlier this month. That case involves a Brazilian national arrested during a traffic stop in Massachusetts last September.

DHS asked the justices to hold Cirrus Rojas’ case until they decide the Massachusetts case.

In Bizzotto’s view, both cases “offer the Supreme Court the opportunity to affirm that the Constitution means what it says.”

A ruling against the mandatory detention policy would open the door for thousands of ICE detainees — at least those within circuits that side with the Trump administration — to request bond hearings in immigration court. It would not require immigration court judges to grant their bond requests.

The Supreme Court also quietly declined this week to revive a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration court judges to pause deportation proceedings for immigrants seeking humanitarian visas or other forms of legal status.

title: Is Donald Trump Preparing to Rule Without Congress – and Could America Be Heading ...
description:
What followed was one of the darkest episodes in modern American political history.
Many participants in the attack were subsequently prosecuted and imprisoned, although President Trump later issued sweeping pardons and commutations for January 6th defendants.
It can develop through a succession of apparently technical decisions that gradually weaken the institutions responsible for restraining executive power.
The fact that it happened once should make Americans particularly alert to the possibility of another confrontation between presidential ambition and constitutional authority.
The question facing America is no longer simply whether Donald Trump can govern without Congress.
text:
1.7K

There is a question that should be troubling every American who cares about the future of their democracy: what happens if Donald Trump decides that Congress is no longer an obstacle he needs to respect?

A Reuters investigation published on November 1st, 2026, raises precisely that concern. According to the report, the White House has spent months preparing ways to continue implementing Trump’s political agenda through executive authority should Democrats win control of Congress in the midterm elections. Senior figures, including presidential adviser Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, are reportedly examining how presidential powers could be used to circumvent congressional opposition.

The areas under consideration reportedly include immigration, tariffs, housing and federal spending. The administration is also preparing for the prospect of congressional investigations into its activities, including possible claims of executive privilege to resist demands for information.

On one level, this is politics as usual. Every American president wants to advance his programme, and executive orders have long been used by administrations of both parties when Congress proves unwilling or unable to cooperate.

But there is a more disturbing dimension to this development. When does a president’s determination to bypass political opposition become an attempt to undermine the constitutional system itself?

And, more importantly, is Donald Trump contemplating something considerably more ambitious than simply governing without Congress?

The lessons of January 6th

Americans have already witnessed what can happen when Trump’s political ambitions collide with the constitutional machinery of government.

On January 6th, 2021, following his defeat by Joe Biden in the presidential election, thousands of Trump supporters descended on Washington. After a rally at which Trump repeated allegations that the election had been stolen, his supporters marched towards the Capitol.

What followed was one of the darkest episodes in modern American political history. The Capitol was breached. Members of Congress were forced to flee or seek shelter. The certification of the presidential election was interrupted as police officers fought to contain the violence.

The objective of the congressional proceedings was straightforward: formally certify Biden’s victory. Yet the process was disrupted by a mob acting in the name of a president who refused to accept his electoral defeat.

The subsequent congressional investigation documented Trump’s pressure on elected officials, his promotion of false election claims and his failure to act promptly to stop the violence. Many participants in the attack were subsequently prosecuted and imprisoned, although President Trump later issued sweeping pardons and commutations for January 6th defendants.

The significance of January 6th extends beyond the violence itself. It demonstrated that the peaceful transfer of power, a principle that had survived America’s civil war and numerous political crises, could be placed under extraordinary pressure by a sitting president. That history cannot simply be dismissed as an unfortunate episode from Trump’s first presidency.

Governing without Congress: a constitutional grey area?

The Reuters revelations raise legitimate questions about the boundaries of presidential authority.

The American Constitution deliberately divides power between the executive, legislative and judicial branches. Congress has the authority to enact legislation, approve federal spending, conduct investigations and exercise oversight over the executive. The president, meanwhile, is responsible for executing the laws passed by Congress. These are not administrative inconveniences. They are fundamental safeguards against the concentration of political power.

Trump’s apparent willingness to explore the limits of unilateral executive action suggests an administration preparing for confrontation with the legislature rather than compromise.

There is nothing inherently unconstitutional about a president using lawful executive authority. However, an administration cannot simply disregard legislation, appropriate money without legal authority or assume that presidential directives automatically override congressional statutes.

The courts remain an essential check on executive power, but what happens if the White House repeatedly tests those boundaries, challenges adverse judicial decisions and treats congressional oversight as illegitimate?

A constitutional crisis does not necessarily begin with tanks outside parliament or soldiers occupying government buildings. It can develop through a succession of apparently technical decisions that gradually weaken the institutions responsible for restraining executive power.

Is Trump planning to hold on to power?

There is an even bigger question. Trump is serving his second presidential term. The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution prohibits anyone from being elected president more than twice. His current term is therefore scheduled to end at noon on January 20th, 2029.

Could he nevertheless attempt to remain in power? There is currently no evidence in the Reuters report establishing that Trump is preparing a coup, planning to cancel elections or intending to refuse to leave office when his constitutional term expires.

It would be irresponsible to present such a conclusion as an established fact. Nevertheless, the possibility deserves scrutiny, particularly given the events of 2021.

Would Trump accept an electoral defeat for his party as a legitimate expression of the American electorate’s wishes? Would he accept a Democratic-controlled Congress investigating his administration? And, looking further ahead, would he accept the constitutional requirement to surrender the presidency in January 2029?

These are questions that should be answered through actions rather than assurances.

The distinction between governing aggressively and undermining democracy is an important one. But it is also a distinction that can become blurred when the executive repeatedly seeks to expand its authority at the expense of other constitutional institutions.

The danger of normalising the extraordinary

One of the greatest dangers facing American democracy is that extraordinary political behaviour can gradually become normalised.

If a president repeatedly challenges the authority of Congress, attacks judges who rule against him, dismisses independent institutions as politically motivated and portrays opponents as enemies of the state, the cumulative effect can be profoundly damaging.

The concern is not simply that Trump might issue more executive orders. It is whether the political culture surrounding his presidency is becoming increasingly intolerant of constitutional restraints.

There is also a distinction between winning an election and acquiring unlimited authority. Even a president with a substantial electoral mandate remains subject to the Constitution. The American system was designed precisely to prevent an individual from exercising unchecked power.

The midterm elections will therefore represent an important test of the relationship between the White House and Congress. A Democratic victory would not deprive Trump of his presidential powers, but it would restore an important mechanism of legislative scrutiny.

And that scrutiny is precisely what the constitutional system is supposed to provide.

America must not wait for another January 6th

Perhaps the most disturbing aspect of the present situation is that America has already experienced a serious attempt to disrupt the democratic transfer of power. January 6th was not an abstract constitutional debate. It was a physical assault on the institution responsible for certifying the outcome of a presidential election.

The fact that it happened once should make Americans particularly alert to the possibility of another confrontation between presidential ambition and constitutional authority.

It would be premature to declare that Trump is planning a coup. The Reuters investigation does not establish that. Governing through executive powers, even aggressively, is not in itself a coup. However, it would be equally complacent to dismiss every warning sign as merely another example of Trump’s unconventional political style.

The fundamental question is whether the president recognises that his authority is temporary, limited and ultimately subordinate to the Constitution.

A president who seeks to govern without congressional cooperation is exercising political power. A president who seeks to govern without constitutional constraints is attempting something altogether different.

A president who refuses to surrender power when his term expires would cross a line that no American president has the right to cross. America’s founding fathers understood the dangers of concentrated executive authority. They created a system of checks and balances because they understood that democracy depends not simply on who wins power, but on whether those who win are prepared to relinquish it.

The question facing America is no longer simply whether Donald Trump can govern without Congress. It is whether America’s institutions, its courts, its elected representatives and ultimately its citizens will be prepared to defend the Constitution if the president attempts to place himself above it.
