title: US attorneys are freeing children from Trump's 'deportation machine' with a new strategy
description:
Organizers of the new movement as well as pro-immigration advocates accuse the government of unconstitutional conduct and plain cruelty, keeping families apart and rushing small children into court without lawyers – to feed Donald Trump’s “deportation machine”.
Researchers estimate nearly all these cases end with a child’s release from federal custody.
As of September, more than 1,800 unaccompanied children have spent six months on average in federal custody, compared with an average of 44 days between 2015 and 2024.
They are swiftly filing habeas petitions to get as many children as possible released to loved ones before it’s too late and the administration bundles them onto deportation flights.
Amid these obstacles to family reunification and fair proceedings, habeas petitions have become a saving grace.
text:
Migrant children stranded alone in prolonged Trump administration custody and targeted by whole-of-government efforts to deport them are starting to win release while they fight their cases – with a fresh legal strategy, the Guardian has found.

A growing army of attorneys across the US is racing around the clock like legal first responders to file petitions of habeas corpus in federal courts demanding freedom for their young clients.

Organizers of the new movement as well as pro-immigration advocates accuse the government of unconstitutional conduct and plain cruelty, keeping families apart and rushing small children into court without lawyers – to feed Donald Trump’s “deportation machine”.

Now they are hitting back with a rare habeas tactic and it is proving surprisingly successful amid the US president’s harsh crackdown that has swept up thousands of minors, according to leaders of the advocacy movement the Guardian first revealed in September.

Researchers estimate nearly all these cases end with a child’s release from federal custody. Some don’t even get as far as a court hearing before the administration backs down and lets the child go, likely in order to avoid having to explain their policy decisions to a judge.

Since Trump retook the White House, officials have taken to keeping children who crossed the US-Mexico border unaccompanied in prolonged custody instead of allowing them to be with relatives or other vetted sponsors stateside while their legal case plays out.

Immigration enforcement activity is also “creating” new unaccompanied children, after sweeping up migrant kids in the country’s interior and separating them from their caregivers.

As of September, more than 1,800 unaccompanied children have spent six months on average in federal custody, compared with an average of 44 days between 2015 and 2024.

“The government is violating the law, and the regulations, and their own policy sometimes in this area,” said Marie Silver, supervising attorney at the Immigration and Human Rights Clinic at Loyola University Chicago School of Law, which is co-managing the new initiative, called the Children’s Due Process Project.

But, Silver continued, “I think the core of what the judges are picking up on and really sort of incensed about is just the true, underlying constitutional problems here when we keep children from their family members for no reason.”

Leading advocates are countering by rallying an expanding band of lawyers, drawn from around a hundred legal organizations, law firms and solo practitioners across the US, who are representing children free of charge. They are swiftly filing habeas petitions to get as many children as possible released to loved ones before it’s too late and the administration bundles them onto deportation flights.

Habeas corpus petitions challenging unlawful imprisonment have become a staple for the many thousands of adults held within the US immigration detention system, the world’s largest. More than 91,000 such petitions have been filed since January 2025, according to a tracker run by ProPublica. Yet until recently, they were far less common for lone migrant children, who historically have been released to family members quickly after arriving in the US and entering federal custody.

In a report published this fall, the Washington DC-based Acacia Center for Justice identified just 33 total habeas petitions filed on behalf of these children before last year, most of them during Trump’s first term. They then tracked “a 3,500% increase in habeas filings” since January 2025, compared with the four years of the Biden administration.

Researchers found at least 72 habeas petitions involving unaccompanied children in government custody across 16 federal district court jurisdictions since the start of the second Trump administration. And, in cases where the outcome was clear, 98% ended with the child released.

“This is the most immediate way to help the kids who are currently being harmed,” said Becky Wolozin, senior attorney at the California-based National Center for Youth Law (NCYL), a co-manager of the Children’s Due Process Project.

Other co-managers include Acacia and The Door, a New York-based comprehensive youth development organization. Through the effort, these organizations are training attorneys and connecting them with young clients who desperately need help with the habeas process.

“Part of what we’re hoping with this project is essentially to build a bench of people who are ready, able and excited to bring these cases, so that more kids have access to this type of vital representation,” Wolozin said.

Children arriving in the US unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian fall under the care of the office of refugee resettlement (ORR), an agency that is part of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and that has typically filled a child welfare role.

US statute and regulations explicitly require that these kids be “promptly placed in the least restrictive setting that is in the best interest of the child”. And so authorities – until recently – put them in congregate shelters, foster care or secure facilities for as little time as possible while vetting prospective “sponsors” – oftentimes parents already in the US – who applied to take care of them after release.

Many of these children have survived abuse, neglect, trafficking, abandonment or other serious harms in their countries of origin or on the way to the US – tragedies that in turn may open the door for them to seek legal immigration pathways stateside.

But now, officials across executive agencies are coordinating efforts to make it much harder for children to receive legal protections before they are ordered deported, including by ending a federal contract that had funded attorneys for over 20,000 of them and plotting to have HHS attorneys represent them instead.

“The immigration judge works for the Trump administration. So does the prosecutor. Under your plan, so would the child’s lawyer. That is unacceptable,” Democratic senators recently wrote in a letter to Robert F Kennedy Jr, the HHS secretary.

In practice the lack of legal representation manifests in cases such as that of a 12-year-old girl from a shelter appearing without a lawyer in the Santa Ana, California immigration court and receiving just one week to find counsel. When children like her are forced to return to court the following week, the chances are that judges will declare them “removable” and order their deportation, said Lindsay Toczylowski, CEO and co-founder of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center.

“She will join so many other children who have no fighting chance in these immigration courts, because this is what a deportation machine looks like – children alone, sitting on the other side of a computer screen, given impossible deadlines, handed useless lists of organizations that have been defunded and rushed toward life-altering orders they cannot understand,” Toczylowski said.

Among such examples are two siblings seeking asylum, ages nine and 13, who spent about six months in government custody and endured significant mental and emotional harms because of their separation from family. Officials knew within days of their arrival that the children’s mother was living in the US, ready to welcome them. Within a month, she had already gone through full federal security vetting protocols without raising any flags, said Matthew Johnson, citywide deputy director of immigrant justice at Legal Services NYC, in New York.

She moved to a more spacious apartment, checked out local schools and built bunk beds for her kids. “Still, her second bedroom sits empty,” the habeas petition his organization filed said, months into the children’s arrival. Weeks of delays piled up, including a technical glitch with a government portal and a government employee ghosting the mother.

“If this was a parking ticket, you would be really frustrated. If it’s your children, it’s inexcusable,” Johnson said. The government even suggested the siblings might pose a safety threat if released, despite there being “no conceivable basis to conclude that these nine- and 13-year-old children were dangerous”, Johnson said. By filing a petition of habeas corpus in federal court, attorneys effectively challenged the administration to justify the siblings’ prolonged time in transitional foster care, roughly 200 miles from their mother.

Just hours before a hearing in August where an official would have had to defend the government’s decision, the children suddenly received the green light to reunite with their parent in Rhode Island.

For their mother, “this was just a painful, and traumatic, and incomprehensible, and inexplicable saga”, Johnson said. “I think she just felt relief that this was over.”

And in another case, a teenager, identified by the initials EHCF in court filings, had lived in Massachusetts for six years before he was moved to ORR custody in Texas, where he was unable to speak to his mother on the phone for days to tell her what had happened.

After months being held against his will, first in San Antonio and then back in a different part of New England, in Connecticut, EHCF was diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, post traumatic stress disorder and attention deficit disorder, which the physician who evaluated him said was likely in part because of his “abrupt and prolonged removal from his family at the age of 15”.

Judge Vernon Oliver wrote in his decision granting the boy’s release: “The Court does not understand why E.H.C.F. is being separated from his mother.”

This is all part of what lawyers are describing as “a deportation assembly line depriving them [the children] of their rights”, where one-year-olds are defending themselves against government attorneys arguing for their removal from the US and some children are breaking down in tears during court, advocates said.

“The conclusion that I have and that other advocates have is that left to its own devices, this agency [ORR] will detain children indefinitely until they’re able to remove them. And so habeas petitions are necessary for that reason,” said Johnson His small team has accepted three referrals from the Children’s Due Process Project.

Meanwhile, Department of Justice and homeland security employees are expediting adjudications. Children’s asylum interviews have been scheduled just 24 hours in advance, sometimes to take place remotely and without notice to their attorneys, legal service organizations said in a lawsuit filed in October – also noting that immigration courts are rushing to complete children’s proceedings before the end of January at the latest. This is despite an enormous backlog of cases and widespread concerns that the fast-tracked decisions could hinder due process.

US district judge Brendan Hurson granted a temporary restraining order last week requiring the federal government to give unaccompanied children at least three weeks’ notice before an asylum interview and allow them to reschedule if needed. But that order only lasts until 13 November.

Amid these obstacles to family reunification and fair proceedings, habeas petitions have become a saving grace. And lawyers who hear about the Children’s Due Process Project are eager to sign up, advocates said.

“There’s just a huge need for the project,” said Beth Baltimore, interim managing director of The Door’s legal services center. “Kids were not getting out of custody. Family members are scared. Family members are targeted. It’s a really difficult process.”

title: 'We spend our days in silence': fear and repression in Ohio as ICE terrorizes Haitian immigrants
description:
The family went without electricity during daylight hours out of fear that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers might come knocking on her door to deport them.
“We spent our days in silence.” For months, ICE has terrorized members of Springfield’s immigrant community, speeding after vehicles down normally placid streets and causing crashes.
In September, Markwayne Mullin, the US homeland security secretary, said 380 people had been detained by ICE agents in Springfield.
But many of the ICE officers operating in Springfield at the time were moved out of state and the judicial order ran out on 18 September.
Two of those people, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were, like Moorman, monitoring the actions of Ice agents.
text:
Michaelle Louis’s feet and legs are aching. She can barely walk.

Surrounded by corn fields and the distant hum of a busy highway, the native of Haiti and dozens of other activists are 23 miles into a 45-mile march from Springfield to Ohio’s statehouse in Columbus to demand better rights for Haitian immigrants.

But the pain she’s feeling now is nothing compared to the mental anguish and fear she was subjected to last summer.

In August, she spent five days huddling with her daughter and brother in the basement of her Springfield home. The family went without electricity during daylight hours out of fear that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers might come knocking on her door to deport them.

“I closed the curtains. I didn’t want anyone to know there was people living in our house,” she recalls.

“We spent our days in silence.”

For months, ICE has terrorized members of Springfield’s immigrant community, speeding after vehicles down normally placid streets and causing crashes. Chief among those being targeted are the city’s Haitian community, who began immigrating to the struggling town of 60,000 residents eight years ago to fill hundreds of open blue-collar jobs.

But a supreme court ruling allowing the Trump administration to end temporary protected status (TPS) for more than 350,000 Haitian nationals in July meant they could no longer work legally, and within days, dozens of ICE agents descended on Springfield. In September, Markwayne Mullin, the US homeland security secretary, said 380 people had been detained by ICE agents in Springfield.

Louis grew up in Haiti’s capital city Port-au-Prince, and says she came to Springfield in 2021 having entered the country legally through the southern US border. Her 31-year-old brother was murdered by a gang in Haiti in December 2018.

“I had so many threats from the gangs. I left three months after he was killed,” she recalls.

“It was very hard for my mom and dad to lose their son.”

It’s not only Haitians who feel harassed by federal immigration agents in Springfield. When ICE began patrolling city streets in August, resident Sean Moorman set about monitoring their activities and following their vehicles around town.

But that soon drew unwanted attention from arguably the most powerful federal law enforcement agency in the country today.

In a lawsuit filed on his behalf by the American Civil Liberties Union of Ohio against seven ICE officers last month, Moorman claimed agents swerved one of their vehicles towards his, “as if to ram him”, took photos of his car and used several of their vehicles to corner Moorman in his car, “making him fear for his life”.

Agents also allegedly drove by and photographed his home while his wife was inside.

Last month, a federal judge ordered ICE to stop “retaliatory action” against Moorman and granted a temporary restraining order against seven of its agents, all of whom remained unnamed.

But many of the ICE officers operating in Springfield at the time were moved out of state and the judicial order ran out on 18 September.

“It is disappointing, but unfortunately not surprising, that ICE chose to play a shell game by shuffling their officers around rather than allowing them to face accountability in court for their lawless actions,” says David Carey, managing legal director at the ACLU of Ohio and Moorman’s legal representative in the case against the ICE agents.

“We certainly disagree with the court’s decision to entertain that shell game, but the fact that the court had already entered and extended a temporary restraining order against these officers also sent the most important message: ICE does not have a blank check to violate first amendment rights.”

Moorman declined an interview with the Guardian, fearing further retaliation from ICE. His lawsuit was thrown out by a federal judge on 2 October.

ICE says it “is aware of the lawsuit filed by the ACLU in Ohio and is reviewing appropriate next steps in coordination with the Department of Justice”.

“Every day, [the Department of Homeland Security] is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe,” an ICE spokesperson said.

“Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”

Around the country, ICE “watchers” such as Moorman have become essential in bringing to light the agency’s dangerous and often homicidal actions in their attempts to detain immigrants.

More than two dozen people have been shot by ICE officers, many in front of their children, since the beginning of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in February 2025. Among them are three US citizens who were shot dead in Minneapolis and Texas. Two of those people, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were, like Moorman, monitoring the actions of Ice agents.

For Louis, the false statement Trump made during his presidential election campaign in September 2024 about immigrants in Springfield eating people’s pets hurt her the most.

“That opened my eyes. Until then, all I did was go to work and come home. I wasn’t that interested in community issues. I was helping people – Americans facing domestic violence. I served the nation; I served citizens,” she says.

Millions of immigrants from dozens of countries around the world have lost their ability to work legally in the US under the Trump administration. According to the Migration Policy Institute, ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have deported 980,000 people since the beginning of Trump’s second stint in office.

“And when you say I’m eating dogs and cats and I’m coming illegally, that’s something that’s shaken me. I was sleeping and now I woke up for my community.”

Louis says the three-day march across Ohio is to raise awareness for activists’ demands to end ICE’s detention of and use of ankle monitors on immigrants, for its agents to leave Springfield and for authorities to establish a permanent residency pathway for Haitians who have contributed to life in the US.

On day two of the march, as a large Amazon warehouse where dozens of Haitians were employed before the Trump crackdown comes into view, Louis talks about a Haitian woman she knows whose husband was recently deported to Haiti, where violence and political unrest has reigned for more than a decade.

“They had bought a house here [but] now they are moving back to Haiti,” she says.

“I think this is a method by ICE – take the man and the family will follow.”

title: Trumponomics: A Midterm Report Card - Paul Krugman
description:
If the polls are any indication, many of those voters now feel betrayed: Public approval for Trump’s economic management is incredibly low.
As Trump might say, it’s like nothing anyone has ever seen before.
But exactly how bad is the Trump economy?
Today’s primer, then, will be a pre-midterm report card on Trumponomics.
Grading Trump’s performance Some readers may note that I’m not covering Trump’s oligarch-friendly tax cuts and the ballooning budget deficit.
text:
Donald Trump won in 2024 because millions of swing voters foolishly believed his economic promises, especially his promise to reverse the rise in prices that took place as the aftermath from Covid snarled global supply chains. If the polls are any indication, many of those voters now feel betrayed: Public approval for Trump’s economic management is incredibly low. As Trump might say, it’s like nothing anyone has ever seen before.

But exactly how bad is the Trump economy? That’s a slightly tricky question to answer. The current state of the U.S. economy isn’t disastrous. We have relatively low unemployment by historical standards. Inflation, while uncomfortably high, isn’t as high as it was during the supply chain shocks of 2021-2022, let alone during the stagflation of the 1970s.

True, many families are facing serious problems of affordability that aren’t fully captured by the Consumer Price Index, especially because of the exploding health care disaster.

Beyond that, Americans are surely angry because of two extreme dissonances: the stark dissonance between what Trump promised and what he has actually delivered, and the equally stark dissonance between Trump’s insistence that we’re experiencing a Golden Age and the definitely not golden financial reality of ordinary Americans’ lives. (And while I won’t discuss it here, Americans are surely angry that as their financial precarity worsens, the Trump family and its minions are raking in billions in graft: polls show that corruption has become a major political issue.)

Furthermore, while the public usually gives presidents too much credit when the economy does well and assigns them too much blame when it does badly, this time around the economy’s problems are Trump all the way. We’d be in much better shape economically if a Democrat or even a sane Republican (if such people still exist) were sitting in the White House.

Today’s primer, then, will be a pre-midterm report card on Trumponomics. I’ll start with a brief overview of the overall state of the economy, then move on to an assessment of Trump policy in four areas where Trump policies have had large effects. Beyond the paywall I will address the following:

1. How the overall economy has changed under Trump II

2. Energy policy and prices

3. Immigration and deportations

4. Tariffs

5. Health care

6. Grading Trump’s performance

Some readers may note that I’m not covering Trump’s oligarch-friendly tax cuts and the ballooning budget deficit. They’re important, but not yet having much political traction. So they’re topics for another day.

text:
New York civil rights activists are applauding a judge’s findings in California that there was “a mountain of evidence” showing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents racially profiled Latinos in the Los Angeles area, in violation of constitutional protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.

Amy Belsher, director of Immigrants Rights Litigation at the New York Civil Liberties Union, said the findings in the much-watched Central District of California case “confirms that ICE has an unconstitutional policy of stopping people based only on the color of their skin.”

She added, “We don’t live in a ‘show me your papers’ country. That’s why we have challenged that same unlawful policy on behalf of New Yorkers (in court filings) — because the Constitution protects all of us from unlawful stops and detentions.”

U.S. District Court Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong issued a temporary order, dated Oct. 23 and made public on Thursday, barring ICE and other federal officers from stopping people “just because they look Latino or because they look Latino and working class.”

Concluding plaintiffs challenging the arrest "will likely prevail" in the ongoing litigation, the judge issued a temporary order barring the government from enforcing “their policy and practice” of making enforcement stops based on racial stereotyping and which lack the required “individualized, particularized assessment,” based on reasonable suspicion, that the people being stopped are in violation of U.S. immigration law.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a Gothamist request for comment. The LA Times reported that the Trump administration was appealing the order – a follow up to an earlier directive from the same judge that also sought to rein in ICE agents making enforcement stops in California. That measure was ultimately blocked by the Supreme Court in an emergency order.

The LA Times quoted a Justice Department official who said Frimpong’s new order would hinder immigration enforcement.

Frimpong’s directive applies only in the Central California district, but it addresses longstanding charges brought by immigration advocates and civil rights attorneys across the country that ICE agents, including in New York and New Jersey, have engaged in racial profiling in furtherance of the Trump administration’s mass deportation initiative.

Frimpong concluded the plaintiffs, including immigrants’ rights groups and Latino individuals who were stopped by federal authorities, cited a “mountain of evidence” showing agents “routinely make detentive stops of individuals because those individuals appear Latino or Latino and working class.”

Relying in part on body-worn camera evidence, the judge’s opinion referenced dozens of instances where federal officers “explicitly use apparent Latino race” as a basis of stopping and detaining people, without the officers’ asking or securing any additional information.

The stops included people in a wide range of circumstances: Latinos dressed in work clothes; Latinos present at low-wage job sites, including car washes; and Latinos riding bicycles or driving their children to school. She also cited evidence, in support of her findings, of officers using racial slurs and "dehumanizing language" in referring to those they stopped.

“The Court’s order makes clear that Latino workers have the right to go about their lives without being detained because of the color of their skin,” Lauren Michel Wilfong, staff attorney with the National Day Laborer Organizing Network and co-counsel for the plaintiffs, said in a statement.

Wilfong added, “This win was made possible by the Plaintiffs and dozens of class members who spoke truth to power to expose DHS’s unlawful actions and safeguard our fundamental rights.”

text:
HOUSTON -- A federal immigration officer charged with aggravated assault after he ran over a Mexican man with his car in Houston will turn himself in on Monday, according to his attorney.

Mario Alberto Morales, a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old construction worker, with his unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as he chased Parra Hernandez through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales on Friday on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

SEE ALSO: ICE agent indicted after running over man with vehicle, Harris County officials announce

Morales is planning to turn himself in at a courthouse sometime on Monday, David Lindenmuth, his attorney, told The Associated Press. Lindenmuth previously told the AP that the incident was "clearly just an accident" and that local officials had "invented a crime out of thin air."

Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told reporters on Friday.

ICE has said Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales' car.

Previously released surveillance camera video shows Morales' vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away.

Teare played footage from Morales' body camera on Friday that showed the agent making sharp turns with his steering wheel. He then stops and exits the vehicle and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is lying on the ground, screaming.

"I was coming in, and I hit him with the car," Morales can be heard saying after another ICE agent arrives.

Parra Hernandez told deputies that he fled the traffic stop when Morales started pulling on a mask, and Morales "threw the car" at him, according to a Harris County Sheriff's Office incident report reviewed by the AP. Morales told deputies that he did not brake before he hit Parra Hernandez, but that he did not intentionally strike him, according to the report.

ICE said after the incident that the target of the operation was a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who the agency said was seen getting into a car with Parra Hernandez. Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told the immigrants' rights group FIEL that her father has been dead for nearly a decade.

READ MORE: Lawyer for man run over by ICE-driven SUV says her client never met ICE's alleged target

Morales is among a small number of federal agents who have been criminally charged for wounding people during the Trump administration's aggressive immigration crackdown. ICE agent Christian Castro pleaded not guilty last month to charges that he lied to the FBI after he shot and wounded a Venezuelan man as immigration agents swept Minneapolis earlier this year.

Many other ICE shootings, including some that were fatal, have not ended in charges for the agents involved.

Morales, 33, has served as an ICE agent for a little over a year, according to Lindenmuth.

Teare said on Friday that authorities have a "significant amount of information" on Morales, and that, in his experience, law enforcement agencies would not hire someone with his background. He did not elaborate.

Morales was charged with a misdemeanor in 2013 for stealing four DVDs, according to Harris County Court records. Those charges were dismissed after he paid a $270 fine and struck a plea deal.

Morales unsuccessfully ran to represent Texas' 34th congressional district in this year's election cycle under the name "Bam Morales," which Lindenmuth confirmed. Morales served in the U.S. Army's 82nd Airborne Division and later as a corrections officer and law enforcement officer, he wrote in a Ballotpedia candidate survey. He wrote that his top priorities were veterans' rights, economic issues and service guided by the Christian principles of "compassion, integrity, service, and accountability." He listed illegal immigration as one of the country's greatest challenges.

Morales also wrote in the survey that he was endorsed by an organization called "Make America Godlier Again."

Morales appeared at a 2024 Christian conference held by televangelist Johnson Suleman. In video of the conference, Morales appears to act as a Spanish translator as Suleman serves free food and "extends his touch of love to migrants."

"I want to pray for the immigrants," Suleman said, as Morales translated those words into Spanish. "I bless you. May the lord grant your request and open your doors."

text:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally striking a man in Houston earlier this month is expected to surrender on Monday morning, his attorney, David Lindenmuth told ABC News.

Mario Alberto Morales was indicted by a grand jury in Houston on a charge of second-degree aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office.

Lindenmuth said Morales did not intend to strike Miguel Parra Hernandez when he was pursuing him and another person who were attempting to flee on foot on Oct. 10.

“It was an accident. It was nothing more than accident, but the DA to score political points right before elections decided to bring charges,” Lindenmuth said.

At a press briefing on Friday, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare alleged that Morales' body-camera footage shows the officer "aggressively steered his vehicle" into Parra Hernandez.

The district attorney played graphic video from the officer's body-worn camera alongside surveillance footage of the incident during a press briefing.

The body-camera footage appears to show Morales behind the wheel, pursuing Parra Hernandez and another individual who are fleeing on foot.

"Got a runner, got a runner," the officer can be heard saying. "On foot. Both of them."

Seconds later, the body camera footage shows the officer appearing to turn his steering wheel toward the left. Authorities say that’s when the vehicle struck Parra Hernandez and then came to a stop.

Morales is then seen approaching Parra Hernandez, who is lying on the ground crying in agony, and moving his leg.

When asked about the video, Lindenmuth said Morales had two detainees in the back seat and was trying to avoid striking a vehicle and did not intend to hit him.

“Clearly there is contact but the contact wasn’t intentional. It wasn’t knowingly,” Lindenmuth said. “It was in reaction to him trying not to strike a vehicle.”

Lindenmuth said Morales served in the army, was a paratrooper, and is a Christian pastor who does missionary work overseas.

He said he believes the charges against his client are politically motivated.

“This is a good man, so why are you attacking his character and his background? You know why? When you don’t have evidence, you have to vilify somebody,” he said. “So he has to make him the boogeyman, a monster, because he knows he cannot prove intent because there was none.”

Speaking at the press briefing, the DA told reporters: "I've reviewed hundreds of cases, some very similar to this. The evidence that we have in this case is as clear as any that I've ever prosecuted or investigated."

Attorney Kim Bruno, who's representing Parra Hernandez, her client suffered fractures and nerve damage and underwent surgery following the incident.

“All he wants is accountability,” Bruno said. “He wants assurance that this will not happen to anybody else. He is so sympathetic, and all he cares about are the other people. But he is the one in the bed suffering.”

Parra Hernandez is currently detained and remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility.

According to Lindenmuth, Morales is a former corrections officer who enlisted in the Army.

Morales also worked as a detention and processing officer at the Port Isabel Detention Center and worked with DHS as an ICE contractor, Lindenmuth said.

He joined ICE as a federal immigration officer in August 2025, Lindenmuth said.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s official social media accounts have posted a provocative Halloween-themed video pairing horror movie monsters with footage of immigrants being detained by federal agents.

Set to Michael Jackson’s hit “Thriller,” the minute-long video opens with famous film villains, including Freddy Krueger, Jason Voorhees and Pennywise the clown before flashing a graphic reading “ICE’s Halloween Spooktacular,” teeing up macabre footage of immigrants being detained.

The video cuts to footage of ICE arrests and enforcement operations, showing agents detaining people, escorting them away and taking them into holding facilities. Several clips show men sitting on the floor of a mass detention area with their faces in their hands.

One shot features a man being escorted by masked officers with the caption “This guy was wanted for homicide.” The next image flashes the word “Seriously” across the screen.

The video also throws in other Halloween imagery, including glowing jack-o’-lanterns and zombies followed by a cartoon of an ICE agent handcuffing a green alien.

The video ends with an animated ICE officer holding a pair of handcuffs next to the words “Happy Halloween.”

“Happy Halloween from your friends at ICE,” the agency captioned the post.

The video sparked conflicting opinions in the comments, with ICE supporters calling it “pretty funny” while critics condemned the stunt as inhumane.

“I don't celebrate Halloween, but I definitely like this video,” one supporter wrote on Facebook.

“#F***ICE,” the comment right below it reads.

Another person denounced the video on X, writing: “Man, I’m all for deporting illegal immigrants. But this is f****d up. Literally normalizing identifying South Americans as monsters. This is not the conduct of a mentally healthy government.”

The Independent has requested comment from ICE and Jackson’s estate.

President Donald Trump and his administration have frequently used provocative clip-based posts intended to “troll” critics and increase engagement across social network sites and other media outlets.

The latest video comes as ICE faces heightened scrutiny over a reported increase in immigration enforcement activity across the country in the weeks leading up to November’s midterm elections.

Cities and states including New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Illinois, Detroit and California have reported an uptick in federal immigration operations, according to recent reporting from NPR.

Asked about the reported increase, a spokesperson for Homeland Security told NPR: “ICE agents uphold our nation’s immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day.”

The rise in ICE activity also has raised concerns about how the operations could affect voters ahead of the midterms. Some civil rights advocates warn that high-profile raids could scare immigrant communities and discourage people from voting.

In court filings this week, Department of Justice officials said there are no plans to deploy ICE agents to serve as poll monitors — but officers from the Drug Enforcement Administration and other federal law enforcement agencies that have participated in immigration operations will join Justice Department personnel across the country.

They will not be armed, but for voters in Arlington County, Virginia, “these threats have already had serious impacts,” officials said in a recent lawsuit.

“Threatening to send armed agents to polling stations is unlawful and contravenes the bedrock values of free and fair elections we hold dear in this country,” Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said in a recent statement.

Wendy Weiser of the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law School has said there is no sign that the enforcement activity has reduced voter participation, pointing to a surge in early voting among communities of color.

text:
President Donald Trump's administration is planning to deport Afghans detained in the US back to their home country via Pakistan, according to court documents obtained by The Associated Press - a move advocacy groups say could put their lives at risk.

Immigrant rights organizations say those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban. Thousands fled persecution in Afghanistan and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.

"This is absolutely unconscionable," said Shawn VanDiver, a US Navy veteran and president of the advocacy group #AfghanEvac. "It seems like there's no end to their willingness to break the law and violate people's human rights."

The US intends to initially deport Afghan immigrants as early as Monday on flights from Louisiana, where the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan, according to court documents.

The plan to deport Afghans to Pakistan was first reported by Bloomberg on Monday. On Friday, The New York Times reported that the immigrants were going to be sent to Afghanistan after arriving in Pakistan.

A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security said in an email to the media on Saturday that ICE does not comment on future immigrant-removal operations, citing operational security and personnel safety. Officials at the Pakistan embassy in Washington did not immediately return email messages.

US officials confirmed the Afghan deportations in sealed court documents obtained by the media.

In a document filed in federal court in Virginia on Friday, a senior ICE official acknowledged that an Afghan immigrant had been scheduled to be on an upcoming charter flight from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan, "with further transport onward to Afghanistan." The document was filed in the case of an immigrant who is not in custody and is challenging efforts to deport him.

In another federal court case in Oklahoma, federal prosecutors filed a document on Monday disclosing that another Afghan immigrant was scheduled to be deported to Afghanistan sometime next week.

The Trump administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. It has done this in some instances when it is unable to send them to their own countries because the US does not have formal relations, like with the Taliban government in Afghanistan. In other instances, it has been used as a deterrent.

In many cases, a U.S. immigration judge has determined their lives would be in jeopardy if sent to their home countries. It was not immediately clear if any designated for return to Afghanistan have protective orders against being sent there.

Human Rights First, an advocacy group for refugees and asylum seekers that tracks U.S. deportation flights, said Saturday that it had confirmed a scheduled flight from Louisiana to Pakistan on Tuesday carrying Afghan immigrants.

"It is beyond egregious that this administration plans to carry out an unprecedented mass deportation flight of Afghans, forcibly sending them through Pakistan and into the hands of the Taliban," Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee & immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said in an email to the media.

"This follows previous unconscionable deportation flights we have tracked under this administration, including Iranian Christian converts and political dissidents removed via Qatar and Kuwait to Iran, as well as a Russian political dissident removed via Egypt to Russia," Arvey said.

Some Democratic members of Congress took to social media to criticize the Afghan deportations after seeing the Times story on Friday.

"It is reprehensible that the Trump Administration plans to deport hundreds of Afghans, including women, children and those who supported U.S. forces, to Pakistan - who then risk being sent back into the hands of the Taliban. Congress must stand against this," Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire posted on X.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut added in his own X post, "We made a promise to our Afghan allies - that after aiding & protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them. This Administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture & death."

In September, Trump's administration finalized a last-minute reprieve to avoid the closure of a camp in Qatar that houses more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted America's war effort or are the relatives of US service members. The administration extended for nine months the life of Camp As Sayliyah, which had been due to close Sept. 30 at the end of the U.S. budget year.

Upon entering his second term, Trump, a Republican, paused his Democratic predecessor's Afghan resettlement program as part of a series of executive orders cracking down on immigration, including dramatically altering refugee admissions to focus on white South Africans.

The refugee changes left thousands of people who fled war and persecution - and had gone through yearslong vetting processes to start new lives in America - stranded at places worldwide, including the base in Qatar.

NORTH ALABAMA, Ala. (WAFF) - Around 180 people were arrested across four North Alabama counties during a weeklong coordinated operation involving local deputies and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Last week, immigration enforcement sparked protests and concerns among families in Franklin County.

During the operation, Russellville Mayor David Grissom reported increased student absences and temporary business closures as some families and workers expressed concerns.

Marshall County Sheriff Phil Sims announced Saturday that his deputies actively participated alongside federal agents in Marshall, Franklin, Lawrence and Colbert counties to locate and apprehend individuals.

According to federal authorities, those taken into custody included individuals previously deported as well as those with criminal records involving violent crimes, domestic violence, sexual offenses, and DUI convictions.

“Our deputies were not simply providing support from the sidelines,” Sims said in a statement. “Marshall County will not be a safe haven for individuals who repeatedly violate our laws or engage in criminal activity that threatens our communities.”

text:
California’s 34th Congressional district includes much of Central and East LA, including historic areas such as Echo Park, Little Tokyo, Downtown and Boyle Heights. The district is about 65% Latino.

Eagle Rock resident and incumbent Jimmy Gomez faces off against Highland Park native Angela Gonzales-Torres. Gomez has held his position in Congress since 2017, but is currently under fire for sexual misconduct allegations that prompted an investigation by the House Ethics Committee.

Both candidates are running on a platform to create pathways to citizenship for immigrants and increase affordable housing. Gomez is a long-time Democratic stronghold in the state who placed first in the June primary, while Gonzales-Torres identifies as a democratic socialist and is a first-time candidate.

Jimmy Gomez

Eagle Rock resident Jimmy Gomez began his career as an organizer and was elected to the U.S. Congress in June 2017, and has served as the Chair of the Assembly Appropriations Committee. Before that, he became one of the youngest members of the California State Assembly.

Gomez authored the Medicare for All Act and filed the first lawsuit against the Trump Administration for its obstruction of congressional oversight into federal immigration detention centers.

Gomez advocates for and is a co-sponsor of the College for All Act to eliminate tuition and fees at four-year public colleges and universities for families who make up to $150,000 and make community colleges tuition and fee-free for students.

His platform focuses on issues like affordable housing, healthcare, education (including cancelling student loans) and paid family leave.

Gomez faces sexual misconduct allegations that prompted an investigation by the House Ethics Committee. The allegations first came to light in April, when the New York Post reported Gomez was seen kissing a young staffer at a party in Sacramento in 2023.

Gomez denies any wrongdoing.

Gomez’s endorsements include:

U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

U.S. Senator Adam Schiff

California Teachers Association

Planned Parenthood Action Fund

The California Democratic Party

The American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (AFL-CIO)

Angela Gonzales-Torres

Gonzales-Torres grew up in Highland Park and is the daughter of a deportee and single mother who relied on social services such as SNAP and Medicaid. She said she is fighting on behalf of working families like her own.

She has experience working in the LA Mayor’s office as well as being a regional representative on Metro’s Public Safety Advisory Committee. She also served as president of the Highland Park neighborhood council.

Gonzales-Torres serves as an Advocate for Equity and Justice Academic Counselor at Pasadena’s City College CORE program supporting formerly incarcerated and system-impacted students in navigating higher education. She is also the program director for a permanent affordable housing project set in Altadena assisting elderly tenants impacted by the recent fires.

Her grassroots campaign focuses on affordable housing, healthcare and education. She also focuses on the experience of immigrants and pledged to work on legislative solutions to create more pathways for citizenship. If elected, she said she would work to abolish ICE.

Some of Gonzales-Torres’s endorsements:

LA City Controller Kenneth Mejia

The Democratic Socialists of America — LA County chapter

California Working Families Party

Justice Democrats

East Area Progressive Democrats

Lucha Action

text:
President Donald Trump's administration is planning to deport Afghans detained in the U.S. back to their home country via Pakistan, according to court documents obtained by The Associated Press — a move advocacy groups say could put their lives at risk.

Immigrant rights organizations say those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban. Thousands fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.

“This is absolutely unconscionable," said Shawn VanDiver, a U.S. Navy veteran and president of the advocacy group #AfghanEvac. “It seems like there’s no end to their willingness to break the law and violate people’s human rights.”

Article continues below this ad

The U.S. intends to initially deport Afghan immigrants as early as Monday on flights from Louisiana, where the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan, according to court documents.

The plan to deport Afghans to Pakistan was first reported by Bloomberg on Monday. On Friday, The New York Times reported that the immigrants were going to be sent to Afghanistan after arriving in Pakistan.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in an email to the AP on Saturday that ICE does not comment on future immigrant-removal operations, citing operational security and personnel safety. Officials at the Pakistani Embassy in Washington did not immediately return email messages.

Afghans caught up in Trump's immigration crackdown

U.S. officials confirmed the Afghan deportations in sealed court documents obtained by the AP.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

In a document filed in federal court in Virginia on Friday, a senior ICE official acknowledged that an Afghan immigrant had been scheduled to be on an upcoming charter flight from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan, “with further transport onward to Afghanistan.” The document was filed in the case of an immigrant who is not in custody and is challenging efforts to deport him.

In another federal court case in Oklahoma, federal prosecutors filed a document on Monday disclosing that another Afghan immigrant was scheduled to be deported to Afghanistan sometime next week.

The Trump administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. It has done this in some instances when it is unable to send them to their own countries because the US does not have formal relations, like with the Taliban government in Afghanistan. In other instances, it has been used as a deterrent.

In many cases, a U.S. immigration judge has determined their lives would be in jeopardy if sent to their home countries. It was not immediately clear if any designated for return to Afghanistan have protective orders against being sent there.

Immigrant groups and Democrats decry deportation plan

Human Rights First, an advocacy group for refugees and asylum seekers that tracks U.S. deportation flights, said Saturday that it had confirmed a scheduled flight from Louisiana to Pakistan on Tuesday carrying Afghan immigrants.

“It is beyond egregious that this administration plans to carry out an unprecedented mass deportation flight of Afghans, forcibly sending them through Pakistan and into the hands of the Taliban,” Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said in an email to the AP.

“This follows previous unconscionable deportation flights we have tracked under this administration, including Iranian Christian converts and political dissidents removed via Qatar and Kuwait to Iran, as well as a Russian political dissident removed via Egypt to Russia,” Arvey said.

Some Democratic members of Congress took to social media to criticize the Afghan deportations after seeing the Times story on Friday.

“It is reprehensible that the Trump Administration plans to deport hundreds of Afghans, including women, children and those who supported U.S. forces, to Pakistan — who then risk being sent back into the hands of the Taliban. Congress must stand against this," Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire posted on X.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut added in his own X post, “We made a promise to our Afghan allies — that after aiding & protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them. This Administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture & death.”

Thousands fled war and persecution in Afghanistan

In September, Trump's administration finalized a last-minute reprieve to avoid the closure of a camp in Qatar that houses more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted America’s war effort or are the relatives of U.S. service members. The administration extended for nine months the life of Camp As Sayliyah, which had been due to close Sept. 30 at the end of the U.S. budget year.

Upon entering his second term, Trump, a Republican, paused his Democratic predecessor’s Afghan resettlement program as part of a series of executive orders cracking down on immigration, including dramatically altering refugee admissions to focus on white South Africans.

The refugee changes left thousands of people who fled war and persecution — and had gone through yearslong vetting processes to start new lives in America — stranded at places worldwide, including the base in Qatar.

text:
Podcaster Joe Rogan criticized President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement policies on Saturday, warning that masked federal agents were "snatching up" people, including American citizens, and setting dangerous precedents that could be exploited by future administrations.

Speaking with British comedians and political commentators Francis Foster and Konstantin Kisin, co-hosts of the popular politics and culture podcast TRIGGERnometry, Rogan argued that Americans should be concerned about the expansion of federal law enforcement powers, even if they support Trump's efforts to crack down on illegal immigration.

Rogan, who endorsed Trump in the 2024 presidential election, has become increasingly critical of some of the administration's policies, particularly its aggressive immigration enforcement tactics and war with Iran. The podcaster is seen to have significant influence over young male voters, a demographic Trump successfully courted in 2024, and his remarks come just days before the November 3 midterm elections, with Republicans trailing Democrats in national congressional polling.

Read More on Politics

What Joe Rogan Said About ICE

"Most people in this country don't like the idea of a militarized police force with no identification, just pulling people over," Rogan said. "It opens up a world of problems. It sets terrible precedents."

The podcast host argued that supporters of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) should consider how the same tactics could be employed by future administrations.

"You're allowed to have a militarized police force with masks on, and they don't have any identification. And they're snatching up people," Rogan said. "And some of them happen to be American citizens."

Rogan suggested that Americans who support such tactics because they believe aggressive enforcement is necessary to achieve Trump's immigration objectives could be overlooking the long-term consequences.

"If you're supporting this, because I got to crack a few eggs to make an omelet. Okay, well, you just opened up the fucking hen house," he said.

"If you're allowing that, and that's normalized in society, that's not good," Rogan added.

However, Rogan also defended the need for immigration enforcement targeting dangerous criminals.

He pointed to the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua and other criminal organizations allegedly involved in kidnapping, illegal activities and cartel violence within the United States.

"That's real too," Rogan said. "So like, support of ICE to go after that is pretty strong."

The Trump administration has defended its immigration crackdown as necessary to remove dangerous criminals and protect public safety, while critics have raised concerns about due process, accountability and the detention of American citizens.

Newsweek reached out to ICE for comment via email on Saturday.

American Citizens Detained by ICE

Rogan's concerns follow numerous reports of American citizens being detained during immigration enforcement operations.

An investigation by ProPublica identified more than 500 U.S. citizens detained by federal immigration agents since Trump returned to office in January 2025.

Leonardo García Venegas, a Florida-born American citizen, was detained during an immigration operation at an Alabama construction site in May 2025. Venegas said agents dismissed his identification as fake before releasing him hours later.

The Department of Homeland Security disputed his account of an improper arrest, saying he had obstructed agents attempting to detain another individual.

In September, two 17-year-old American citizens said they were assaulted and detained for approximately eight hours after stopping to record an ICE operation in Alamo, Texas. The teenagers said they had been traveling to a Marine Corps recruiting office.

DHS maintained that the teenagers had interfered with the enforcement operation.

Aliya Rahman, an American citizen, said federal immigration officers forcibly removed her from her vehicle in Minneapolis while she was traveling to a medical appointment.

DHS has repeatedly defended its enforcement practices, maintaining that American citizens are not targeted for immigration arrests and that individuals who obstruct law enforcement can face arrest regardless of citizenship.

What Joe Rogan Said About the Iran War

Rogan also suggested that Trump's decision to enter the war with Iran had severely damaged his presidency.

"It was the Iran decision that f***ed everything," Rogan said during the discussion. His remarks follow months of criticism of the conflict, which Rogan has argued contradicts Trump's campaign promises to avoid new foreign wars.

During an October 14 conversation with actor Michael Douglas, Rogan said he believed Trump's promise of avoiding new wars had proven untrue.

"What Trump stood for, some of it turned out to not be real," Rogan said, pointing specifically to the Iran conflict.

Rogan's History of Breaking With Trump

Despite his 2024 endorsement, Rogan has repeatedly criticized the administration's immigration policies.

In January, he described the fatal shooting of Renee Nicole Good by an ICE agent in Minneapolis as a "terrible tragedy" and questioned whether aggressive immigration enforcement risked resembling the tactics of the Gestapo.

During a May podcast, Rogan similarly warned that heavily armed immigration agents wearing masks and lacking visible identification represented a dangerous expansion of government authority.

He reiterated those concerns in October, criticizing ICE recruitment incentives and what he described as inadequate training for armed federal agents.

Rogan has also opposed Trump's Iran war, questioning its benefits for the United States and warning about the consequences of prolonged military involvement.

Nevertheless, the relationship between Rogan and Trump has remained more complicated than a straightforward political break.

In April, Rogan appeared alongside Trump at the White House as the president signed an executive order accelerating research and regulatory review of psychedelic treatments, including ibogaine.

Trump publicly acknowledged that Rogan had personally urged him to pursue the policy, while Rogan said he had exchanged text messages with the president about the potential medical benefits.

Rogan's Influence and the Midterm Elections

Rogan was widely viewed as an important figure in Trump's successful efforts to build support among younger men during the 2024 presidential election. Trump's nearly three-hour appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience attracted tens of millions of YouTube views, while Rogan endorsed the Republican shortly before Election Day.

Following Trump's victory, UFC President Dana White publicly thanked Rogan and other influential podcasters for their support.

Trump made substantial gains among young male voters in 2024, a demographic his campaign aggressively targeted through appearances on popular podcasts, such as Rogan's show. According to Edison Research exit polling for NBC News, Trump won approximately 49 percent of men ages 18 to 29, roughly matching Kamala Harris and improving significantly on his 2020 performance against Joe Biden.

Recent polling suggests that support has weakened considerably. An October YouGov survey across eight battleground states found young men favoring Democratic candidates over Republicans by 55 percent to 35 percent.

Rogan's latest criticism comes as Republicans face a difficult political environment nationally ahead of Tuesday's midterms.

The RealClearPolling average as of October 29 showed Democrats leading Republicans by approximately eight points on the generic congressional ballot. An October Pew Research Center survey also found Trump's approval rating had fallen to 30 percent.

Although Rogan's comments do not indicate how his audience will vote, his warning about ICE detaining American citizens and criticism of the Iran War brings into focus the challenges Trump and Republicans faces in maintaining support among key voters who helped them win just two years ago.

description: Dishonesty to influence
text:
When I first heard about the Legislature kicking the tires l…

Wyoming and Colorado share a border and a mountain range, bu…



I have one question. Why would anyone vote for a candidate who does not repudiate lies in ads made by a PAC in his favor?

I'm speaking about U.S. House candidate Chuck Gray. If this person or his PAC is so desperate to mislead voters, what dishonesty will that person pursue in the future when he "represents" us?

Wyomingites are smart. We know that honesty is important. A friend just sent me two ads the PAC supporting Gray produced, which stated unfounded information about me. I am not offended because of the PAC's lies, not denied by Gray, have nothing to do with me.

However, I am angry — dumbfounded by the dishonesty trying to influence voters by scaring them. This kind of behavior is un-Wyoming.

For one example, I have spent years working on rural healthcare (Oct. 10, 1991, Laramie Daily Boomerang). The PAC claims Gray did something for rural healthcare. What? No showing. Regardless of these actions, thank you voters, for your vote. Wyomingites don't tolerate ignorance or dishonesty. Thanks again.

Lisa Kinney

Candidate for U.S. House of Representatives

Laramie

I am writing as a concerned voter about the recent dirty politics being carried on by Rep. Trey Sherwood and the shill of an organization PAC for a Better Wyoming on her behalf. I grew up in politics and perfectly understand what is going on here. I don’t like it.

What bothers me most as a voter is that this PAC is openly misconstruing a candidate’s positions, specifically Wyoming House District 14 candidate Emily Study. It shows in the attack mailers the PAC has been distributed recently in my district.

I was surprised that the incumbent herself took the same route. The PAC is counting on the average voter to be aghast on what it is saying Study represents and how she will destroy our beloved Wyoming and its ways. Like the old adage says, ”say it enough and people will start believing it even if it is not true.”

This PAC has stated positions for Study which have no reference to her public record, either legislatively or during her campaign. Much of accusations are inferred. Further, this PAC has clearly provided a large financial backing to an incumbent that can easily overwhelm a person seeking to do right for the community. This is where money in politics needs to be limited. In my view, if this PAC is doing what it is, it is for a questionable reason backed by money.

I hold to my belief that candidates should be stating what “they” represent and what “they” have done. We need to get away from this way of dirty politics, which the intent is to smear good people trying to do right for their community.

State where you stand, how you differ and stop the attacks. If you are going to vote for a candidate, understand clearly what they support and not according to some pie in sky slogans. This holds true to both Sherwood and Study.

When you go to vote, ask yourself what the present incumbent has done for you and the community. Equally well, know what the opponent says or promises. Ignore the attacks.

David A. DePastina

Laramie

One of the most important decisions Albany County voters will make Tuesday is who will be our sheriff for four years. You need to know a couple of things about Darron Wyatt.

One, he has sworn his allegiance to the Republican Party platform, which sanctions discrimination against the LGBTQ community. The members of that community, and those who care about them, have reason to be concerned about whether Wyatt would protect their rights as sheriff.

Two, Wyatt recently met with President Donald Trump's corrupt head of the FBI, Kash Patel as the guest of ICE's favorite Wyoming sheriff Brian Kozak of Laramie County. I don't believe this office should be partisan, but clearly Wyatt sees it as such and has signaled he would enforce the law as a partisan MAGA.

On the other hand, his opponent Aaron Appelhans has a record of fair and just law enforcement. Before you decide how to vote, Google Wyatt's name and learn how he "enforced the law" as a southern California cop. Appelhans is a Laramie guy. He learned law enforcement among us.

I for one do not want a partisan sheriff employing law enforcement techniques he learned and practiced in California. I voted for Aaron Appelhans and urge you to do the same.

Rodger McDaniel

Laramie

The fur is flying fast and furious in the Albany County Sheriff’s race. Consider the following anyone can verify, among the many reasons I already voted for Aaron Appelhans are:

His opponent, Daron Wyatt, worked in the Anaheim, California police department at a time when it was one of the deadliest in the country for its size.

He is mentioned specifically in the “Anaheim Police Department Use of Force Report, 2017” published by the ACLU of Southern California:

“In 2004, Daron Wyatt, then employed as a police sergeant by the Placentia Police Department, was involved in an incident in which Placentia police officers shot and killed Brian Charles Smith. Sgt. Wyatt did not fire his gun, but used his TASER, and was the supervising officer on scene. Anaheim PD hired Wyatt in 2008. The following year, Wyatt shot and killed Adolph Anthony Gonzalez, who was unarmed.”

Wyatt was subsequently acquitted of civil liability in the death of Gonzalez, in a case that went on for years because of inconsistencies in the testimony of the officers involved and the inability of a dead man to testify:

“In Gonzalez v. City of Anaheim, the Ninth Circuit held that inconsistencies in the officers’ testimony regarding the physical confrontation raised a genuine dispute of material fact concerning the immediacy of the threat that Gonzalez posed to the officers and others. As a result, the court held that summary judgment was not proper.” (“Dead Men Tell No Tales,” lira.bc.edu/works/publication-article/j0t3s-htk38 ).

We are approaching a poignant anniversary on Nov. 4 when, eight years ago, an unarmed Laramie resident was shot and killed by a sheriff’s deputy. The deputy should never have been hired due to previous incidents of violence, all “exonerated.”

Appelhans has restored the professionalism of the Albany County Sheriff’s Office. He hires and trains deputies with clean backgrounds to de-escalate potentially violent situations and interact positively with our community.

That’s the direction I want to keep by voting for Sheriff Appelhans.

Sarah Gorin

Laramie

text:
US president Donald Trump’s administration has been slammed online, following a report from The New York Times, citing US officials, which says the Republican’s government has detained Afghan immigrants in Louisiana and “relatives of those who helped the US military”, with a view to deport them to Afghanistan.

The NYT’s report, published on Friday, cites three US officials and says of the “dozens” of people detained, some of them “could face discrimination or persecution under the Taliban”, including one gay man.

Homosexuality is illegal in Afghanistan, and punishable by death.

One official said more than 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be deported, in a move which would see them sent to Pakistan, which would then send them to Afghanistan.

The newspaper added that the first deportation flight is expected to leave on Monday (November 2).

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told the NYT in a statement that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) “does not comment on prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details”.

The news has since been condemned as an “unforgivable betrayal” by social media users:

text:
Immigration advocates are suing the state of Tennessee, arguing a new policy is unfairly preventing some non-U.S. citizens who are here legally, from obtaining temporary driver's licenses.

The lawsuit challenges changes made by the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security that advocates say could leave thousands of immigrants unable to drive — despite having federal permission to be in the United States.

Under the previous policy, Tennessee accepted work permits and other federal documents as proof of legal authorization to remain in the country.

But advocates say the state is now limiting the types of documents certain noncitizens can use to qualify for a temporary driver's license.

Under the new requirements, applicants must present a valid visa, an I-94, an I-94W or a temporary green card.

That leaves some people who have held Tennessee driver's licenses for years, or even decades, suddenly being denied when they attempt to renew.

"Under its new rule, TDOS will only issue driver's licenses to certain non-citizens who present a valid visa, an I-94 or an I-94W or somebody with a temporary green card," said Jazmin Ramirez, advocacy director for the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition.

"As a result, people who have held driver's license for years or even decades are now being turned away and denied renewals for the first time."

The Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition filed the lawsuit, arguing the policy excludes people who have federal authorization to live and work in the United States.

Immigration attorney Kathleen Martinez says the state is effectively treating people with work permits as if they do not have authorized immigration status.

"They're treating everyone with a work permit as if they are not here with authorized stay," Martinez said in a post on social media.

DACA recipients among those affected

During a virtual news conference, advocates described how the changes are affecting immigrants who depend on their ability to drive to work, take their children to school and handle everyday responsibilities.

DACA recipients are among those potentially impacted. Many have federal work authorization but are not issued the specific immigration documents Tennessee now requires.

One person who spoke during the news conference, but asked to remain anonymous, described how losing their license has affected their job.

"Currently, I am employed at a Level 1 trauma center but cannot show up to work because I am without a license and live an hour away," the person said.

Advocates say the consequences could extend to thousands of people who previously qualified for temporary licenses but no longer meet the state's revised documentation requirements.

Lawsuit questions state's authority to make changes

The lawsuit argues Tennessee officials implemented the new restrictions without following the proper legal procedures.

Attorneys contend the Department of Safety and Homeland Security overstepped its authority by changing which federal documents are accepted and failed to give the public an opportunity to weigh in before the policy took effect.

The legal challenge comes after Tennessee passed sweeping immigration legislation that went into effect this year.

State officials have reportedly interpreted the new law as allowing the department to impose stricter requirements for temporary driver's licenses.

However, advocates argue the state cannot use the legislation to deny licenses to people who have otherwise been authorized to live and work in the country under federal law.

The lawsuit asks the court to intervene and challenge the state's new licensing requirements.

WZTV reached out to the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security for comment.

The department responded that it does not comment on ongoing litigation.

text:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed his department is investigating 300,000 cases of potential noncitizens voting, with 1,600 active investigations.

The Trump administration has made potential noncitizens voting its central message heading into the midterm elections Tuesday, repeatedly claiming without evidence that it is widespread. The administration has used those allegations to try to interfere with states’ constitutional authority to administer elections.

“All we’re trying to do is make sure we secure our elections,” Mullin said in a Fox News interview.

In reality, repeated studies have shown that noncitizens voting is exceedingly rare and never happens in sufficient numbers to change the outcome of an election.

The Trump administration sent five states lists of alleged noncitizens who are supposedly registered to vote illegally. The administration sued California after the state refused to remove 20,000 people from the voting rolls that the Department of Justice (DOJ) claimed were “likely” noncitizens. It filed a separate suit alleging Washington failed to remove 400 people from its voting eligibility list.

“They’re not being transparent with their elections. They’re not being transparent with who voted in past elections,” Mullin said.

Both California and Washington said a cursory examination of the lists found several errors, including American citizens, inactive voters and people who never registered to vote.

Mullin has made grandiose claims about noncitizens voting in the past that later fizzled under closer scrutiny. In July, Mullin claimed that DHS had identified over 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in California, New Jersey, Nevada and Pennsylvania. Specifically in Nevada, he claimed his department identified more than 15,000 noncitizens registered to vote. That number was revised to 185 people, all of whom were later shown to be American citizens.

Despite that, Mullin pressed on, blaming Democrats for fostering sanctuary cities that become a “melting pot for criminal activity.”

“The Democrats, the only thing they’re for is sowing chaos and disruption. They’re not for anything else,” Mullin said.
