text:
HOUSTON -- A federal immigration officer charged with aggravated assault after he ran over a Mexican man with his car in Houston will turn himself in on Monday, according to his attorney.

Mario Alberto Morales, a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old construction worker, with his unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as he chased Parra Hernandez through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales on Friday on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

SEE ALSO: ICE agent indicted after running over man with vehicle, Harris County officials announce

Morales is planning to turn himself in at a courthouse sometime on Monday, David Lindenmuth, his attorney, told The Associated Press. Lindenmuth previously told the AP that the incident was "clearly just an accident" and that local officials had "invented a crime out of thin air."

Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told reporters on Friday.

ICE has said Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales' car.

Previously released surveillance camera video shows Morales' vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away.

Teare played footage from Morales' body camera on Friday that showed the agent making sharp turns with his steering wheel. He then stops and exits the vehicle and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is lying on the ground, screaming.

"I was coming in, and I hit him with the car," Morales can be heard saying after another ICE agent arrives.

Parra Hernandez told deputies that he fled the traffic stop when Morales started pulling on a mask, and Morales "threw the car" at him, according to a Harris County Sheriff's Office incident report reviewed by the AP. Morales told deputies that he did not brake before he hit Parra Hernandez, but that he did not intentionally strike him, according to the report.

ICE said after the incident that the target of the operation was a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who the agency said was seen getting into a car with Parra Hernandez. Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told the immigrants' rights group FIEL that her father has been dead for nearly a decade.

READ MORE: Lawyer for man run over by ICE-driven SUV says her client never met ICE's alleged target

Morales is among a small number of federal agents who have been criminally charged for wounding people during the Trump administration's aggressive immigration crackdown. ICE agent Christian Castro pleaded not guilty last month to charges that he lied to the FBI after he shot and wounded a Venezuelan man as immigration agents swept Minneapolis earlier this year.

Many other ICE shootings, including some that were fatal, have not ended in charges for the agents involved.

Morales, 33, has served as an ICE agent for a little over a year, according to Lindenmuth.

Teare said on Friday that authorities have a "significant amount of information" on Morales, and that, in his experience, law enforcement agencies would not hire someone with his background. He did not elaborate.

Morales was charged with a misdemeanor in 2013 for stealing four DVDs, according to Harris County Court records. Those charges were dismissed after he paid a $270 fine and struck a plea deal.

Morales unsuccessfully ran to represent Texas' 34th congressional district in this year's election cycle under the name "Bam Morales," which Lindenmuth confirmed. Morales served in the U.S. Army's 82nd Airborne Division and later as a corrections officer and law enforcement officer, he wrote in a Ballotpedia candidate survey. He wrote that his top priorities were veterans' rights, economic issues and service guided by the Christian principles of "compassion, integrity, service, and accountability." He listed illegal immigration as one of the country's greatest challenges.

Morales also wrote in the survey that he was endorsed by an organization called "Make America Godlier Again."

Morales appeared at a 2024 Christian conference held by televangelist Johnson Suleman. In video of the conference, Morales appears to act as a Spanish translator as Suleman serves free food and "extends his touch of love to migrants."

"I want to pray for the immigrants," Suleman said, as Morales translated those words into Spanish. "I bless you. May the lord grant your request and open your doors."

text:
Footage has emerged of a masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent pulling their handgun on a dogwalker during the arrest of a suspected illegal migrant in North Hollywood, Los Angeles, on Friday.

ICE adopted more aggressive tactics after Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 having vowed to crack down on illegal immigration during the 2024 presidential election campaign.

This period has coincided with a sharp decrease in illegal crossings of the U.S.-Mexico border, but has also seen a number of controversial ICE shootings of activists and suspected illegal migrants.

Read More on News

Newsweek contacted ICE, the Department of Homeland Security and California Governor Gavin Newsom for comment on Saturday by email outside of regular office hours.

What The Video Shows

On Friday the Los Angeles Times published a video it said had been recorded earlier that day during an ICE operation in North Hollywood, credited to Damari Butler. It had been filmed from an elevated position, possibly a building, above the ICE agents, who are wearing tactical gear reading "ICE Police," and has since circulated widely on social media.

The footage begins with one ICE agent detaining a man who had been pinned down on the sidewalk, while a second aims a can of spray at a bystander with two dogs on leads who had stopped at the scene.

The dogwalker backs away commenting “I’m not bothering you” while an unknown party loudly shouts “ICE, ICE.”

It then cuts to two agents dragging the detained man, who is shouting in Spanish and appears to be moaning in pain, towards a vehicle. During the commotion a can of an unidentified spray is dropped by one of the agents, and the dog walker moves over and picks it up.

He is swiftly grabbed by an ICE agent and throws the can further down the road, after which a second agent pushes him into a bush and points a pistol at his head from a range of several inches. The dogwalker is released after which four ICE agents are seen dragging the detained man to a vehicle while the dogwalker once again approaches.

In the background repeated whistles can be heard, a tactic used by anti-ICE activists to warn people the federal agency is in the area. One of the officers again approaches the dogwalker, holding up what appears to be a can of spray, causing him to swiftly back off.

Speaking to the Los Angeles Times Butler said they began filming the scene after the ICE agents bundled their suspect to the ground. Butler commented: “There was no asking what his name was, no ID, nothing. They just grabbed him.”

Referring to the dogwalker who had a gun pointed at him, Butler added: “The guy with the dog, I guess he moved the pepper spray out of the way, and then the other ICE agent ran over.”

Reaction

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass shared the Los Angeles Times story on X adding: “This is egregious and will not be tolerated in LA. I’m engaging the Attorney General’s Office to investigate and prosecute any wrongdoing by these federal agents.

Additionally, I referred this matter to the Office of U.S. Representative Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat leading oversight on federal immigration enforcement abuses.

“We beat Trump and ICE in court, and new state laws have implemented accountability measures for ICE agents to protect our communities.”

LA City Councilmember Nithya Raman on X commented: “I am outraged by reports of violent ICE kidnappings in North Hollywood. LA is not a playground for the Trump regime’s inhumane operations, and Angelenos should not have to live in fear of going to work, taking their kids to school, or living their life.”

ICE Shootings

Since Trump returned to office in January 2025 over 20 people, both suspected illegal migrants and U.S. citizens, have been shot by ICE agents, with a number of these incidents being fatal.

ICE-involved shootings became particularly controversial in January when two anti-ICE activists, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Jeffrey Pretti, were shot dead in unrelated incidents in Minneapolis, Minnesota. In both cases federal officials argued they acted in self-defense but this was contested by local politicians.

Following the shootings hundreds of ICE agents were withdrawn from the city, a move described by former U.S. border patrol chief Greg Bovino as a “surrender.”

Earlier this week a federal immigration officer in Texas was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after allegedly deliberately driving an SUV into a fleeing man on October 10. The charges were brought against Mario Alberto Morales following the incident that injured Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old Mexican national, who remains in ICE custody.

Initially ICE officials said Hernandez had run in front of the vehicle, but Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said this account was contradicted by video evidence.

Illegal Border Crossings Fall

According to data released by the Department of Homeland Security in October 2025 following the Trump administration’s illegal immigration clampdown unauthorized crossings of the U.S.-Mexican border fell to their lowest level since 1970.

In the 2025 fiscal year U.S. Border Patrol recorded just under 238,000 apprehensions of suspected illegal migrants attempting to enter the country, down from around 2.2 million in the 2022 fiscal year.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found 40 percent of registered voters believed Republicans have the better immigration policy against 38 percent for Democrats. This was a substantial decline for Republicans from January 2025 when they led on the issue by 26 percentage points.

title: U.S. plans to deport Afghans back to their home country through Pakistan, documents show
authors: DAVE COLLINS Associated Press, ABC News
description:
President Donald Trump's administration is planning to deport Afghans detained in the U.S. back to their home country via Pakistan, according to court documents obtained by The Associated Press — a move advocacy groups say could put their lives at risk.
Immigrant rights organizations say those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban.
Thousands fled persecution in Afghanistan and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.
The plan to deport Afghans to Pakistan was first reported by Bloomberg on Monday.
U.S. officials confirmed the Afghan deportations in sealed court documents obtained by the AP.
text:
President Donald Trump's administration is planning to deport Afghans detained in the U.S. back to their home country via Pakistan, according to court documents obtained by The Associated Press — a move advocacy groups say could put their lives at risk.

Immigrant rights organizations say those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban. Thousands fled persecution in Afghanistan and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.

“This is absolutely unconscionable," said Shawn VanDiver, a U.S. Navy veteran and president of the advocacy group #AfghanEvac. “It seems like there’s no end to their willingness to break the law and violate people’s human rights.”

The U.S. intends to initially deport Afghan immigrants as early as Monday on flights from Louisiana, where the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan, according to court documents.

The plan to deport Afghans to Pakistan was first reported by Bloomberg on Monday. On Friday, The New York Times reported that the immigrants were going to be sent to Afghanistan after arriving in Pakistan.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in an email to the AP on Saturday that ICE does not comment on future immigrant-removal operations, citing operational security and personnel safety. Officials at the Pakistan embassy in Washington did not immediately return email messages.

U.S. officials confirmed the Afghan deportations in sealed court documents obtained by the AP.

In a document filed in federal court in Virginia on Friday, a senior ICE official acknowledged that an Afghan immigrant had been scheduled to be on an upcoming charter flight from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan, “with further transport onward to Afghanistan.” The document was filed in the case of an immigrant who is not in custody and is challenging efforts to deport him.

In another federal court case in Oklahoma, federal prosecutors filed a document on Monday disclosing that another Afghan immigrant was scheduled to be deported to Afghanistan sometime next week.

The Trump administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. It has done this in some instances when it is unable to send them to their own countries because the US does not have formal relations, like with the Taliban government in Afghanistan. In other instances, it has been used as a deterrent.

In many cases, a U.S. immigration judge has determined their lives would be in jeopardy if sent to their home countries. It was not immediately clear if any designated for return to Afghanistan have protective orders against being sent there.

Human Rights First, an advocacy group for refugees and asylum seekers that tracks U.S. deportation flights, said Saturday that it had confirmed a scheduled flight from Louisiana to Pakistan on Tuesday carrying Afghan immigrants.

“It is beyond egregious that this administration plans to carry out an unprecedented mass deportation flight of Afghans, forcibly sending them through Pakistan and into the hands of the Taliban,” Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee & immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said in an email to the AP.

“This follows previous unconscionable deportation flights we have tracked under this administration, including Iranian Christian converts and political dissidents removed via Qatar and Kuwait to Iran, as well as a Russian political dissident removed via Egypt to Russia,” Arvey said.

Some Democratic members of Congress took to social media to criticize the Afghan deportations after seeing the Times story on Friday.

“It is reprehensible that the Trump Administration plans to deport hundreds of Afghans, including women, children and those who supported U.S. forces, to Pakistan — who then risk being sent back into the hands of the Taliban. Congress must stand against this," Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire posted on X.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut added in his own X post, “We made a promise to our Afghan allies — that after aiding & protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them. This Administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture & death.”

In September, Trump's administration finalized a last-minute reprieve to avoid the closure of a camp in Qatar that houses more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted America’s war effort or are the relatives of U.S. service members. The administration extended for nine months the life of Camp As Sayliyah, which had been due to close Sept. 30 at the end of the U.S. budget year.

Upon entering his second term, Trump, a Republican, paused his Democratic predecessor’s Afghan resettlement program as part of a series of executive orders cracking down on immigration, including dramatically altering refugee admissions to focus on white South Africans.

Los Angeles leaders are speaking out after video captured the moments when what appeared to be U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers pointed a gun at a bystander as a different man was detained in North Hollywood on Friday.

The cell phone footage shows a man being taken away by several masked officers just seconds before the bystander, who was walking two dogs, appeared to pick something up off the ground. He was then rushed by two agents, one of whom pushed the man into some bushes while holding what looked to be a handgun. The bystander tossed the item almost instantly, at which point the agent backed away.

As the video continues, the dog walker can be heard yelling at the officers before one approached him again, holding what witnesses said was pepper spray, causing him to run down the street. As he's running, he can again be seen bending down to pick something up, which he tosses further down the street. It's unclear what the object was.

In the video, the agents are seen wearing vests that say "ICE Police" while dragging the detained man towards an unmarked SUV parked in the street.

It happened at around 8:30 a.m. near the Ivy Apartments on Vineland Place and Otsego Street. Damari Butler, who lives in the area, said he watched the entire ordeal.

"He draws his gun and puts it right in the guy's face," Butler said. "Which was insane. At that moment, I realized how real this was, because, respectfully, I didn't know what was about to happen to that guy."

In a statement provided to CBS LA Saturday on the incident, DHS said agents arrested Angel Luis Gonzalez Lobo from Venezuela during a targeted operation.

"He was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge after failing to show up for his court date. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings and will receive due process," DHS said in its statement.

DHS also addressed the incident with the bystander, claiming he was armed with pepper spray, creating "a moment of chaos."

"These actions by these individuals created an unnecessarily dangerous, and precarious environment for federal law enforcement as they endeavored to carry out their lawful duties and effect an arrest," DHS said.

Several L.A. city leaders also addressed the incident Friday night after the video began to gain traction on social media.

"It is alarming to see the images and reports coming out of North Hollywood this morning," said Mayor Karen Bass in a statement. "Every Angeleno deserves to feel safe in their own community. No one should have to live in fear because of where they come from, what language they speak, or how they look."

Congresswoman Luz Rivas, who represents the area, called the video "horrifying."

"ICE is violating the fundamental rights and safety of individuals across the San Fernando Valley to carry out Donald Trump's anti-immigrant agenda," Rivas said in a statement. "Families are being ripped apart and hardworking residents are being terrorized on their own streets by masked thugs. ICE needs to get out of L.A. and it must be abolished for good."

Mayoral candidate and Los Angeles City Councilwoman Nithya Raman also shared her "outrage" on social media.

"LA is not a playground for the Trump regime's inhumane operations, and Angelenos should not have to live in fear of going to work, taking their kids to school, or living their life," Raman's statement said.

text:
(ABC 6 News) – A state preliminary report says Minnesota’s Truth Council is documenting harm tied to two federal immigration operations and preparing final recommendations.

According to a preliminary report from the Governor’s Council on Recording the Truth of Operation Metro Surge and Operation PARRIS, the council says federal immigration activity violated constitutional rights and caused broad harm across Minnesota.

The report says harms included more than 70 Minnesota children detained between Dec. 1, 2025, and March 10, and $244 million in lost wages in Minneapolis and Saint Paul alone. It also says fear, school absences, reduced health care access, business losses and social isolation followed the operations.

“Minnesotans know what happened in their communities, but too many stories have yet to be heard, documented, and shared. For months, families lived in fear, children were separated from their parents, and our neighbors were subjected to racial profiling and unlawful detentions. At the same time, people showed up for one another with compassion, courage, and resilience. This council will make sure we document Minnesota’s history,” said Gov. Tim Walz.

What has the council done?

The report says Gov. Tim Walz signed Executive Order 26-05 on March 25 creating the Minnesota Truth Council to build a public record of the impact of the two operations. The 15-member council is chaired by Peter Cahill and includes Vice Chair Jennifer Prestholdt of The Advocates for Human Rights.

The report says 150 people applied to serve, and appointments were announced June 1. It also says the council does not have subpoena power and is not a law enforcement body.

“In particular, the Council will not engage in reporting around the shootings of Renee Good, Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, or Alex Pretti,” said the executive order.

The preliminary report says more than 3,000 federal agents were sent into Minnesota and that many residents remain afraid to speak because immigration enforcement is still ongoing. It also says some people are still sheltering in place or have left the state.

Story collection and meetings

The report says The Advocates for Human Rights developed the story collection process, including translated materials in Somali, Hmong and Spanish. As of October, the process involved more than 2,500 people and more than 185 community organizations.

More than 700 Minnesotans shared individual stories, 330 story collectors were trained through more than 26 trainings and at least 290 people joined 20 community dialogues, according to the report. Outreach events were also held in cities including Minneapolis, Falcon Heights, The Med City, Willmar and St. Cloud.

Across four public meetings, the council heard testimony from 74 people over 13.5 hours, according to the report. The state’s cross-agency data team also met with 17 agencies and produced eight data reports plus other supporting materials for the council.

What happens next?

The report says the council is preparing a final report and recommendations due by Dec. 1. It says that final report will be delivered to the governor, legislative leaders and Minnesota’s congressional delegation under the executive order.

“Our goal is that this work can be a source of truth and an example for future efforts to prevent harm and support the long-term recovery of people and communities across Minnesota,” said Chair Peter Cahill.

ABC 6 News has reached out the to U.S. Department of Homeland Security for a response and is still waiting to hear back.

text:
A new court filing has cast further doubt on the accuracy of a list of “likely non-citizen” voters that the administration of United States President Donald Trump sent to the state of California ahead of the midterm elections.

On Saturday, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA), an advocacy group, submitted an analysis to the court conducted by two data scientists from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).

It found that more than four in every 10 names on the list were not on California’s voter rolls.

It also found that thousands of potentially eligible US citizens were incorrectly identified as ineligible to vote.

The Trump administration’s list, delivered to California in early October, had suggested that as many as 20,930 “likely non-citizens” were registered on the state’s voter rolls.

That list has formed the basis of a lawsuit, filed on October 15, that calls on California to sequester any ballots sent to those “likely non-citizens”, preventing them from being tallied as part of voting results.

The lawsuit is unfolding in the final days before Tuesday’s pivotal midterm elections, which will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local offices.

Trump has expressed fear that, if his Republican Party loses its majorities in the two chambers of Congress, he could be impeached.

The Republican leader also has a track record of spreading false information about elections, including that his defeat in the 2020 presidential race was the result of a “rigged” vote.

He has often targeted California in his criticism. The state – the most populous in the country – is considered a longtime left-wing stronghold. It will elect 52 seats to the 435-member House of Representatives in Tuesday’s elections.

Already, Trump has accused California of “cheating” in its June 2 primary elections, after several Republican candidates underperformed, including Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt.

Under the US Constitution’s Elections Clause, election administration falls solely to the states, though Congress may pass regulations governing voting.

Critics, including California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom, have cited that fact in their rebuttal to Trump’s lawsuit.

All 50 states already prohibit non-citizen voting in federal elections and undertake measures to prevent voter fraud, which is considered exceedingly rare.

Other states that have received similar lists of “likely non-citizen” voters have also found significant errors in the Trump administration’s accounting. Nevada, for example, found that none of the names included on that list were non-citizen voters.

Such errors have raised concerns that eligible citizens would see their votes denied if the Trump administration wins its California lawsuit.

Still, the Trump administration has threatened state officials with prosecution over the potential for non-citizen voting.

It has also vigorously pursued its lawsuit through federal court. On Friday, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco rejected the complaint a second time, determining it unconstitutional.

“We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the court majority wrote in its ruling.

In Saturday’s court filing, the data scientists from UCLA’s Voting Rights Project found that 8,880 names on the list were not listed anywhere in California’s current voter files, a proportion of 42 percent.

Many other names on the list were either confirmed as US citizens or may correspond to US citizens.

“This review proves, at least as a preponderance of the evidence, that demands of election officials under criminal and civil threats, endangers the voting rights of plaintiff CHIRLA’s members and clients,” the filing said.

It was co-signed by the Democratic candidate to succeed Newsom as governor, Xavier Becerra.

text:
WASHINGTON -- More than 4 in 10 names flagged as possible noncitizen voters in California by the Trump administration cannot be found on the state's voter rolls, according to a legal filing Saturday by an immigrant-rights group.

It's the first outside analysis of a list that the Department of Justice has used to threaten prosecution of election officials. The analysis also found that thousands of U.S. citizens appear to be flagged as ineligible to vote on the government's list.

The contention was made in a filing by two data analysts at UCLA. They analyzed the 20,930 names that the department demanded that California election officials treat as possible illegal voters by separating their ballots during the vote count on Election Day.

Multiple judges have rejected the demand as unconstitutional and a threat to democracy, and local and state officials have said the list appears riddled with errors.

Court filing outlines problems with government list

The breadth of the problems with the list was outlined in Saturday's filing. It describes an analysis by two members of UCLA's Voting Rights Project, who filed a lawsuit challenging it with the Los Angeles-based Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA.

The research found that 8,880 of the names, representing 42% of the entire list, do not correspond to anyone in California's current voter file. It also found at least 22 are U.S. citizens, and many more may correspond to those of confirmed citizens.

"The expert analysis further makes clear that the mandated voter list endangers a significant number of eligible California voter," said the filing, which was cosigned by Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for California governor and an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.

The Trump administration had objected to sharing the list, calling it a "fishing expedition" and noting that it included sensitive information. On Saturday, the federal prosecutor who spearheaded the Trump case in California called the analysis "bogus."

"This is a bogus report by the activist illegal immigrant rights group CHIRLA," Bill Essayli, who runs the U.S. Attorney's office in Los Angeles, posted on X.

Also on Saturday, President Donald Trump bemoaned the legal rulings against his effort to force California to separate votes from the individuals his administration labels suspected noncitizens, even though one came from a judge he himself nominated.

In a social media post, Trump claimed his Justice Department found "20,000, but potentially Hundreds of Thousands, and maybe even Millions," of fraudulent votes, "and the Court has just ruled against it. Why would they reject fixing Election Fraud?"

The Trump administration has also urged Washington state to remove what it says were 400 possible noncitizens on its rolls, though state election officials there say that list is also unreliable and includes one voter who cast ballots in the 1990s.

The Justice Department has warned California election officials they could face criminal liability if they let noncitizens vote and issued subpoenas of election offices there.

Election officials say they have no time to investigate

Election officials have complained that the Trump administration has confronted them with lists of possible illegal voters at the last minute before Election Day, with no time to conduct the painstaking investigation required by law before removing someone from the rolls.

Multiple lawsuits have been filed to stop the administration from continuing to threaten local election officials.

On Friday, a federal judge in California ordered the Justice Department to stop sending demands to state officials, a decision the Trump administration appealed Saturday. Several counties in the state had run quick checks of the Trump list and found numerous errors.

Saturday's broader analysis was possible because a federal judge on Friday ordered the Trump administration to share the list with the plaintiffs in the case.

CHIRLA and the UCLA project sued the Homeland Security Department in early October to prevent it from using federal immigration data to challenge state voter rolls. The lawsuit cited examples in other states where the federal government's data has been proven to mistakenly include thousands of citizens.

Case argues that government's methods pose risk to voting

The case argued that the data-matching methods risk disenfranchising or deterring citizens from voting. On top of that, plaintiffs argued, the lists could disproportionately target naturalized citizens who are legally entitled to vote.

Applying the government's methodology, the UCLA researchers found that nearly 7,500 naturalized citizens in the state were "highly likely" to be incorrectly flagged as ineligible.

The researchers noted that the administration apparently removed the voter identification number from the names, making it harder for election officials to determine whether the flagged individuals were already on their rolls or were duplicates in the Justice Department list. They described the voter ID number as the most crucial data point.

The Justice Department argues that there is just as much to lose if the ballots aren't separated.

"Every ballot cast by an ineligible voter cancels out the vote of an American citizen," Kiersten V. Pels, a spokesperson for the department, wrote in an email. "The Department makes no apology for protecting those votes."

Local election officials at the United States's crucial midterm elections are preparing to confront armed federal agents if they are deployed to polling booths by the Trump administration.

In the US state of Colorado, Denver chief election official Paul López said voters were concerned by the threat of federal agents showing up at the polls, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.

"They're authoritarian tactics," López told Four Corners.

"It is absolutely illegal per US federal law for any federal agent, for any troop or anybody trying to intimidate voters at the polls.

"And it's my expectation, if somebody violates that and refuses that order, that they be arrested."

With US President Donald Trump's approval rating at a record low, and polls suggesting the Democrats will win the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate, some fear he may meddle in the midterms or even reject the results.

One leading US civil society group told Four Corners they were prepared to rush to court if Trump tried to interfere.

"We have seen this administration, the president and his enablers' willingness to incite violence.

"We're working with local election officials and law enforcement to prepare for [it]."

Trump administration has not ruled out deploying ICE agents

When asked in May about the prospect of federal agents being deployed for the midterms, Trump said he would do anything necessary to ensure "honest" elections.

The president's Homeland Security Secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said in September that ICE officers could be deployed across the country.

"ICE isn't there to patrol the polling places," he said.

"We're there to enforce specific threats."

At a fiery congressional hearing in September, FBI director Kash Patel refused to rule out the deployment of FBI agents at the polls.

In Denver, López is taking the threat seriously.

He is part of a coalition that has filed a lawsuit aimed at blocking federal officers from turning up at the polls.

"It's against federal law and it's punishable by prison time," López said.

Denver officials have also been conducting training with election workers to prepare them for polling day scenarios, including possible intimidation and meddling in the vote.

"We feel prepared … [for] anybody showing up at the polls that tries to intimidate somebody, federal agent or otherwise," López said.

Luke Ball is a Republican strategist who worked on Trump's successful 2024 re-election campaign.

He said he had no problem with federal law enforcement officers appearing at polling places.

"I think it's fine to have law enforcement at a polling place, especially if they're helping maintain law and order and helping deter illegal voting," Ball said.

"These men and women who are involved in law enforcement and ICE are great Americans. They love their country.

"These are not bogeymen who are here to oppress the vote."

Pro-democracy groups brace for misinformation and 'lies'

The Trump administration has also been attempting to collect states' unredacted voter rolls to try to identify what it calls "non-citizen voting".

Non-citizens have never been allowed to vote in US federal elections, and there is no evidence non-citizens have swayed an election outcome.

Officials in about 30 states have refused to hand over unredacted voter information, arguing it is illegal and a violation of privacy.

Protect Democracy has successfully filed and supported lawsuits against the Trump administration, including its attempts to obtain state voters roles, Vail said.

"They're trying to deceive the American voters about the integrity of our elections," he said.

"The courts have been clear that this is … a federal government intrusion into state powers and a violation of Americans' right to privacy.

"The courts have also struck down the president's unlawful executive order seeking to limit voting by mail."

Protect Democracy is part of a coalition of civil society groups that has been wargaming threats to the elections and how to respond.

That includes the possibility Trump will deny the election results and try to pressure election officials and Congress into refusing to certify legitimate winners.

Vail also said the group was worried about voter intimidation, false national emergencies aimed at disrupting or delaying voting, and efforts to seize ballots or voting machines.

Protect Democracy has analysed nearly 10,000 jurisdictions across the US to try to identify the most at-risk areas on election day.

Vail said the group was prepared to "go to court immediately" in a range of scenarios.

"Unfortunately, we need to be prepared for any scenario, including the prospect of violence," he said.

The US Supreme Court has rejected an urgent request to temporarily restore immigration judges’ authority for administrative closure of certain deportation cases, the Chicago Desavanja portal reported. As a result, the ban imposed after a court proceeding in Texas remains in effect.

The decision was made on October 27, 2026, without a detailed explanation or any publicly expressed dissent from any justice. It does not represent a final ruling on the dispute, as the appeals process is ongoing.

Administrative closure allowed for the temporary removal of a deportation case from the active court docket. This option was used by immigrants awaiting decisions on visas, humanitarian protection, or other requests for legal residence. According to official data cited in the article, from 1990 to 2026, the procedure was applied to approximately 360,000 people.

The Joe Biden administration formalized this practice in 2024, but the Department of Justice changed its legal position after Donald Trump returned to power. Texas then challenged the regulation, which was struck down nationwide by federal judge Reed O’Connor.

The cities of Baltimore, Columbus, and New Haven, together with the organization Centro Legal de la Raza, attempted to challenge this outcome. Their representatives warn that the decision could particularly affect victims of crimes, children, and other vulnerable immigrants.

The Department of Justice claims that the ban does not require the automatic reopening of previously closed cases, although some immigration courts have already begun to review them. Administrative closure does not mean a permanent halt to deportation, and the possibilities for legal protection depend on the circumstances of each individual case.

title: How Would a Democratic Takeover of Congress Change Washington? - الحرة
description:
The U.S. system is based on a division of powers among the president, Congress and the federal courts.
A Democratic takeover of the House of Representatives would be enough to complicate Trump’s legislative agenda, even if Republicans retain control of the Senate.
House Democrats could block bills the administration favors, including those involving taxes and government spending.
Democrats in control of Congress could also seek to impose restrictions on the use of funds or demand greater oversight of military operations.
After the new Congress takes office, however, his ability to secure the funding, legislation and appointments needed to carry out his policies could change.
text:
President Donald Trump could find himself facing a Congress more willing to challenge his policies after the Nov. 3 midterm elections if Democrats manage to win a majority in either chamber or both.

But losing Republican control of Congress would not mean Trump could no longer pursue his agenda, at home or abroad, although it would impose new constraints on some of his decisions for the final two years of his term.

The extent of the constraints Trump might face will depend on whether Democrats take control of the House of Representatives, the Senate or both.

These powers take on particular significance amid the war with Iran and debates over military spending and foreign aid — issues on which Congress can exert influence even as the president retains authority over military and diplomatic decisions.

The U.S. system is based on a division of powers among the president, Congress and the federal courts. Each branch has powers that allow it to oversee the others and constrain some of their decisions, a principle known as “checks and balances.”

What Happens if Republicans Lose the House?

A Democratic takeover of the House of Representatives would be enough to complicate Trump’s legislative agenda, even if Republicans retain control of the Senate.

House Democrats could block bills the administration favors, including those involving taxes and government spending.

They would also control congressional committees, giving them enhanced oversight powers to launch investigations into administration decisions, subpoena officials and request documents related to its policies.

Such investigations could cover the handling of the war with Iran, military spending, economic policies or White House decisions on immigration.

But Democratic control of the House alone would not give the party the power to block presidential nominations. The Senate is responsible for confirming Cabinet members, ambassadors, judges and other senior federal officials.

Nor would investigations into Trump’s policies necessarily enable Democrats to change them. They could increase political pressure on the administration but would need the cooperation of the Senate and the president to turn many of their objections into binding legislation.

What About the Senate?

A Republican loss of the Senate — which polls suggest is possible but less likely than a loss of the House — would pose a different challenge for Trump. If Democrats win the majority in the Senate, they would have direct influence over the president’s choices for senior positions in the administration and the federal judiciary.

The U.S. Constitution gives the Senate the authority to approve a wide range of presidential appointments, including Supreme Court justices, Cabinet members and ambassadors.

If Democrats take control of the chamber, they could reject Trump’s nominees or delay their confirmation, making it more difficult for him to fill vacancies with his preferred candidates.

They would also have a greater role in setting the Senate’s agenda and launching investigations into administration policies, as well as influencing legislation related to national security and foreign policy.

The Senate has the power to approve international treaties by a two-thirds majority of senators present, while the president can conclude other types of international agreements without requiring Senate approval.

But losing the Senate alone would not prevent Trump from issuing executive orders or exercising his authority over foreign policy and as commander in chief of the armed forces.

Federal courts can review some of these decisions, while Congress retains its legislative, spending and oversight powers.

What Could Democrats Do About Iran?

Democrats in control of Congress could also seek to impose restrictions on the use of funds or demand greater oversight of military operations.

But these powers do not mean Democrats could unilaterally halt any military operation ordered by the president. The constitutional and political boundaries between presidential and congressional authority over the use of military force have long been disputed. Imposing legislative restrictions could also require overcoming opposition from the White House.

Democrats could also initiate impeachment proceedings against Trump. But removing him from office would require a conviction by a two-thirds majority of senators present, a threshold that party control of both chambers would not guarantee.

Trump would also retain his veto power over bills passed by both chambers. Congress could override a presidential veto only with a two-thirds majority in each chamber.

Control of both chambers would not automatically allow Democrats to pass all the legislation they seek, either. Most bills in the Senate require the support of 60 senators to end debate and proceed to a vote, unless special procedures apply.

This could lead to legislative gridlock, particularly on taxes, spending and immigration, where the two parties would need to negotiate to reach agreements.

How Many Seats Do Democrats Need?

Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in the House, with 218 seats compared with 214 for Democrats, alongside one independent member and two vacancies.

In the Senate, Republicans hold 53 seats, compared with 45 for Democrats and two independents who caucus with them.

Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 and take control of the Senate, assuming the two independents continue to align with them. If the chamber ends up evenly divided, with 50 seats for each side, Republicans will retain effective control because Vice President JD Vance can cast the tie-breaking vote.

In the House, the new majority will be determined by the results of elections for all 435 seats, rather than simply by changes to the current distribution.

The balance of power in Congress will not shift as soon as Tuesday’s election results are announced. The newly elected Congress is scheduled to begin its term on Jan. 3, 2027.

Until then, Trump will remain constitutionally vested with the powers of the executive branch. After the new Congress takes office, however, his ability to secure the funding, legislation and appointments needed to carry out his policies could change.

The midterm results, therefore, will determine not only which party controls Congress, but also how much political latitude Trump will have during the second half of his term and the extent of the opposition he may face in Washington.

text:
A federal judge in Minnesota has ordered that the Donald Trump administration return a Nicaraguan national from the Central African Republic, where he has been since August despite having never visited or holding any connection to the country.

Kenis Adalberto Lopez Gonzalez came to the U.S. in 2022—immediately turning himself into immigration authorities—and was permitted to remain thanks to a 2024 ruling based on credible fears he could face torture if returned to his home country.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained him in January before he was sent to the African nation—one of dozens the U.S. now has a third-country deportation arrangement with.

Read More on News

But on Friday, the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota ordered the government to arrange his return to the U.S. “as soon as practicable.”

"ICE violated Mr. Lopez's constitutional rights, and hardly even denied it," Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Lopez, told Newsweek in an emailed statement Saturday. "Their main argument was that since he's now been deported, he's beyond the reach of the federal courts. We are pleased that the district judge did not credit that argument, and has now ordered the government to bring him back to Minnesota so that he can finally have his day in court."

Newsweek has contacted ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for comment.

Who Is Kenis Lopez?

As chronicled in court records, Lopez entered the U.S. in late 2022. While he was subject to a removal order, a judge ruled in August 2024 that he could not be deported due to concerns over his safety if he was returned to Nicaragua.

However, Lopez was detained in January 2026 amid the largescale enforcement operation in Minnesota—Operation Metro Surge—and was deported to the Central African Republic in August following several months in detention centers. According to the court’s findings, Lopez previously resided in Shakopee, Minnesota, ran a construction company and had no criminal record.

The court has learned that, during his time in the African nation, he has been “a target for violent criminals,” that he cannot leave the country “for lack of status,” and that he “fears bodily harm if he goes outside.”

The court noted that there exist “serious and known risks to foreigners in the Central African Republic,” and that the U.S. State Department has since January assigned it a Level 4 “do not travel” travel advisory.

While it did not weigh on the broad legality of third-country deportation by the U.S. government, the court finds at this preliminary stage that immigration officials likely violated his due-process rights when Lopez was taken into custody this year.

In Friday’s order, Judge Jeffrey M. Bryan told DHS and ICE to “arrange for and facilitate Lopez’s return to the United States from the Central African Republic by taking all reasonable steps within their control to do so.”

“Defendants shall return Lopez to the District of Minnesota and shall thereafter not remove him from the District while this matter is pending,” the order reads.

“ICE violated Mr. Lopez’s constitutional rights, and hardly even denied it,” Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Lopez, told the Minnesota Reformer.

Third-Country Deportations Under Trump 2.0

The administration has been open in defending third-country deportations, framing this as a necessary and fair enforcement tool in situations where an individual’s country of origin will not accept them, and if the policy is focused on serious criminals.

In a press release last week, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said agreements with several nations now allowed the U.S. to remove “those who are so barbaric that even their home countries won’t take them back.”

“For far too long, illegal aliens ordered removed by a judge have avoided deportation simply because DHS had no place to send them,” Mullin continued.

Federal immigration law does establish circumstances in which individuals may be deported to a country they do not hail from and where they have not previously lived, though the practices has still faced criticism on legal and human rights grounds.

Writing on X, Minnesota Representative Angie Craig said that Gonzalez had “fled political violence” in Nicaragua, and described him as a “business owner” who had a “work permit as well as a court order preventing his deportation.”

Craig called third-country deportations “dangerous and unacceptable,” and said there was “no reason a law-abiding Minnesotan should be deported to a country where they have never been.”

Thanks to agreements with several countries and the Supreme Court lifting bans on third-country deportations, the administration has been able to remove thousands during Trump’s second term. According to the website Third Country Deportation Watch, 20,000 individuals have ended up in Mexico.

As of as of Oct. 27, Third Country Deportation Watch says over 170 individuals have been transferred to the Central African Republic.

text:
HOUSTON – “No one is above the law.” That was the message from FIEL Houston during a news conference Friday, following the indictment of an ICE agent accused of running over Miguel Parra Hernandez with an SUV in northwest Harris County.

The immigrant-led civil rights and advocacy organization joined Parra Hernandez’s family, his legal team and relatives of a witness to address the latest developments in the case and call for greater accountability.

A Harris County grand jury indicted ICE agent Mario Alberto Morales on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, about 20 days after the October 10 incident.

FIEL Houston’s Cesar Espinosa called the indictment a historic moment for Harris County, saying it sends a clear message that federal agents are not above the law.

“Nobody is above the law,” Espinosa said.

He also pushed back against ICE’S claims that the case is politically motivated.

“To ICE, this is not political. This is our lives. And if you think that justice is political, then you have no idea what justice really means,” Espinosa said.

Attorney says video tells a different story

Attorney Kim Bruno, who represents Parra Hernandez and Luis Delfin, said the newly released body-camera footage shows a different account of the incident than what was initially presented by the federal agency.

“From the beginning, the video told a different story than what was offered by the agency,” Bruno said.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare previously said the footage shows Morales aggressively steering his vehicle toward Parra Hernandez, striking him and running over both of his legs.

The agent’s initial account to 911 described Parra Hernandez jumping out of a vehicle and hitting his car.

Bruno said Parra Hernandez’s account of what happened has remained consistent.

Parra Hernandez remains hospitalized and unable to walk

Much of Friday’s news conference focused on the physical and emotional toll the incident has taken on Parra Hernandez.

Bruno said he has suffered fractures, nerve damage and chronic pain and has undergone surgery.

He is also struggling with anxiety and depression following the incident.

Bruno said Parra Hernandez is currently unable to walk. Doctors plan to try getting him back on his feet in approximately three weeks, but whether he will regain the ability to walk remains uncertain.

His attorney also raised concerns about the conditions surrounding his recovery.

Bruno said officers maintain constant surveillance in his hospital room, making it difficult for him to receive confidential mental health care.

She said Parra Hernandez appears apprehensive about what he says and how he communicates, even while receiving treatment.

Bruno said Parra Hernandez’s primary concern is accountability and making sure the same thing does not happen to someone else.

She described him as someone who continues to worry about others despite being the person suffering in a hospital bed.

Family and attorneys demand immediate release

FIEL Houston and the legal team are also calling for the immediate release of Parra Hernandez, Luis Delfin and everyone else connected to the case.

Delfin was one of the people detained inside the ICE vehicle during the incident and is considered a witness.

Espinosa said releasing those involved would allow them to cooperate fully with the investigation.

Cassandra Serrano, the niece of Luis Delfin, also spoke during the news conference, saying federal agencies should be held accountable under the law.

“Just because this is a federal agency, they are not above the law,” Serrano said.

Parra Hernandez’s brother, Rodolfo Parra, thanked the community for its support and said the family wants Miguel released as soon as possible so he can have his family around him during recovery.

Espinosa described the indictment as a moment of hope for a community that has felt overlooked.

“A beaten and broken-down community has had a glimpse of hope,” he said.

Immigration proceedings continue

Bruno also provided an update on Parra Hernandez’s immigration case.

She said immigration authorities were moving forward with an expedited process despite his hospitalization and the pain medication he is taking.

Bruno questioned whether he could meaningfully participate in those proceedings given his medical condition.

A judge granted a continuance, postponing the hearing. A new hearing date had not been set as of Friday’s news conference.

The ICE agent’s attorneys have disputed the prosecution, and ICE has called the indictment a political stunt, questioning the state’s authority to investigate federal officers.

The criminal case remains ongoing, and an indictment is not a conviction.

For Parra Hernandez’s family and legal team, however, Friday’s message was clear: they want accountability, transparency and the opportunity for everyone involved to cooperate with the investigation.

text:
After much uproar, the City of Forest Grove released videos showing an Oct. 7 interaction involving a police officer and an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent at the police department.

The release comes as residents voice concerns about whether local police are working with federal immigration enforcement after an ICE officer was seen entering the city's police station. Both the City of Forest Grove and the Forest Grove Police Department deny assisting or cooperating with any federal immigration enforcement activities.

READ ALSO | Reports of increased ICE enforcement stir concern across Portland metro area

On Oct. 12, during a Forest Grove City Council meeting, Kiley Delgado, who is a resident of Hillsboro, called for the release of videos showing what happened.

"I was there in person. I was the one who filmed this interaction... These officers should be ashamed and they should be held accountable," Delgado said.

In one of the newly released police bodycam videos, a federal officer can be seen pulling up to the station and telling police from his car, "Well, this lady back here seems to be on to what we're doing," and explained, "She's been following me for the better part of 20 minutes. I'm going to come over here and park in an authorized spot for a cop, right, yeah, maybe she'll split, get the picture? Hopefully that works out for you guys?"

We now know that woman was Delgado.

The police officer allowed the federal officer to park in the authorized parking spots. The federal officer then asked police, "Would it be OK if I utilize the [restroom]?" and an officer gave permission.

Surveillance video from the front entrance shows the federal officer walking into the station and then leaving less than two minutes later, based on the video timestamps.

Forest Grove police declined an interview with KATU, saying the city’s public release of information would be their only comment. KATU then emailed asking why the officer was allowed to park in a spot reserved for authorized vehicles, but did not get a response.

Delgado told KATU she wants the city to be more open about how they handle sensitive cases.

"My first thought is how heavily redacted the audio portion of the video is. And the way I understand it, the audio would only need to be redacted if it were to cover sensitive information that was being shared, which I don't believe was the case here," she said.

READ ALSO | 'That is abuse': Salem witness describes ICE clash as council members condemn tactics

In a description for the released videos on YouTube, the city wrote that body-worn cameras have both active and passive recording modes and do not record audio when in passive mode.

PCUN, an immigrants' rights coalition group, issued a statement saying, "This footage puts into question our local law enforcement's commitment to public safety. We know that people are more likely to report crimes when they have trust in police. When immigrants and mixed-status families are afraid to call police, community trust breaks down. As a coalition, we have concerns about the impact this will have and will be following up.”

Forest Grove officials say they are conducting an investigation and reviewing their policies. The city also decided to stop allowing anyone from the public to use restrooms inside the police station.

Forest Grove Mayor Malynda Wenzl addressed the community’s concerns directly.

“My hope is that by releasing these videos, the community feels that we, the City, are acting transparently and responsibly. I am sorry that this incident has caused pain and increased fear and I want to assure everyone that the City is taking this incident seriously and taking decisive action to ensure it does not happen again. I believe that as a result of the review of this incident, the City of Forest Grove will be stronger and better prepared to serve the community going forward," Wenzl said.

In November 2025, the council adopted Resolution 2025-64, which states that Forest Grove is a sanctuary city and ensures that anyone can request help from public safety without being questioned about immigration status or fearing reprisal, consistent with the Oregon Sanctuary Promise Act.

City officials said that more information about Forest Grove’s sanctuary city status is available on the City’s website.

A violent arrest by masked federal immigration agents in North Hollywood has ignited widespread outrage and calls for an investigation after video shows officers dragging a screaming man along the ground and holding a bystander at gunpoint.

What we know:

The incident happened around 8:30 a.m. near the intersection of Vineland Place and Otsego Street, according to authorities.

Federal immigration enforcement agents wearing face coverings dragged a screaming man along the ground while taking him into custody. At the same time, a man walking his dog picked up a canister from the ground and suddenly an agent pushes into the bushes and points a gun in his face just inches away.

Witnesses further stated that the bystander picked up a dropped cell phone to ask if it belonged to the man being detained. At that point, an agent pepper-sprayed the bystander.

What we don't know:

Authorities have not disclosed whether the operation was an intentional, targeted enforcement action or a random arrest.

The identity of the man taken into custody is unknown, and no legal representatives or family members have come forward.

The Department of Homeland Security has not responded to FOX 11's requests for comment.

What they're saying:

"He dragged him like a dog, like with no respect for the man," said witness Joseph Cevallos. "He dragged him like a dog… like with no respect for the man."

He later added, "It gets me mad when I see sh** like that there’s no respect out here for these poor people that are just trying to do something better for themselves."

Another observer, Raven Potters, expressed shock at the aggression directed toward both individuals, noting, "the way they were treating him was disgusting and inhumane ..like there was no reason for him to do that and to shove that guy in the bushes that was horrible."

Witness Enrique Martinez reflected on the broader pattern in the neighborhood, stating, "We as a society keep seeing videos like this show up closer and closer to home and we're like letting it happen and letting it be…".

An additional community member questioned the lack of identification, noting that legitimate operations require agents to identify themselves and display warrants rather than concealing their faces.

City leaders were quick to condemn the operation.

Councilmember Nithya Raman stated via social media, "I am outraged by reports of violent ICE kidnappings in North Hollywood. LA is not a playground for the Trump regime's inhumane operations."

Mayor Karen Bass also responded directly to the confrontation, releasing a statement declaring, "ICE operations have not stopped and neither have we. My office is actively working with immigrant rights leaders to determine what further action we can take to protect Angelenos. Strengthen our city's protections and demand accountability."

What's next:

The investigation is ongoing.

Bass said she is speaking with the California Attorney General's Office to investigate and prosecute any potential wrongdoing committed by the federal agents involved in the altercation.

text:
The Catholic Archbishop of Detroit, Edward Weisenburger, attended a vigil in southwest Detroit meant to show solidarity with immigrants amidst a surge in ICE activity.

The Catholic Archbishop of Detroit attended a vigil Friday evening following an uptick in Immigrations and Customs Enforcement activity this week in southwest Detroit, a surge which some community members said was the worst in about a year and has left local kids and families fearful.

"Part of my spiritual practice is to get up in the morning and say, 'Where would Jesus be today?' ... Yesterday when I heard about this, I decided this is where Jesus would be today, standing with people who are suffering," said Edward Weisenburger.

The vigils, originally organized by a Catholic immigrant advocacy group called Strangers No Longer, began in 2019 and now take place every Friday at Clark Park for around an hour. People hold hand-made signs with slogans of support like "Refugees Welcome" and "Detroit Is Immigrant Powered."

The vigils are meant to be a visible show of support for those in the predominantly immigrant area of southwest Detroit, especially for children as they get out of school, who have been "traumatized" by ICE raids, detentions or deportations, said event organizer Bill O’Brien.

"To show that there are people who care," O'Brien said.

Today's vigil was the first time the archbishop attended in person. His message was one of solidarity with those who have been impacted by ICE amid President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign.

"I think it's less a political statement, and far far far more a moral, ethical and religious statement. The sign I'm holding in Spanish says we are all family, we are all of one God, one heavenly father which makes us brothers and sisters. We as Christians are not permitted not to recognize the face of Christ in others," Weisenburger said.

Weisenburger has been a vocal advocate for immigrants during his time as the leader of the city's archdiocese, beginning in February 2025. He's protested mass detention and marched to ICE offices, calling for an American immigration system that keeps families together, provides people with their due process rights and, above all, maintains human dignity.

At the vigil, the archbishop also spoke in support of a Christianity that holds power to account.

"I don't really believe in a polite religion that maintains the status quo for people in power. ... I'm not a rabble rouser either. But I think sometimes when people want to reduce religion to just sweetness and prayer ... as much as they just want to reduce it to that and carve out, excise out Jesus's message on justice, on dignity of humanity and truth? That's not Christianity anymore," he said.

Since its inception, the vigils held in Clark Park have continued to draw newcomers, including those of different faiths outside of Christianity, O’Brien said.

Lyn Jones, who lives in Lafayette Park, is one of those attendees. She doesn't label herself as any religion, though she grew up in a primarily Christian household that was open to other faiths, she said. Jones attends the vigil every Friday. She said she comes because she feels a sense of responsibility to her neighbors in southwest, to show them there are people who see them as human beings and that "it's not all about what comes down from Washington," she said.

Jones said she knows some people could see the vigil as just a bunch of people standing on a park corner with signs, but she feels like the show of solidarity is a meaningful statement.

"If anyone feels encouraged by seeing us here," she said, "that could be enough to get them through another day."

text:
New Delhi, Oct. 31 -- The November 3 US midterm elections could have implications for thousands of Indian professionals working in, or seeking to move to, the United States.

With President Donald Trump's administration tightening skilled-worker immigration rules, the outcome of the elections will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress or Democrats gain the power to scrutinise and potentially block parts of the president's legislative agenda.

Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the House of Representatives and four in the Senate to take control of each.

Even if Democrats win, they cannot automatically reverse immigration restrictions introduced through presidential orders or executive agencies.

The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign professionals for specialised roles and is widely used by technology companies and IT services firms employing Indian workers.

Several Republican-backed proposals in Congress seek to tighten the programme.

One is the Protecting American Workers Through H-1B Modernisation Act, introduced in both chambers. It seeks to raise the salary threshold for certain H-1B-dependent employers to qualify for an exemption from requirements to first recruit American workers.

Another proposal, the H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act, seeks to sharply increase penalties for serious programme violations and document fraud. It was introduced in the House in October and referred to the Judiciary Committee.

Neither proposal has become law.

If Republicans retain control, these proposals could have a clearer path through Congress, although passage is not guaranteed.

A Democratic-controlled chamber could slow or block them through committee action, hearings and legislative negotiations.

Employment-based green cards are another area to watch, particularly for Indian professionals who face long waits for permanent residency.

The Trump administration has already suspended new and pending PERM labour-certification applications involving major technology and outsourcing companies, including Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. The administration has cited alleged abuse of the immigration system, according to a Reuters report.

The PERM process is an important step in several employment-based green-card applications.

Separately, the proposed SMARTER Act seeks to replace the existing employment-based immigration framework with a skills-based points system. It also proposes restricting family-sponsored immigration largely to spouses and minor children and eliminating the Diversity Visa programme.

The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee after its introduction in September.

If enacted, such a system could change how applicants qualify for employment-based green cards. Its impact on Indian applicants would depend on the points criteria, the treatment of existing applications and any transition provisions.

A Democratic victory could increase congressional scrutiny of the administration's immigration policies, including its treatment of skilled foreign workers, visa enforcement and green-card applications.

text:
Houston-area elected officials said Friday that they hoped the indictment of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent accused of running over Miguel Parra Hernandez would send a message to ICE agents and the White House that on-the-ground enforcement tactics need to be reevaluated. But they were skeptical that things would change immediately.

Mario Alberto Morales was indicted on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, a second-degree felony, in connection to an auto-pedestrian crash that injured Parra Hernandez, 48, on Oct. 10.

ICE INDICTMENT: ICE agent indicted for crash that left Houston immigrant with broken leg following chase by SUV

Morales is accused of driving an unmarked Jeep Grand Cherokee that pursued Parra Hernandez and another man around 7:30 a.m. on Oct. 10 near the intersection of Texas 6 and Clay Road in West Houston.

Parra Hernandez was hit in a strip mall parking lot and one of his legs was broken as the vehicle drove over him, authorities said. The other man escaped on foot.
