title: Trump's quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue before the midterms | Fortune
description:
Amid the rising U.S. cost of living, a destabilizing war in Iran and a disrupted system of global commerce, the now-quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue just in time for midterm elections.
According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026.
During this period, Democrats commonly cited immigrants’ acute vulnerability and their willingness and ability to fill critical low-skilled and high-skilled labor gaps.
After the global pandemic halted most human mobility in 2020, the Biden administration sought to avoid the immigration issue altogether.
No mandate for inaction Should Democrats win majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives in 2026, the issue of immigration is highly unlikely to be resolved.
text:
Scott Shuchart, a Biden appointee who joined the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in 2022, told the newspaper that the White House was “wishing the problem would go away so that they could focus on the things they cared about.”

But two years after Donald Trump leveraged voter dissatisfaction with the Biden administration’s management of the U.S. southern border to win the 2024 election and enforce his immigration crackdown, the issue has suddenly become a secondary matter.

Amid the rising U.S. cost of living, a destabilizing war in Iran and a disrupted system of global commerce, the now-quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue just in time for midterm elections.

From liability to advantage

For the past three decades, the Democratic Party and its candidates have struggled to develop and pass new immigration policies and communicate related political messages.

Bipartisan attempts at comprehensive immigration reform died on Capitol Hill in 2006, 2007 and 2013. Since then, a majority of Americans has trusted Republicans more with governing the issue. That has given the GOP an advantage when the salience of immigration policy has risen due to border crises and related high-profile events, even if that edge has recently narrowed.

In a February 2024 poll, 28% of U.S. respondents told Gallup that immigration was the country’s most important problem – matching the largest share since tracking began in 1981. By May 2026, that figure was 8%, a staggering drop in such a short period.

In a different poll by The Economist/YouGov, the share of U.S. registered voters who identified immigration as the country’s most important issue fell from 14% in October 2024 to 5% in September 2026.

Erik Iverson, a Republican Senate campaign pollster, recently told Axios that declining border crossings have reduced the urgency of immigration, depriving Republicans of an issue that previously energized voters and offered conservatives an advantage.

“You become a victim of your own success,” he said.

But this success is dubious. President Trump’s approval ratings on immigration are underwater.

In the RealClear Polling average from September to October 2026, his net approval was at negative 10.8%. In a recent Fox News poll, most Americans believe the Trump administration has “gone too far” in enforcing immigration laws, including 60% of independents.

Despite Republicans’ insistence that the mass removal of undocumented immigrants and a halt to new migrants would raise wages and make housing more accessible, Americans are experiencing high inflation rates, slow gross domestic product growth and sour consumer sentiment.

Ominously for the White House, Trump’s negative 10.8% net approval score on immigration is actually among his best. On inflation, the economy and foreign policy, his net approval rating is at negative 42.8%, negative 31.7% and negative 27.8%, respectively.

These dynamics bode well for Democrats’ midterm election prospects.

Republicans are now less concerned about immigration – what has been their greatest source of political energy and the left’s greatest political liability – as both parties’ voters are focused on other matters.

Despite the White House’s aggressive and frequently violent pursuit of undocumented immigrants, its proposal to end birthright citizenship, and its near closure of U.S. borders, even Democrats are no more likely to identify immigration as the country’s top issue today than they were previously.

According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026. In October 2024, 3% said the same.

Remarkably, without Democrats’ endorsement of a single new immigration policy idea, independents now express greater trust in Democrats than Republicans on immigration, 41% to 27%, according to a September 2026 Marist survey.

Democrats’ trial and error

Democrats’ sudden edge arises after a decade of trialing different approaches to counter the nativism and popular discomfort that Trump has harnessed.

Before Trump’s 2016 election victory and immediately thereafter, Democratic leaders sought to ameliorate the image of foreigners in the U.S., by highlighting that immigrants start more businesses, file more patents and commit fewer crimes than native-born U.S. citizens on average.

During this period, Democrats commonly cited immigrants’ acute vulnerability and their willingness and ability to fill critical low-skilled and high-skilled labor gaps. But the praise and pity produced resentment among many Americans who did not want an admissions system that elevated foreigners to a higher pedestal.

Toward the end of the first Trump administration, Democrats began citing the immense macroeconomic and fiscal benefits driven by immigrants’ long-term settlement in the U.S.

Economists attribute to immigrants the bulk of U.S. population growth from 1990 to 2015. And economists have shown that continued immigration mitigates inflation and extends the solvency of Social Security and Medicare funds. Immigration also provides workers for industries like construction, agriculture, food production and healthcare.

However, the benefits of these relationships for average voters tend to be diffuse and realized in the medium-to-long run. That makes them hard to recognize.

After the global pandemic halted most human mobility in 2020, the Biden administration sought to avoid the immigration issue altogether. It’s a strategy that Democrats have now carried over while the dynamics of being out of power still permit doing so.

No mandate for inaction

Should Democrats win majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives in 2026, the issue of immigration is highly unlikely to be resolved. As a matter of constitutional oversight, Democrats plan to commence investigations into the Trump administration’s abusive immigration enforcement tactics, questionable case adjudication and alleged corruption.

It will be almost impossible to pass meaningful immigration legislation in such an environment.

The Biden-era approach was a pivotal electoral liability in 2024. And the Obama administration’s series of immigration executive actions instigated a tennis match of such orders between subsequent administrations ever since.

Democrats will soon feel some pressure to develop bipartisan approaches to immigration governance that ensure order at U.S. borders and a strategy for immigrant selection and integration that is designed with the national interest in mind.

Justin Gest, Professor of Policy and Government, George Mason University; Institute for Humane Studies

text:
A liberal-majority appeals court in California handed the Trump administration a victory by blocking a lower court's ruling that ordered the State Department to open its application pool for the 2027 Diversity Visa lottery, which admits roughly 55,000 immigrants from low-immigration countries each year.

In a 2-1 ruling, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals blocked a preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta requiring the lottery pool to be opened after Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a notice in November delaying the program's acceptance of new applications in order to "implement certain changes," but the application period never opened.

A month later, the State Department ordered an indefinite pause on issuing diversity visas after a Portuguese national who was issued a lottery visa in 2017 committed a mass shooting at Brown University, killing two people and injuring nine others. The shooter, Claudio Manuel Neves Valente, was also tied to the murder of a Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) professor two days after the Brown University shooting.

FBI REVEALS BROWN UNIVERSITY MASS SHOOTER BEGAN PLOTTING MASSACRE AS EARLY AS 2022, BLAMED VICTIMS

The Ninth Circuit has been a perennial thorn in the side of President Donald Trump, having ruled against key portions of Trump's 2017 executive order restricting travel from predominantly Muslim countries and blocked a policy barring immigrants from being eligible for asylum if they crossed the southern border between ports of entry.

However, the appeals court ruled that the lower court's preliminary injunction could not be enforced, finding that the immigration law firm Red Eagle, which represents individuals going through the visa lottery process, did not have standing to sue the federal government. The appeals court ruled that the program was intended to "encourage immigration, not generate revenue for law firms."

LIBERAL COURT STUNS WITH RULING THAT HANDS TRUMP MAJOR IMMIGRATION WIN

The court wrote, "If Red Eagle Law were allowed to allege standing based upon its hypothetical or conjectural collateral injury, we would be opening the floodgates, allowing all lawyers to ‘roam the country in search of governmental wrongdoing.’"

However, the court made clear that its ruling was based on procedural grounds and did not weigh whether the State Department failed to follow the law.

"We do not endorse the Department’s failure to open the lottery registration period," the court wrote.

Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor and partner at Holtzman Vogel, said the decision by the liberal court was a "very easy call" in a post on X.

"Here, the plaintiff was a law firm not bringing a claim on behalf of someone in the diversity visa lottery but on behalf of the firm itself," Kambli wrote. "The district court should have never gone beyond standing but CA9 corrected this one."

TRUMP ADMIN ANNOUNCES EXPANSION OF VISA RESTRICTION POLICY IN WESTERN HEMISPHERE

President Donald Trump has been vocal about his opposition to the Visa Lottery Program for years. During his January 2018 State of the Union address, he called for ending the program, arguing that visas should be issued based on merit.

Earlier that same month, Trump said during a bipartisan meeting with lawmakers at the White House that lottery visas allow the "worst of the worst" to come into the country.

"They call it ‘visa lottery,’ I just call it ‘lottery.’ But countries come in and they put names in a hopper," Trump said. "They’re not giving you their best names; common sense means they’re not giving you their best names."

text:
Very early on Wednesday morning, Dover, N.J., Councilwoman Sandra Wittner started getting messages about immigration agents. A dozen or more were gathering outside a Walgreens, according to the messages she was getting. Throughout the day, neighbors in north New Jersey saw a spike in Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity.

And New Jersey is not alone. In the weeks ahead of the midterms, various cities and states across the country are reporting a notable rise in ICE activity, according to reports gathered by NPR and its member stations.

"The tactics that the administration has been deploying in communities really appear to be designed to try to intimidate voters," says Wendy Weiser of the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law School. Despite that, early turnout is surging.

"There was definitely a lot of apprehension and fear," Wittner recalls. "We just really weren't sure if something huge was about to happen. People were not feeling very comfortable or safe."

Wittner is not sure who was detained or where, which is unsurprising: these days it's difficult to report on ICE crackdowns as they happen, because the Department of Homeland Security no longer publicly shares timely information on its operations.

NPR wrote to the agency to ask if there has been a recent surge. It responded: "ICE agents uphold our nation's immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day."

And yet NPR and its member stations have received tips from rural Illinois,Oregon,Detroit andCalifornia about surges in ICE enforcement, throughout October.

An official within New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office who was not authorized to speak publicly confirmed that they have noted a surge in ICE activity in the city.

"We're certainly witnessing an uptick in activity, and have been since the summer," says a member of a volunteer group of neighbors in New York. She asked that NPR not use her name, as she is worried about retaliation. Her group goes to the scene where an ICE operation is happening, documents it, reminds those being detained of their rights, and alerts neighbors.

"In the past few weeks we've seen numerous large operations, or what we call cluster raids, multiple agents going to one spot and then the next," she said.

On the other side of the country, Oregon Public Broadcasting reporter Troy Brynelson has reported on a similar trend. "What we were seeing in early October and what we've seen continue, at least anecdotally throughout this month, is that ICE activity has really picked up in Portland." Brynelson says it seems to be concentrated in commercial areas. "I'd say it's a noticeable uptick compared to what we've seen over the summer."

Juan Proaño of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), a civil rights organization says he's concerned because this is happening so close to the midterm elections. "It's not about ICE at the actual polling station, it's ICE at the perimeter of the polling station," he says.

"Mass enforcement actions could be away from the polls, but with social media and the news, it could be enough to dissuade somebody from actually going out to vote."

Weiser of the Brennan Center says there's no indication the raids are affecting turnout. On the contrary, she says there has been a surge in early voting in minority communities across the country. "The good news is: it isn't working. Americans are tuning this out and we are not seeing a significant impact on participation. And we are actually seeing huge surges in participation in communities of color, and in Latino communities, and in all the communities that have been targeted by ICE and DHS."

Even so, she says that intimidation at the polls is illegal, and should be reported.

text:
Elia smiles as she speaks, moving her scrunchie-laden wrists to describe two things that bring her joy: math and basketball. She pauses a moment to ask her foster mom how to say volleyball in English.

The 17-year-old from Central America is a recipient of Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, a humanitarian protection for immigrant children who survived neglect, abuse or abandonment from one or both parents. She’s had nearly two years of stability here in the U.S.. But now, that’s in jeopardy.

“My attorney called and said I have to be at the court hearing, so I went, but my attorney did the speaking to the judge,” Elia said in a video interview, tugging at the pink rose on her purple sweater. GBH News is using a pseudonym for Elia since she is a minor.

“I’m afraid I’m going to lose the opportunity to study. I’m just really confused,” she said.

In April, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services rescinded a Biden-era policy that deferred deportation proceedings for youth who are current and future Special Immigrant Juvenile petitioners for green cards.

Elia is one of many immigrant youth and children who have been ordered removed from the country as a result, despite having already gained humanitarian relief to be in the U.S. legally. Other youth and children who have the same immigration status, or are in the process of getting it, fear they will be ordered to a court hearing and told to leave the country.

An hour before getting the life-changing call from her attorney, Elia was talking about college majors with Stacey, her foster mother. Right after the call, Stacey, connected with Elia’s therapist to get her additional emotional support. GBH News is not using Stacey’s real name due to concerns of repercussions on Elia from the Trump administration.

Federal immigration authorities ordered Elia to appear in court earlier this month, where she joined many children at a room in an Ascentria Care Alliance location in Worcester for a virtual immigration court hearing. Immigration Judge Omar Karram ordered her deported, but that’s on hold while she appeals the decision.

Worcester-based Ascentria is the only foster care service provider for the state’s Unaccompanied Refugees Minors Program. Staff there are used to representing children in routine immigration hearings. Recently, staff there say more children are being forced to miss school to attend hearings.

“These are children who are victims of extreme abuse, abandonment, neglect, trafficking, all kinds of things. And their escape to the United States was quite frankly the only option, and it is not an option that comes easily for them, “ Angela Snyder, supervising attorney at the Immigration Legal Assistance program at Ascentria. “There has been a systematic attack on the rights for these youth through the immigration system.”

The Trump administration cut funding to support unaccompanied minors’ legal representation with the organization in 2025. Some of the immigration policy changes have also caused adult Special Immigrant Juvenile visa recipients to have their work permits cancelled.

So far, no one in the program has been deported, but they’re concerned that could change, and more children have been ordered to hearings.

From immigrant to foster care

To gain that status, there are many requirements, including an order from a state court that children can’t return and live safely in their county of origin in order to get the status.

When unaccompanied immigrant children arrive in the U.S., they’re held at facilities run by the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which works with local provides to establish state guardianship and bring them into the specific state’s foster care system.

Two agencies co-administer the program, the state Department of Children and Families and the federal Office of Refugees and Immigrants. The Executive Office of Health and Human Services, which houses both DCF and ORI, told GBH News that the Office of Refugees and Immigrants has opened its help desk services for children with SIJs.

“Since the 1990s, Massachusetts has hosted children in foster care on behalf of the federal government’s Unaccompanied Refugee Minor program,” said a spokesperson for DCF. “The federal government has long held the responsibility to provide legal services for unaccompanied immigrant children, including those in the federal URM program. But the Trump Administration has cut that funding and rolled back longstanding protections against deportation, leaving vulnerable young people across the country without legal representation.”

The office said that for decades, immigration enforcement action against SIJ holders was deferred and Judges regularly cancelled deportation hearings for those children and young adults with SIJS, who were on a lawful pathway to a green card.

“Simultaneously, Immigration Court Judges have been ordering these children deported, when in previous years their hearings would be delayed while they await their green card process,” said the spokesperson. “In Massachusetts, we are working to provide access to legal services for unaccompanied immigrant children and DCF-involved young adults through the Massachusetts Access to Counsel Initiative, the ORI Help Desk, and our contracted partners. This includes those in the care of the Department of Children and Families and other unaccompanied youth who hold Special Immigrant Juvenile Status.”

Elia spent a month at a federal facility in Texas for minors who arrived in the U.S. without parents. Then she was connected with her foster parents.

Stacey says of Elia, “she’s just pure joy and innocence.” She said Elia had an education gap, but has been able to make up at least four grade levels in less than two years. She’s now hoping to go to college after high school, and the family is supporting that dream with extra tutoring. Stacey proudly mentioned an award Elia recently got at school, and says the family was already planning her next birthday with a prom theme.

“We want to make sure she has that experience because we don’t know what’s going to happen. She has this deportation order. We don’t know if that means that it’s going to be appealed or there’ll be some legislation that stops it or that she’ll have to leave,” said Stacey.

Ascentia Care Alliance has 30 days to appeal her order of removal. Then the Board of Immigration Appeals, the highest court in immigration court system, must issue a timeline with deadlines for parties to file arguments.

Change affects older immigrants, too

People over 18 who have Special Immigration Juvenile status are nervous about what the changing policies can mean for them as adults, and their foster families are trying to be preemptive in supporting them.

One of those is Juan, a 20-year-old student from Central America who is studying to be an HVAC technician. GBH News isn’t using his real name because he’s afraid of being detained. He’s been in Central Massachusetts living with a foster parent since he was 15.

“I’ve done everything that has been asked of me, all of my responsibilities,” said Juan. He said he’s nervous about an upcoming court hearing in December, and doesn’t understand if it’s routine or not.

“I really don’t want to leave my studies, my dreams. My foster mom is my family,” he said. Juan is hoping to one day own his own business, and is working at a restaurant until he can finish the degree. “We’re here to work hard, build a future, and not hurt anyone, or take anything from anyone,” said Juan.

Grace, his foster mother, launched a change.org petition with over 1,200 views. GBH News is not using her last name due to her concerns of retribution of the Trump administration on Juan, and repercussions as a state employee. She wants to see the deferred action policy reinstated by the federal government, and accountability in the immigration courts.

The petition urges Gov. Maura Healey, the Department of Children and Families, and state legislators to take action to protect the youth from deportation. It is unclear what can be done on a state level, however. The Governor’s office referred to Health and Human Services’ comment to GBH News. A spokesperson said the administration had spoken with the petition creator and spoke to her again on Friday.

“I’m hoping that they’ll be able to either connect me with the right contacts in order to find procedural safeguards for these kids or get the word out there to people to know that this is happening right here in Massachusetts,” said Grace.

text:
A Harris County grand jury on Friday indicted an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in connection with an Oct. 10 crash in northwest Houston that left an immigrant wailing in pain from a broken leg after he was hit by the agent’s SUV, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office.

Mario Alberto Morales, 33, is believed to be the first federal agent to be charged in Texas over an incident related to the agency’s recent ramped up enforcement actions during the Trump administration. It represents a rare instance of a state prosecutor pursuing charges against immigration authorities.

During a news conference announcing the charge, Teare said Morales "aggressively" steered his vehicle into Miguel Parra Hernandez, seriously injuring him. Teare, a former vehicular crimes prosecutor, said "the case is as clear as any that I've ever prosecuted or investigated.

"As long as I am district attorney, this office will prosecute any law enforcement officer who violates the law," Teare said. "An ICE badge does not give you free reign to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone.”

David Lindenmuth, a McAllen-based attorney representing Morales, criticized the indictment as a rushed "political prosecution" and defended the agent's actions during the chase.

Lindenmuth called the crash an accident and contended Morales had swerved in Parra Hernandez’s direction to avoid an idling truck in front of him. He accused Teare's office of guiding the investigation to the indictment.

Teare “basically told the investigators where he wanted them to go -- and they went there," Lindenmuth said.

MORE ON THIS CASE:Who is Mario Alberto Morales? What to know about ICE agent accused of hitting Houston immigrant with car

Lindenmuth said Morales, whom he described as a military veteran and pastor, is in the Houston area and is expected to surrender himself once the case is assigned to a court. He was placed on administrative leave from ICE following the incident.

Lindenmuth expects proceedings that could remove Morales' state prosecution to federal court as the agent is a federal employee. Similar legal maneuvers have taken place in prosecutions involving other federal law enforcement officers.

Following the indictment, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz in Houston mirrored Lindenmuth's sentiment that Teare targeted the agent.

"The Harris County District Attorney now appears determined to put a different federal agent's scalp on the wall," Reitz said in a statement. "This time he's pursuing what looks like a political prosecution of an ICE agent for doing his job — exactly what his allies have been agitating for."

Reitz said he conducted his own review of the evidence and declined to pursue federal charges.

An unidentified ICE spokesman called the indictment a "political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians" and called the allegations that Morales intentionally hit Parra Hernandez "reckless and false."

Morales is accused of severely injuring the 48-year-old Parra Hernandez, a Mexican immigrant who worked as a construction worker in Houston, during a chase around 7:30 a.m. on Oct. 10 through a strip mall parking lot at the intersection of Texas 6 and Clay Road.

Morales is alleged to have driven his Jeep Grand Cherokee into Parra Hernandez, who has been recovering at a rehabilitation facility under the watch of ICE agents since the crash.

The crash was investigated by the Harris County Sheriff's Office, which responded to the scene after ICE called an ambulance for Parra Hernandez.

MORE ON THIS CASE: Search warrant details Harris County investigation into ICE agent for crash that injured Houston immigrant

Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez, who joined Teare at the news conference, said the indictment was an example of holding law enforcement officers responsible for upholding their "extraordinary authority."

“Our responsibility is not to be guided by politics or public pressure," Gonzalez said. "Our responsibility is to follow the facts, uphold the law, and do what is right.”

ICE agent was wearing body camera

The indictment coincided with an unusual step by Teare's office to make public evidence in the case before a trial or other court proceedings. The office shared portions of a 911 call that Morales made following the crash, as well as footage from his body-worn camera.

Teare credited the use of the body-worn camera for allowing the investigation to progress sooner for a grand jury to issue an indictment in less than a month.

The agent's body-worn camera footage, as well as security video from a nearby business, showed Morales' vehicle going after the occupants of a white pick-up truck that came to a stop on the wrong side of the road. The two men inside then got out of the driver's side door and bolted.

Moments later, Morales jumped the elevated median of Clay Road and turned into a parking lot they ran into.

RELATED: Texas leaders react to ICE agent's indictment in crash that injured immigrant

The surveillance footage from a nearby bakery appeared to show Morales turn into Parra Hernandez as he ran, though a view of the actual collision was obscured by another vehicle that authorities believe isn't connected to the incident.

A former law enforcement official, Bryan Corb, who now works in private investigations, estimated the agent was going anywhere from 20 to 25 mph at the time of the impact after reviewing the surveillance footage.

The body-worn camera showed a closer look at Morales' actions not seen from the surveillance footage, such as Morales notifying other ICE agents that the the two men inside the vehicle were running away on foot. Less than five seconds later, Morales can be seen veering to the left in the direction of Parra Hernandez just moments before striking him.

After the collision, Morales stepped out of the Jeep and in Spanish asked Parra Hernandez, who was on the ground and crying out in pain, “where’s the other one” before telling him to show him his hand.

Parra Hernandez then turned on his back and said, “You ran over me.” Parra Hernandez later screamed in pain “my foot.”

"He got hit with a car, bro," Morales told another ICE agent. "I was coming in and I hit him with the car."

The other man Morales sought managed to escape as other authorities rushed to the scene. He remains in the country and not in ICE custody, Teare said.

'He hit my car'

During Friday's press conference, Teare also played parts of Morales' 911 call that he made seeking an ambulance for Parra Hernandez's injuries.

“I tried to get around him and he hit my car,” Morales told the dispatcher. “He’s fine, he’s just complaining of the pain”

As Parra Hernandez’s screams can be heard in the background, Morales told the dispatcher that he wanted to move the injured man to his government vehicle. The dispatcher told Morales not to move him and to wait for paramedics to arrive.

Representatives with FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights group, reported that Parra Hernandez's leg was broken in three places and required surgery in the days after the crash.

MORE COVERAGE: Man struck by ICE vehicle lived in Houston more than 30 years

Throughout the chase, Morales had two detainees in the back of his Jeep that have since been deported. The video doesn't make clear that the men are there, and they're never heard in the footage shared by Teare's office.

Investigators went to Port Isabel to interview one of the men, José Presa Cañada, before they were removed from the country, Teare said.

The other detainee was identified by NBC News and Telemundo as Luis Delfin Martinez. They were arrested earlier that morning before Parra Hernandez was hit.

Teare previously said it would be against most law enforcement agency protocols for a police officer to participate in a vehicle chase with detained individuals aboard.

Rare indictment of federal agent

Morales’ indictment is a rare case of state prosecutors seeking charges against federal agents who injure, or even kill, people in the line of duty.

However, the charges aren’t without precedent.

Earlier this year, prosecutors in Minneapolis charged an ICE agent, Christian Castro, with assault and making a false statement after he allegedly fired a gun through a home’s front door and shot a man in the leg. He was also indicted on charges of lying to the FBI.

In February, after Cameron County prosecutors in South Texas presented evidence, a grand jury declined to indict federal agents over the March 2025 killing of Ruben Ray Martinez. He was fatally shot by agents with a Department of Homeland Security subagency near a traffic accident scene in South Padre Island.

Investigation into ICE shooting of Salgado continues

Morales’ indictment comes as Teare’s office continues to investigate ICE agents who were involved in the July shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo.

Salgado was shot at the end of a chase through Houston’s East End. In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, DHS claimed Salgado “weaponized” his vehicle against the agents pursuing him. That claim was disputed by three men who were in Salgado’s van when he was shot.

The men, including Salgado’s brother, were held in ICE custody for days before being ordered released from custody by federal judges. All three men were later spotted entering a grand jury area of Houston’s downtown courthouse in September, but weeks have passed with no news of an indictment.

The grand jury that is believed to have heard evidence about the Salgado shooting had been scheduled to end its term on Friday, but a district court judge granted their request to extend their term for 90 days.

Teare expects evidence gathering and evaluation of the Sagaldo shooting to end before Thanksgiving.

text:
The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement flights that have been happening almost daily in recent months at Akron-Canton Airport are soon coming to an end.

The private contractor handling Homeland Security deportation flights at the Akron-Canton Airport has announced its intentions to stop servicing those flights at the end of November, airport officials said Oct. 28.

For nearly six months, prison buses have been arriving almost daily at the Avflight hangars on West Airport Drive to transfer Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees to Eastern Air Express, Air Wisconsin and Global X jets usually headed to Alexandria, Louisiana. Alexandria is the site of a major immigration detention facility and serves as a primary hub for deportations out of the country.

The flights have drawn protesters, who hold signs like “Ice out,” “Immigrants are welcome here,” and “Stop ICE flights.”

“Akron-Canton Airport (CAK) has been made aware that Avflight has notified the ICE flight operator, AEG Fuels, of its decision to discontinue providing ground-handling services at CAK effective November 30, 2026. ICE flights will cease from CAK beyond that date,” airport Vice President Lisa Dalpiaz said in an email Oct. 28.

Avflight, based in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and the private contractor that manages ICE flights, AEG Fuels based in Miami, did not respond immediately to questions.

Avflight is a major operator at the airport with additional hangars on the east side servicing dozens of private planes daily.

Deportation flights began at Akron-Canton at the end of April when Youngstown Warren Regional Airport closed a portion of its longest runway and tarmac for repairs.

Flights were expected to return there when work was completed in August, but that did not happen until a Sept. 29 collision of two Eastern Air Express planes outside the Avflight facility at the Akron-Canton Airport.

The tip of one wing scraped a stabilizer wing on the rear of the other and both planes had to be sidelined for inspection and repairs.

For two weeks, deportation flights were moved to Youngstown Warren until both 737s were repaired and removed from Akron-Canton. On the day before President Donald Trump was to arrive at Youngstown Warren for a campaign rally Oct. 12, planes were transferred from Youngstown Warren to Akron-Canton, as were daily flights.

Since then, at least 20 Eastern Air Express Boeing 737s and Air Wisconsin CRJ200s have landed at the airport in the city of Green, according to the fight-tracking application FlightAware.

The Western Reserve Port Authority, which manages the Youngstown Warren airport, said it was not aware of the Akron-Canton developments and referred questions to the private operator at the airport that serviced ICE flights in the past. The private contractor, JetsFBO, did not respond immediately, nor has it responded to any previous requests of the last two months.

Meanwhile, Akron-Canton officials learned that the bills for landing fees sent to the three charter companies will not be paid. The airport had accumulated more than $46,000 in landing fees through September.

The Federal Aviation Administration in a memo released in early 2026 said that private contractors working for the government would not be required to pay landing fees.

Airport officials said that the loss is insignificant.

The Akron-Canton airport authority has been the only organization forthcoming with information since news coverage began in July, though officials have maintained an arms length from the deportation activity.

Officials said that as a public agency and partly funded by the federal government the airport cannot obstruct any legal business activity that fits with the airport’s purposes. However, they said that they had no intention of trying to convince deportation contractors to stay at the airport because it did not fit their long-term business model.

Doug Oplinger is a retired Akron Beacon Journal reporter and editor. He can be emailed at oplingerdoug@gmail.com

text:
When Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, thousands of people nationwide took action. Many took to the streets to protest. Others posted on social media, or called or wrote to their elected officials.

The First Amendment protects all these activities, and no one who engages in these nonviolent forms of protest should face fear, intimidation, or consequences for exercising their right to speak out.

That’s why two New Yorkers who expressed their anger over ICE’s killings were shocked when federal agents tracked them down and gave them official warnings that what they did was potentially illegal.

It’s also why we sued for all records relating to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) investigation into one of these New Yorker’s social media posts.

DHS’ actions make clear that going after these individuals was not about protecting federal agents. It was an effort to scare them into shutting their mouths. These scare tactics from the Trump administration are unlawful and undermine our most basic freedoms.

A Post, an Email – Then a Knock at the Door

On January 8, the day after ICE agents shot and killed Renee Good in Minneapolis, Syracuse-based activist Paigelynne Gonyea posted a photo of the officer who killed Good. She added the following caption: “The ICE agent who shot and killed Renee Good in broad daylight has been identified as Jonathan Ross by the Minnesota Star Tribune. I think today is a great day for Jonathan to be indicted!” She had every right to publish the post, which constitutes protected speech under the First Amendment.

More than five months later, Gonyea was working at a polling site when she received a voicemail from a DHS agent who said he was at her home. He had come to talk to her about a post she made that he said “doxxed” a federal agent. A group of agents then arrived at the polling site to speak with Gonyea. They produced a copy of her post and a document labeled “WARNING NOTICE” that explained it is illegal to make “restricted personal information” about a federal official “publicly available.” The agents asked Gonyea to sign the document. She refused.

DHS later claimed that in a different post, a copy of which only they have produced, Gonyea shared Jonathan Ross’ address. Gonyea denies having made such a post and the post could not be found on her account. And because no media outlet found the post, and agents did not show Gonyea the post when they confronted her, we have serious questions about whether DHS may have fabricated it.

That’s why we’ve filed our lawsuit. We want to understand the basis for DHS’ assertion that Gonyea’s social media activity constituted “a federal crime,” and we want to prevent them from chilling protected speech by coming after people just for speaking out against ICE’s violence.

What happened to Gonyea is not an isolated incident. On the same day agents confronted Gonyea at the polling site, they came looking for David Streever at his Rochester home. Five months earlier, Streever had written an email to acting ICE director Todd Lyons in which he warns Lyons will be “tormented” by having protected murderous agents and “will never know peace.”

Like Gonyea, Streever wasn’t home when agents arrived with a warning similar to the one Gonyea received. He was returning from vacation with his 7-year-old daughter. Another agent later tracked Streever down at the hotel where he and his daughter were staying and left a business card at the front desk.

Fighting to Protect the Freedom of Speech

The impact of these threats extends far beyond one email or one Instagram post. Left unchecked, these won’t be the last times DHS threatens people who speak out against ICE’s killings. Countless others will be scared into silence.

At a moment when ICE agents are flooding our streets and shooting people in broad daylight, we must fight back against any effort to muffle protest.

title: Search warrant identifies ICE agent who ran over man in Houston area - Click2Houston
description:
The documents identify the ICE agent involved, describe his account of the collision and outline what an investigator with the Harris County District Attorney’s Office observed while reviewing surveillance footage.
No criminal charges against the ICE agent have been announced.
According to the document, the ICE agent told a Harris County sheriff’s deputy he was looking for a man identified as Jose Mendoza.
Authorities also sought to examine the 2025 Jeep Grand Cherokee driven by the ICE agent.
No criminal charges have been announced against the ICE agent.
text:
Nearly three weeks after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent ran over a man in northwest Harris County, newly obtained court documents provide a detailed account of the moments leading up to the collision and reveal how investigators’ efforts to examine the federal agent’s SUV were delayed.

KPRC 2 News obtained a search warrant and the sworn affidavit connected to the Oct. 10 incident involving 48-year-old Miguel Parra-Hernandez near Highway 6 and Clay Road.

The documents identify the ICE agent involved, describe his account of the collision and outline what an investigator with the Harris County District Attorney’s Office observed while reviewing surveillance footage.

The investigator reported seeing the agent accelerate toward Parra-Hernandez, make a clear turn to the left and line up his Jeep directly toward the man before striking him.

The description differs from ICE’s previous public statement, which said Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle.

The records also reveal a separate issue in the investigation. Although authorities obtained a warrant to search the Jeep Grand Cherokee, an Oct. 23 court filing confirms local investigators had not been given access to the SUV.

No criminal charges against the ICE agent have been announced.

KPRC 2 is withholding his name because he has not been charged.

The sworn affidavit provides details about why federal agents were in the area and how the encounter developed before Parra-Hernandez was struck.

According to the document, the ICE agent told a Harris County sheriff’s deputy he was looking for a man identified as Jose Mendoza.

The agent said he had been following a Chevrolet Silverado pickup truck. During the encounter, the Silverado traveled the wrong way onto Clay Road before eventually stopping.

The people inside the pickup ran away.

According to the agent’s account, he drove his Jeep Grand Cherokee over a median, crossed the street and headed toward the fleeing men.

The agent acknowledged striking Parra-Hernandez with the front driver’s side of his SUV.

He also told the deputy the Jeep rolled over Parra-Hernandez.

The affidavit documents what the agent reported to law enforcement. Investigators separately reviewed surveillance footage to determine how the collision occurred.

One of the most significant portions of the affidavit describes an investigator’s review of surveillance video from the shopping center.

According to the sworn statement, the investigator observed the Jeep accelerating toward Parra-Hernandez as he ran through the parking lot.

The investigator described the SUV making a clear turn to the left and lining up directly toward Parra-Hernandez.

The affidavit also states Parra-Hernandez was running away, with his back to the Jeep, when the vehicle struck him.

Those observations are significant because ICE previously offered a different description of the collision.

The federal agency said Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle.

The affidavit, by contrast, describes the SUV changing direction toward a man who was running away.

The two accounts raise questions about the vehicle’s path, the driver’s actions and the circumstances immediately preceding the collision.

The investigator’s observations are part of a criminal investigation. They do not constitute a finding of guilt.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare previously told KPRC 2 News his office had obtained surveillance footage and was working to collect additional video from nearby businesses.

Teare, who previously led the district attorney’s vehicular crimes division, said his assessment of the available footage was that Parra-Hernandez had been intentionally struck.

“I’ve personally handled hundreds of auto-pedestrian crashes,” Teare said during an Oct. 14 interview with KPRC 2.

He said his assessment was shared by other investigators who reviewed the footage.

Teare also disputed ICE’s description of Parra-Hernandez running in front of the vehicle.

His statements represent the district attorney’s assessment during an ongoing investigation. A charging decision has not been announced.

The investigation extends beyond the surveillance footage.

Authorities also sought to examine the 2025 Jeep Grand Cherokee driven by the ICE agent.

The search warrant authorized investigators to look for evidence associated with the collision, including electronic crash data.

Such information is important because vehicle systems sometimes record information associated with a collision, including vehicle speed, braking and other operating conditions.

Investigators wanted to examine the SUV to determine what evidence was available and whether the vehicle’s electronic systems contained relevant information.

Teare previously explained why investigators sought to secure the Jeep before federal agents drove away.

“The Sheriff’s Department had a wrecker ready to take it,” Teare said during the Oct. 14 interview.

He explained that crash data and other forensic evidence risk being lost when a vehicle is driven again following a collision.

According to Teare, investigators informed the ICE agents of their intention to examine the vehicle.

The agents did not consent to the download of the vehicle’s data, he said.

Investigators then began preparing a search warrant.

But before the vehicle was secured, the agent drove away in the Jeep.

The sworn affidavit provides additional information about what happened after the Jeep left the shopping center.

According to the document, federal agents drove the vehicle back to an ICE office before local investigators had an opportunity to examine the SUV.

A Harris County Sheriff’s Office captain subsequently contacted the ICE field director about the vehicle.

The affidavit states the captain was told the Jeep would remain at the federal office behind a secured, locked gate.

The vehicle’s removal became a major point of disagreement between federal authorities and the Harris County District Attorney’s Office.

During his interview with KPRC 2, Teare said he had never encountered a comparable situation in his 20 years of law enforcement experience.

He also expressed concern that driving the Jeep after the collision might have affected electronic evidence investigators hoped to recover.

Asked whether the information might have been lost, Teare said he believed that was likely.

The court documents do not establish whether any specific electronic data was permanently erased.

Teare has publicly criticized ICE’s handling of the Jeep.

“ICE was never cooperating,” he said during an earlier KPRC 2 interview.

Teare said the agency answered some questions, but its cooperation ended when federal agents removed a critical piece of evidence over the objections of other law enforcement agencies.

He also said local authorities had identified the driver and other ICE agents involved in the incident.

At the time, Teare declined to release identifying information about the agent while prosecutors evaluated the evidence and considered whether charges were appropriate.

The district attorney’s concerns about access to the Jeep are now reflected in the court records obtained by KPRC 2.

The search warrant was forwarded to the Department of Homeland Security.

According to the court documents, DHS acknowledged receiving the warrant and indicated that the matter would be referred to its legal team.

But a return filed with the court on Oct. 23 indicates the search had not taken place.

The document states:

“Access to 2025 Jeep Grand Cherokee has not been provided — no search of vehicle.”

The filing establishes that investigators had not been given access to the SUV as of Oct. 23, despite obtaining judicial authorization for the search.

KPRC 2 News is seeking an updated response from federal authorities about whether access has since been provided, whether the Jeep has been examined and whether any electronic crash data has been preserved.

The collision left Parra-Hernandez with multiple fractures to his right leg and an ankle injury, according to information previously shared with KPRC 2.

His family reported that he required medical treatment and surgery following the incident.

During an Oct. 13 news conference, relatives and advocates also raised concerns about his continued detention by ICE while receiving treatment.

His brother, Rodolfo Parra, described the family’s distress over the injuries and the circumstances surrounding his brother’s detention.

The family and advocates also challenged the suggestion that Parra-Hernandez was connected to the person federal agents were seeking.

During the news conference, an advocate said Parra-Hernandez did not recognize the individual ICE had identified as the target of its operation.

The advocate said Parra-Hernandez had been picking up workers that morning.

Those statements reflect the family’s and advocates’ accounts. The search warrant establishes the name of the person the agent said he was pursuing, but does not establish that Parra-Hernandez was that person.

The search warrant identifies possible offenses under investigation, including aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, aggravated assault causing serious bodily injury and reckless driving.

The offenses listed in a search warrant identify potential violations investigators are examining. Their inclusion does not mean prosecutors have determined that a crime occurred.

No criminal charges have been announced against the ICE agent.

The district attorney’s office has previously said investigators were gathering surveillance footage, witness accounts and physical evidence before making a charging decision.

The unanswered questions now include whether investigators have obtained the Jeep, whether relevant vehicle data remains available and whether the evidence supports criminal charges.

KPRC 2 News continues to seek answers from ICE, the Department of Homeland Security and the Harris County District Attorney’s Office about the status of the investigation.

text:
Very early on Wednesday morning, Dover, N.J., Councilwoman Sandra Wittner started getting messages about immigration agents. A dozen or more were gathering outside a Walgreens, according to the messages she was getting. Throughout the day, neighbors in north New Jersey saw a spike in Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity.

And New Jersey is not alone. In the weeks ahead of the midterms, various cities and states across the country are reporting a notable rise in ICE activity, according to reports gathered by NPR and its member stations.

“The tactics that the administration has been deploying in communities really appear to be designed to try to intimidate voters,” says Wendy Weiser of the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law School. Despite that, early turnout is surging.

“There was definitely a lot of apprehension and fear,” Wittner recalls. “We just really weren’t sure if something huge was about to happen. People were not feeling very comfortable or safe.”

Wittner is not sure who was detained or where, which is unsurprising: these days it’s difficult to report on ICE crackdowns as they happen, because the Department of Homeland Security no longer publicly shares timely information on its operations.

NPR wrote to the agency to ask if there has been a recent surge. It responded: “ICE agents uphold our nation’s immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day.”

And yet NPR and its member stations have received tips from rural Illinois,Oregon,Detroit andCalifornia about surges in ICE enforcement, throughout October.

An official within New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office who was not authorized to speak publicly confirmed that they have noted a surge in ICE activity in the city.

“We’re certainly witnessing an uptick in activity, and have been since the summer,” says a member of a volunteer group of neighbors in New York. She asked that NPR not use her name, as she is worried about retaliation. Her group goes to the scene where an ICE operation is happening, documents it, reminds those being detained of their rights, and alerts neighbors.

“In the past few weeks we’ve seen numerous large operations, or what we call cluster raids, multiple agents going to one spot and then the next,” she said.

On the other side of the country, Oregon Public Broadcasting reporter Troy Brynelson has reported on a similar trend. “What we were seeing in early October and what we’ve seen continue, at least anecdotally throughout this month, is that ICE activity has really picked up in Portland.” Brynelson says it seems to be concentrated in commercial areas. “I’d say it’s a noticeable uptick compared to what we’ve seen over the summer.”

Juan Proaño of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), a civil rights organization says he’s concerned because this is happening so close to the midterm elections. “It’s not about ICE at the actual polling station, it’s ICE at the perimeter of the polling station,” he says.

“Mass enforcement actions could be away from the polls, but with social media and the news, it could be enough to dissuade somebody from actually going out to vote.”

Weiser of the Brennan Center says there’s no indication the raids are affecting turnout. On the contrary, she says there has been a surge in early voting in minority communities across the country. “The good news is: it isn’t working. Americans are tuning this out and we are not seeing a significant impact on participation. And we are actually seeing huge surges in participation in communities of color, and in Latino communities, and in all the communities that have been targeted by ICE and DHS.”

Even so, she says that intimidation at the polls is illegal, and should be reported.

text:
California doesn’t have a ban on ICE agents wearing masks or raiding homes in plain clothes.

The state legislature pushed a ban through earlier this year but a federal judge tossed it because it singled out the federal immigration agency and did not apply to all law enforcement agencies.

And while the progressive Bay Area state senator who launched the now-suspended mask ban says a similar, more robust ban is already in the works, little progress has been reported publicly.

That’s bad news for Fresno-area immigration advocates who say recent ICE raids in the Central Valley in the runup to Tuesday’s power-tipping midterm elections only serve as more evidence that the law is needed for the public’s safety.

“You’re picking up people off the streets in a way that is so violent that you don’t know if it’s another organized crime group,” said Dr. Lizbeth De La Cruz Santana. “We don’t know if it’s immigration because again, they’re not having their cars marked or anything. So of course, people are going to be scared.”

De La Cruz Santana, regional partnerships specialist at the Central Valley Immigrant Integration Collaborative (CVIIC), said the public needs protection and suggested that if the state law doesn’t work then perhaps a city-level law could establish protocols for federal agents operating locally.

“ICE agents not wearing identification, are masked or others who are impersonating ICE, affect the way that people interact with immigration or the perception that we have of ICE specifically,” De La Cruz Santana said.

Reports of people impersonating immigration agents only fuel those concerns, she said, noting that costumes and equipment sold online, including on Etsy and Amazon, make it easy for bad actors to pose as federal agents.

She also raised concerns about civilians forming patrol groups and using easily obtained gear or AI-generated fake identification to impersonate authorities.

Fake ICE agents and unknown masked men with guns

Earlier this month, daycare worker Victoria Ford witnessed a traffic stop in which a man in plain clothes first identified himself as being an agent with the fictional and nonsensical “Kerman County Parole.”

She said the unidentified man wore a cami-green bulletproof vest with the words “police work,” when Ford witnessed him stop a woman of color outside Ford’s workplace near Shields and West in early October. She said the man posing as law enforcement ordered the driver out of her car under threat of physical removal.

Ford also said the man quickly changed his story when questioned by witnesses at the scene. He was then joined by two other men who also vaguely claimed to be law enforcement. She said one of them wore a police badge that she said looked like a Halloween costume – and the other man wore a face mask.

“Were they ICE agents, traffickers? We still don’t know,” Ford said in a community assembly hosted by United San Joaquin (USJ) on Oct. 19. “What I do know is that these kinds of tactics are terrorizing our communities, and I can only imagine what might have happened to that young woman, but no one had been there to stand up for her.”

Ford and her colleagues called the Valley Watch Network and provided the license plate numbers of the vehicles, as well as the woman’s, in case something happened.

“If you have no identification on you, all you’re doing is just feeding the terror of, ‘I don’t know who you are. I can’t trust you,’” Ford said. “I think it’s a growing problem because of the fact that, like for myself, I was pretty confident that we had a law that said that they can’t have masks.”

But currently there is no valid law requiring ICE agents to identify themselves during routine raids.

Critics say the problem is far from new and people posing as federal officers aren’t the only problem created by maskless and unidentifiable immigration agents.

Protesters have posted their interactions with agents on social media to encourage the community to join them to speak out against ICE and to provide more information about the raids the federal government refuses to discuss.

Many say the masks give even legitimate ICE agents cover to act at least unprofessionally and aggressively.

On Oct. 13, video shows agents shining bright lights at the activists and agents surrounding one individual, and calling another activist, “a bitch.” In another clip, Fresno Resistance co-founder Alfred Aldrete accused agents of pepper-spraying both his brother, Noah, and himself on Oct. 14. On the same day, the agents pushed Noah into a car and knocked Alfred’s phone from his hand and threw him down. A police car is seen parked in clips as the incident occurred.

“These masks give these goons just enough confidence to become physical and abuse not only the kidnapped community members but also become physical with peaceful protesters and assault some,” said Aldrete, who, along with others like Rehop Fresno, have been working to document ICE encounters in and around Fresno.

Activists have begun shining lights in agents’ faces, with the caption, “expect us to shine a light upon your darkness. To light you up.”

A tough spot for local-level law enforcement

The masks and fear over unidentifiable agents creates problems for local-level police and sheriff’s deputies, too.

Sheriff John Zanoni, at the Oct. 19 USJ assembly, urged residents to be responsible when sharing information on social media, saying videos have incorrectly identified sheriff’s deputies on the department’s auto theft task force as ICE agents.

“I ask that people be responsible,” Zanoni said. “When you see this uniform, you see the sheriff’s office. Know that we are not immigration enforcement officers.”

Zanoni said that it’s important for people to know who they’re interacting with for their own safety and to avoid potential legal liability, especially when distinguishing federal agents from people falsely posing as law enforcement.

“We need to be readily identifiable and have our badge and other identifications visible,” Zanoni said.

He also acknowledged concerns about federal agents wearing face masks or not identifying themselves, and shared “that’s not how we do business or major operations.”

Zanoni added that ICE could do a better job communicating with the sheriff’s office about its enforcement activities.

Mayor Jerry Dyer, the city’s longtime former police chief, has not been shy about his criticism over tactics used by federal immigration agencies in recent years.

“If they want to focus on immigration, it should be on the worst of the worst,” Dyer said at the Oct. 19 assembly hosted by United San Joaquin. “And in terms of working together, that we continue to have a unified voice, that we not blame one another.”

Dyer also called for local governments to maintain a unified response and have realistic expectations about what they can do to challenge federal immigration enforcement.

“We’re not going to go out and arrest ICE,” Dyer said. “We can’t do anything that’s going to be positive not to wear masks. But we need to be very vocal and say that we don’t want ICE doing what they’ve been doing within our community.”

‘Avoiding accountability for their harm they cause’

California’s federal mask ban would have eliminated claims of law enforcement immunity in lawsuits if the agents covered their face while on duty.

In February a federal judge ruled that the state could not enforce SB 627 because the law treats federal officers differently from state and local police. The ruling means federal officers can continue wearing masks while the legal fight continues.

“There has been multiple accounts of people impersonating ICE across the nation and we must be able to prevent that,” Aldrete said. “We must be able to hold these terrorists accountable if and when they break the law.”

Aldrete said that upholding the mask ban could help prevent unwarranted ICE arrests, reduce the risk of physical harm to people, and improve safety for immigrant communities, including parents and children.

Ford also stressed the importance of identification in helping families locate loved ones detained by immigration agents.

“If I have no identification to go off of, I can’t find my family member,” Ford said. “I would need to know who you are and what department you’re working for, so that I can go find whoever you are detaining.”

Trump’s administration previously sued to block the mask ban, prompted by concerns over forcing agents to reveal their identities would put the agents at risk.

Throughout California last year, a huge number of the federal agents detaining people wore masks over their faces. California lawmakers in at least 30 other states have introduced, considered, voted on, or even passed similar legislation.

New Jersey, Oregon, and Washington, all passed mask bans earlier this year. Los Angeles County and Saint Paul, Minnesota have passed local bans.

On Oct. 14, a federal appeals court ruled against a California law requiring ICE officers to show visible identification, a final ruling after the law was previously put on hold after the Ninth Circuit separately blocked enforcement in April.

State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, who authored the legislation, called the ruling “a huge win.” He said the judge’s decision supports the law’s constitutionality and could pave the way for its application to law enforcement officers at all levels of government. Wiener now plans to introduce a new bill that would extend the ban to state officers as well but no new deadlines have been announced.

Aldrete hopes city officials will push for greater accountability for ICE agents, citing concerns about out-of-town agents bringing detained community members to the facility and blending in with local agents.

He said communities do not feel safe “while ICE operates under the cover of masks avoiding accountability for their harm they cause.”

text:
Immigration detainees held at Indiana’s Miami Correctional Facility are suing state and federal agencies for what they say are inhumane and unconstitutional conditions.

The 72-page court filing details medical neglect, cells flooded with human waste, and abusive punishments detainees claim to have experienced at the maximum security prison used by the Trump administration for its immigration enforcement policies.

The lawsuit also alleges conditions at the facility violate the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment due process clauses because the detainees are civil detainees, not under criminal convictions, and are facing punitive punishments like lockdowns and solitary confinement.

The ACLU of Indiana and Illinois filed a class action lawsuit Thursday, Oct. 29, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana. The lawsuit covers the three named plaintiffs and all other detainees at the correctional facility north of Kokomo.

“Frankly, they are experiencing physical decline, potential long-term medical consequences, and, like, severe emotional distress and suffering,” said Katie Hickey, an attorney with the ACLU of Illinois representing the plaintiffs.

Officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE and Indiana Department of Correction are listed as plaintiffs. Representatives for the agencies did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit comes after continued reports from detainees, lawyers and advocates about the conditions at the prison. This summer Gov. Mike Braun called for an audit to review the private healthcare provider the state contracts to work in the facilities after reports from the IndyStar on delays in medical care for detainees.

Indiana began housing Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees at Miami Correctional in October 2025 through a two-year contract with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Miami Correctional is a maximum security facility for men.

Since detainees began to arrive, there have been two reported deaths.

In the lawsuit, plaintiff Cynthia Acevedo said healthcare providers at the facility switched her to a different seizure medication that is ineffective at preventing seizures. Even then, Acevedo, a transgender woman, does not regularly receive the medication and has multiple seizures a week. When she goes to get medical treatment, no Spanish translator is made available.

Sergei Vasenin and Kemoye Muslar, the other plaintiffs, share their experiences of slow and limited medical care and regular solitary confinement and lockdowns.

During a 10-day lockdown, Muslar said his cell flooded over with sewage for three days. He was not provided cleaning supplies or hygiene products.

The detainees also allege guards call them racial slurs, threaten death and physically beat them without any reason.

The lawsuit details a case of a recent suicide attempt by a detainee. It alleges, staff were notified of concerns for the man’s mental health. It goes on to say that guards locked him alone in his cell where he went on to use a cable and hang himself according to witnesses. The lawsuit says the condition and whereabouts of the detainee remain unconfirmed.

The plaintiffs are asking for the court to declare the facility’s medical and mental health care and conditions inadequate and in violation of the the Fifth Amendment and Fourteenth Amendment due process clause.

‘Further litigation forthcoming’

Hickey said she hopes this lawsuit forces changes but also gets answers to what has occurred at Miami Correctional Facility.

“The people who have died, the recent suicide attempt. There’s been no transparency from the government about all of that, so we hope that we can learn a lot more about all of these things in Miami over the next; over the coming months,” Hickey said.

For more than a year religious leaders have gathered monthly at or near the prison to pray for the detainees being held there and their families. André Carson visited Miami Correctional in April demanding answers to the deaths in the facility. After speaking with people held at the prison he said the state needed to end its holding of ICE detainees there.

Other groups including the Indiana Organizing Project have held events across the state calling on the governor to end the contract with ICE or at least not renew it.

Indiana Organizing Project Executive Director Stuart Mora said nothing in the lawsuit surprised him and it comes as conditions fail to improve.

“I think that there will be further litigation forthcoming,” said Mora. “Our team has not seen significant changes in Miami Correctional, since the governor called for an investigation several months ago.”

The ACLU was joined by the National Immigrant Justice Center, Macarthur Justice Center and law firm Dunn Issaacson Rhee in filing the lawsuit on behalf of the detainees.
